story_idea.candidate: Benjamin Franklin's will (codicil of 1789; he died 17 April 1790) left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia, to be lent at 5% to young married tradesmen for 100 years and then 200; he projected Boston's fund at about £131,000 after a century and about £4 million after two. When the funds were wound up around 1990, Boston's held roughly $4.5-5 million.
story_idea.why: How can £1,000 plausibly become millions with no new money added, and why did the real funds fall far short of Franklin's arithmetic?

days.headline_hint: Franklin left Boston £1,000 and a 200-year plan to turn it into £4 million. Here is his arithmetic

story.title: Benjamin Franklin's 200-year bet
story.hook: In a codicil to his will dated 23 June 1789, Benjamin Franklin left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia, to be lent at 5% a year to young married tradesmen under 25 who had served an apprenticeship in the town. He died in Philadelphia on 17 April 1790. Franklin worked out that if the loans were repaid, Boston's £1,000 would be £131,000 after 100 years: £100,000 of it was then to go on public works, and the other £31,000 was to be lent out for a second century, by the end of which it would be £4,061,000. Nobody was to add a penny.
story.puzzle: How can £1,000 become £131,000 with nothing added, when 5% of £1,000 is only £50 a year — £5,000 of interest over a century? And why, when the second century ran out around 1990, did Boston's fund hold only about $4.5–5 million and Philadelphia's about $2 million?
story.payoff: Interest earns interest. FV = 1,000 × 1.05^100 = 1,000 × 131.5013 = £131,501.26: Franklin's £131,000 is 5% a year compounded for a century, rounded down, and his £4,061,000 is £31,000 × 131, the same 100-year growth factor applied again (the unrounded factor gives £4,076,539). Simple interest would have given only 1,000 + 1,000 × 0.05 × 100 = £6,000. The real funds fell short because they never earned a steady 5%: borrowers were hard to find, some never repaid, and the managers eventually put much of the money into ordinary investments. Over 100 years a lost point is enormous: 1.04^100 = 50.50 and 1.03^100 = 19.22, against 131.50 at 5%.
sources: Franklin's codicil of 23 June 1789 (terms, 5% loans to married artificers under 25, £131,000 and 'four millions and sixty one thousand pounds'), as quoted in: When & Where in Boston, 'Franklin Fund is established', whenandwhereinboston.org/entry/franklin-fund-is-established
Unsung History podcast, 'The Unusual Codicil in Benjamin Franklin's Will', unsunghistorypodcast.com/ben-franklins-will/ (£100,000 public works / £31,000 relent)
Michael Meyer, Benjamin Franklin's Last Bet (Mariner Books, 2022); review by Terry W. Hartle, Christian Science Monitor, 2 June 2022 (defaults, poor management, shortfall vs projection)

days.module: LM4 The Time Value of Money in Finance
days.title: Discounting: present value and implied rate
days.concept: Present value PV = FV_N / (1 + r)^N is compounding run backwards, and the same equation solves for the rate r = (FV/PV)^(1/N) − 1 or the number of periods N = ln(FV/PV)/ln(1 + r).
los: Present value of a single sum: PV = FV_N / (1 + r)^N
Discount factor DF = 1/(1 + r)^N
Implied rate of return: r = (FV/PV)^(1/N) − 1
Number of periods: N = ln(FV/PV)/ln(1 + r)
Rule of 72 as a sanity check for doubling time
Higher rate or longer horizon → lower PV

story_idea.candidate: Pieter Schaghen's letter of 5 November 1626 to the Dutch States General reports that Peter Minuit's colonists bought the island of Manhattan from its native inhabitants 'for the value of 60 guilders' (the source of the famous '$24').
story_idea.why: Was 60 guilders a bargain or a fair price? The answer depends entirely on the rate of return the money could have earned since 1626 — what rate makes the two sides equal?

days.headline_hint: Sixty guilders for Manhattan: the one interest rate that decides whether it was a steal

story.title: Sixty guilders for Manhattan
story.hook: On 5 November 1626 Pieter Schaghen, a Dutch official in Amsterdam, wrote to the States General in The Hague that the colonists of New Netherland 'have purchased the Island Manhattes from the Indians for the value of 60 guilders'. The letter does not say what changed hands, and it is the only known contemporary record of the deal. In the 1840s American historians converted the sum at the exchange rate of their day, about 40 cents to the guilder, and '$24' entered the schoolbooks. In 2018 the economists Jason Barr, Fred Smith and Sayali Kulkarni estimated that the land of Manhattan alone, without its buildings, was worth about $1.4 trillion in 2014.
story.puzzle: Was $24 a steal, or would the sellers have done just as well investing it? There is one annual rate at which $24 in 1626 and $1.4 trillion in 2014 are worth exactly the same. What is it?
story.payoff: Run compounding backwards. From FV = PV(1 + r)^N, r = (FV/PV)^(1/N) − 1 = (1.4 trillion/24)^(1/388) − 1 = 6.60%. Above that rate, $24 invested in 1626 would have outgrown the island; below it, the buyers got a bargain. Discounting the $1.4 trillion back 388 years shows how completely the answer hangs on the rate: at 6% it was worth $212.55 in 1626, at 7% $5.56, at 8% about 15 cents. The sum itself is rough (a 19th-century exchange rate set against 2014 dollars), but the lesson is exact: over long horizons the rate decides everything.
sources: Pieter Schaghen, letter to the States General, 5 November 1626 (Nationaal Archief, The Hague); translation: New York State Library, nysl.nysed.gov/newnetherland/schaghentrans
New Netherland Institute, 'Peter Schagen letter', newnetherlandinstitute.org (only record of the purchase; goods worth 60 guilders)
New Amsterdam History Center, 'The Schaghen Letter', newamsterdamhistorycenter.org/education/schaghen.html (1840s conversion at 40 cents a guilder = $24)

Jason Barr, Fred Smith and Sayali Kulkarni, 'What's Manhattan worth? A land values index from 1950 to 2014', Regional Science and Urban Economics 70 (2018), 1–19; reported as about $1.4 trillion for 2014 by The Real Deal, 6 January 2016

Recompute everything that used $1.4 trillion: the implied rate is about 6.6573% over 388 years (1626-2014); in the walkthrough use FV = 1,740,000,000 in $ thousands with PV = -0.024.

days.module: LM1 Returns of Financial Assets and Instruments
days.title: Required returns: real, nominal, after-tax
days.concept: A nominal required return is the real risk-free rate plus premiums for expected inflation, default, liquidity and maturity, and real and nominal rates are linked exactly by (1 + nominal) = (1 + real)(1 + inflation).
los: Required rate = real risk-free rate + inflation premium + default risk premium + liquidity premium + maturity premium
Nominal risk-free rate ≈ real risk-free rate + expected inflation
Exact Fisher relation: (1 + r_nominal) = (1 + r_real)(1 + π)
Real return = (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation) − 1
After-tax return = pre-tax return × (1 − tax rate)
An interest rate read three ways: required return, discount rate, opportunity cost
Return types (LM2): gross return (before management and administrative fees) vs net return (after them); pre-tax vs after-tax; nominal vs real

story_idea.candidate: On 16 December 2021 the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye cut its policy rate to 14% while official annual consumer inflation for December 2021 came in at about 36%; the lira lost roughly 44% against the dollar that year.
story_idea.why: A saver earning 14% while prices rise 36% is 'earning' interest — so is he getting richer or poorer, and by exactly how much?

days.headline_hint: Türkiye paid 14% while prices rose 36%. How much poorer did savers get, exactly?

story.title: Türkiye's 14% that lost money
story.hook: On 16 December 2021 the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye cut its policy rate, the one-week repo rate, from 15% to 14%, its fourth cut since September and 500 basis points in all. On 3 January 2022 the statistics office, TurkStat, reported that consumer prices had risen 36.08% in the year to December, the fastest pace since 2002. Over 2021 the lira lost about 44% of its value against the dollar, its worst year in two decades.
story.puzzle: Picture a saver earning the policy rate, 14%, while prices rise 36.08%. Is he richer or poorer at the end of the year — and is 14% − 36.08% = −22.08% the right answer?
story.payoff: Rates multiply; they do not subtract. (1 + real) = (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation) = 1.14/1.3608 = 0.8377, so the real return is −16.23%: the saver's money buys about 16% less. The shortcut's −22.08% overstates the loss by 5.85 percentage points, because at 36% inflation the cross term (real × inflation) is large. To earn even a 2% real return, a lender would have needed (1.02)(1.3608) − 1 = 38.80% — the nominal rate must carry the real rate plus compensation for inflation, and riskier loans add default, liquidity and maturity premiums on top.
sources: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye rate decision, 16 December 2021 (one-week repo rate 15% → 14%), reported by Hürriyet Daily News and Daily Sabah, 16 December 2021, and Business Standard, 17 December 2021 (fourth cut; 500 bp since September)
TurkStat consumer price index, December 2021 (36.08% year on year, highest since 2002), released 3 January 2022; reported by Bianet, Daily Sabah, SeeNews and Euronews, 3 January 2022
Reuters, 'Turkey's lira logs worst year in two decades under Erdogan', 31 December 2021 (via Gulf News, Investing.com, Free Malaysia Today): lira down about 44% against the dollar in 2021

days.module: LM4 The Time Value of Money in Finance
days.title: Stated, effective and continuous rates
days.concept: Compounding m times a year turns a stated annual rate r_s into a larger effective annual rate EAR = (1 + r_s/m)^m − 1, which rises toward e^(r_s) − 1 as compounding becomes continuous.
los: EAR = (1 + r_s/m)^m − 1
FV with m compounding periods per year: FV_N = PV(1 + r_s/m)^(mN)
Continuous compounding: FV_N = PV e^(r_s N); EAR = e^(r_s) − 1
Back from EAR: r_s = m[(1 + EAR)^(1/m) − 1]; continuously compounded rate r_cc = ln(1 + EAR)
Compare rates only on an effective (or common-frequency) basis

story_idea.candidate: In 1683 the Swiss mathematician Jacob Bernoulli asked what happens to a loan at 100% a year if interest is credited more and more often — yearly, half-yearly, monthly, every instant. He showed the result stays bounded, between 2 and 3 times the principal: the first appearance of the number now called e (about 2.71828).
story_idea.why: If more frequent compounding always earns more, why doesn't compounding every instant earn an infinite amount?

days.headline_hint: Bernoulli's 1683 riddle: credit interest every instant and you still can't triple your money

story.title: Jacob Bernoulli and the interest that never runs away
story.hook: In 1683 Jacob Bernoulli, a mathematician in Basel, Switzerland, asked a lender's question. Lend 1 at 100% a year and credit the interest once, and the debt doubles to 2. Credit half the interest at six months and let it earn interest too, and the debt is 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25. Credit it monthly, daily, every instant, and the debt keeps growing — but Bernoulli showed it stays between 2 and 3. Leonhard Euler later identified the limit as the number now called e, and in 1748 worked it out to 18 decimal places: 2.71828…
story.puzzle: If crediting interest more often always earns more, why doesn't crediting it every instant earn an infinite amount?
story.payoff: Because each finer slice adds less than the one before. With m credits a year the debt is (1 + 1/m)^m: m = 1 gives 2, m = 2 gives 2.25, m = 4 gives 2.4414, m = 12 gives 2.6130, m = 365 gives 2.7146, and crediting continuously gives e = 2.7183. In CFA terms, 100% stated is an effective annual rate of 161.30% compounded monthly, 171.46% daily and e^1 − 1 = 171.83% continuously: the EAR climbs toward e^(r_s) − 1 and stops there.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'e (mathematics)', britannica.com/topic/e-mathematics (Bernoulli's compound-interest problem; limit between 2 and 3; Euler)
Plus Magazine (University of Cambridge), on e, plus.maths.org (Bernoulli, 1683, compound interest; first number defined as a limit)
Wikipedia, 'e (mathematical constant)' (Bernoulli 1683; Euler's 1748 value to 18 decimal places)

story_idea.candidate: Irene Triplett, who died on 31 May 2020 in North Carolina aged 90, was the last person drawing a pension from the American Civil War: $73.13 a month from the Department of Veterans Affairs, inherited through her father Mose Triplett, who had fought in the 1860s.
story_idea.why: A small monthly cheque paid for decades — what single sum today is that stream of payments worth, and what does the answer depend on?

days.headline_hint: The last Civil War pension: $73.13 a month until 2020. What is a stream like that worth?

story.title: Irene Triplett's $73.13
story.hook: Irene Triplett died on 31 May 2020 in a nursing home in Wilkesboro, North Carolina, aged 90 — the last person drawing a pension from the American Civil War, which had ended 155 years earlier. Her father, Mose Triplett, fought first for the Confederacy and then for the Union; she was born in 1930, and he died in 1938 at 92. Because of her cognitive disability the Department of Veterans Affairs classed her as a 'helpless child' of a veteran, and every month it paid her $73.13.
story.puzzle: A small cheque, arriving every month for decades. If someone offered one lump sum today instead of the next ten years of cheques, what would be a fair price — and what does the answer depend on?
story.payoff: Each cheque is a single sum to discount, and adding 120 of them is exactly the ordinary-annuity formula. At 4% a year (4/12% a month), ten years of $73.13 is worth PV = 73.13 × [1 − (1 + 0.04/12)^−120]/(0.04/12) = $7,223.06 — well below the $8,775.60 paid out in total, because later cheques are worth less today. The answer depends on the rate (at 8% the same ten years are worth $6,027.48) and on the length (30 years at 4% are worth $15,317.90; even forever only $21,939.00 — Day 8's perpetuity).

story_idea.candidate: On 8 November 2022 Edwin Castro of Altadena, California, held the only winning ticket for a $2.04 billion Powerball jackpot, the largest in history. He could take $997.6 million in cash now, or 30 annual payments over 29 years — the first paid immediately, the rest growing 5% a year — totalling $2.04 billion.
story_idea.why: Why is '$2.04 billion' worth only about half that in cash, and how does a first payment made today change the comparison?

days.headline_hint: $2.04 billion or $997.6 million today? The Powerball choice, and the payment that comes first

story.title: The $2.04 billion ticket from Altadena
story.hook: The Powerball draw of Monday 7 November 2022 was held nearly 10 hours late, on the morning of 8 November, because the Minnesota Lottery needed more time to verify its sales. It produced the largest lottery jackpot in history, $2.04 billion, won by a single ticket sold at Joe's Service Center in Altadena, California; in February 2023 the winner was named as Edwin Castro. He had a choice: $997.6 million in cash, or the annuity — one payment straight away and 29 more once a year, each 5% bigger than the last, adding up to $2.04 billion. He took the cash.
story.puzzle: Why is '$2.04 billion' worth less than half that in cash — and how much does it matter that the first payment comes today rather than a year from now?
story.payoff: Simplify the annuity to 30 level payments of $68 million (the $2.04 billion spread evenly). Because the first comes today, it is an annuity due: at 4%, PV = 68 × [1 − 1.04^−30]/0.04 × 1.04 = $1,222.9 million, against $1,175.9 million if every payment came a year later — exactly 1.04 times bigger. The rate that makes the level stream worth the $997.6 million cash is 5.94%. The real schedule is more back-loaded — about $30.7 million first, rising to about $126.4 million — so the rate that makes it equal to the cash is only about 4.4%. Most of the headline $2.04 billion is money far in the future.

story_idea.candidate: In March 2015 the UK Treasury redeemed the 3½% War Loan — about £1.9 billion still outstanding, descended from the 5% War Loan of 1917 and converted in 1932 into a bond with no fixed repayment date — and in July 2015 it redeemed the last consols, some tracing back to debts consolidated in the 1750s. Holders had received fixed coupons for generations with no maturity date.
story_idea.why: If a bond never matures, what is it worth — and why did it suddenly make sense for the government to pay it off after a century?

days.headline_hint: Britain paid its First World War loan for a century and never had to repay it. So why did it?

story.title: The bond Britain could keep forever
story.hook: On 3 December 2014 the UK Debt Management Office announced that the 3½% War Loan would be repaid at par — £100 for every £100 of stock — on Monday 9 March 2015; £1,938.6 million was still in issue. It descended from the 5% War Loan sold in 1917 to pay for the First World War, converted in 1932 into a 3½% stock that never had to be repaid: the government could choose to repay it at any time after 1 December 1952, but did not have to. On 5 July 2015 the last undated gilts, including the 2½% Consolidated Stock (consols, with roots in 18th-century borrowing), were repaid too, completing the repayment of about £2.6 billion of historical debt.
story.puzzle: A bond that never has to be repaid pays £3.50 a year forever. What is that worth — and why did it suddenly pay the Treasury to hand back £100 for it after more than 80 years?
story.payoff: A level payment forever, starting next year, is worth PV = A/r, because the discounted payments form a geometric series that converges. In December 2014 the 30-year gilt yield hit a record low of 2.639%, so £3.50 a year forever was worth about 3.50/0.02639 = £132.63 per £100 at market rates. The Treasury could instead pay holders £100, borrow that £100 at well under 3.5%, and stop paying 3.5% forever. When long rates were above 3.5%, the stream was worth less than £100 (at 4%, 3.50/0.04 = £87.50) and repaying at par would have been a gift to the holders.

story_idea.candidate: In October 1981, as the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker fought double-digit inflation, Freddie Mac's survey recorded the highest average 30-year fixed US mortgage rate ever: 18.63%.
story_idea.why: At 18.63%, how much of a homeowner's first monthly payment actually paid off the house — and how long before principal outweighed interest?

days.headline_hint: 18.63%: the 1981 mortgage whose first payment paid off about $6 of the house

story.title: The 18.63% mortgage
story.hook: In the week of 9 October 1981, Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the average US 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 18.63%, the highest since the survey began in 1971 and a record that still stands. The Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker had pushed interest rates to around 20% to break double-digit inflation, and banks' prime rate reached 21.5%. As home sales collapsed, builders mailed chunks of two-by-four lumber to Volcker and to members of Congress in protest; one addressed to Volcker is catalogued in the St. Louis Fed's FRASER digital library.
story.puzzle: Take a $100,000, 30-year loan at 18.63%. How much of the first monthly payment actually pays off the house — and how many years pass before principal outweighs interest?
story.payoff: Each payment first pays interest on the balance still owed. Month 1's interest is 100,000 × 0.1863/12 = $1,552.50 of a $1,558.58 payment, leaving $6.08 for principal. After a full year of payments ($18,702.99) the balance is still $99,920.44: only $79.56 repaid. Principal grows by just 1.5525% a month, so it first exceeds interest in payment 317, more than 26 years in, and the borrower pays about $461,090 of interest in all on a $100,000 loan.

days.title: Uneven cash flows: NPV and IRR
days.concept: An uneven stream is valued by discounting each cash flow separately and adding (cash-flow additivity), and its internal rate of return is the single discount rate that makes that net present value zero.
los: NPV = Σ CF_t / (1 + r)^t (CF_0 usually negative)
Cash-flow additivity: PVs at the same date can be added or split
IRR: the r that solves Σ CF_t / (1 + IRR)^t = 0
CF worksheet with frequencies (repeated cash flows)

story_idea.candidate: On 23 November 1998 the four largest US tobacco companies signed the Master Settlement Agreement with 46 states, promising about $206 billion over the first 25 years in uneven annual payments; many states then sold their future payments to investors for cash up front by issuing 'tobacco bonds'.
story_idea.why: A state trades decades of uneven payments for one cheque today — how do you put a single price on an uneven stream, and what return does the buyer earn?

days.headline_hint: 46 states, $206 billion, one uneven stream: how Ohio turned tobacco payments into cash today

story.title: Selling the tobacco settlement
story.hook: On 23 November 1998 the four largest US cigarette makers — Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds, Brown & Williamson and Lorillard — signed the Master Settlement Agreement with 46 states, the District of Columbia and five territories, settling the states' claims for the health-care costs of smoking. They agreed to pay about $206 billion over the first 25 years in annual instalments, each adjusted for inflation and for how many cigarettes are sold, so the payments are anything but level. Many states sold their future payments for cash now: in October 2007 Ohio's Buckeye Tobacco Settlement Financing Authority sold $5.53 billion of bonds backed by Ohio's share, reported at the time as the state's largest borrowing ever.
story.puzzle: How do you put one price on a stream of payments that changes every year — and what return does the buyer of that stream actually earn?
story.payoff: Discount each year's payment separately and add (cash-flow additivity); subtract the price and you have the NPV at the buyer's required rate. The single rate that makes the NPV zero is the IRR, the return the buyer earns if the payments arrive as projected. In today's illustration a buyer pays 470 for 120, 120, 115, 110 and 105: NPV at 6% = +12.16 and IRR = 6.97%. If every payment came in 10% lower, the IRR would fall to 3.06%. That is what happened to tobacco bonds: smoking fell faster than projected, so the payments shrank. By 2012 Moody's was projecting defaults on many tobacco bonds if cigarette sales kept falling about 3% a year, and Ohio's bonds drifted toward default until a refinancing of about $5.4 billion in February 2020.
sources: Philip Morris Companies Inc., Form 8-K, November 1998 (SEC EDGAR): the Master Settlement Agreement with 46 states, D.C. and five territories; original participating manufacturers
Congressional Research Service, RL30058, 'Tobacco Master Settlement Agreement (1998)': about $206 billion through 2025

days.title: Holding-period returns and chain-linking
days.concept: Returns over successive periods compound by multiplying growth factors, (1 + R_1)(1 + R_2)…(1 + R_n) − 1, which is why a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to recover and why a period return is annualized as (1 + R_period)^c − 1.
los: Holding-period return HPR = (P_1 − P_0 + D_1)/P_0 = income yield + price return
Multi-period (chain-linked) return = (1 + R_1)(1 + R_2)…(1 + R_n) − 1
Annualizing: R_annual = (1 + R_period)^c − 1, c = periods per year (or 1/years)
Gain needed to recover a loss L: L/(1 − L)
Percent change and compound growth with the Δ% worksheet

Forgetting the dividend or coupon in the HPR

story_idea.candidate: The Nasdaq Composite closed at a record 5,048.62 on 10 March 2000, then fell to 1,114.11 on 9 October 2002, a drop of about 78%. It did not close above its 2000 high until 23 April 2015.
story_idea.why: If the index fell 78%, why wasn't a 78% rise enough to get back — and why did recovery take fifteen years?

days.headline_hint: The Nasdaq lost 78% in 31 months — and needed a 353% gain and 15 years to get back

story.title: Fifteen years to climb back
story.hook: On 10 March 2000, at the top of the dot-com boom, the Nasdaq Composite closed at a record 5,048.62. Thirty-one months later, on 9 October 2002, it closed at 1,114.11 — about 78% lower. Then it climbed for more than twelve years. It finally closed above the old record on 23 April 2015, at 5,056.06: fifteen years, one month and thirteen days after the peak.
story.puzzle: The index fell 78%. Why wasn't a 78% rise enough to get it back — and why did the climb take so long?
story.payoff: Returns multiply, they don't add. The fall left 1,114.11/5,048.62 = 0.2207 of the peak: an HPR of −77.93%. A 78% rise from the low only reaches 1,114.11 × 1.78 = 1,983.12, only 39% of the old peak. Getting back needs 5,048.62/1,114.11 − 1 = +353.15%, which is L/(1 − L) = 0.7793/0.2207. From the October 2002 low to the April 2015 record (4,579 days, about 12.54 years) the index compounded at 12.82% a year. That is a strong return, and it still took twelve and a half years just to break even.

days.module: LM2 Types of Financial Returns
days.title: Arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means
days.concept: The arithmetic mean answers 'what is a typical one-period return', the geometric mean answers 'what constant return gives the same ending wealth', and the harmonic mean gives the average cost per share when the same amount of money is invested each period.
los: Arithmetic mean R̄ = ΣR_t/n
Geometric mean R_G = [(1 + R_1)(1 + R_2)…(1 + R_n)]^(1/n) − 1
Harmonic mean X̄_H = n / Σ(1/X_i) (cost averaging)
Harmonic ≤ geometric ≤ arithmetic (equal only if all values equal)
Geometric ≈ arithmetic − σ²/2; arithmetic for forecasting one period, geometric for past compound growth

Applying the harmonic mean to returns rather than to prices paid with equal money each period

story_idea.candidate: Cathie Wood's ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) gained about 152.5% in 2020, then lost about 23.4% in 2021 and about 67.0% in 2022, ending 2022 below where it began 2020.
story_idea.why: The fund's 'average annual return' over the three years was strongly positive, yet a buyer at the start lost money. Which average tells the truth?

days.headline_hint: ARK's average year was +20.7%, yet $10,000 shrank to $6,383. Which average tells the truth?

story.title: The fund whose average year was +20.7%
story.hook: Cathie Wood's ARK Innovation ETF (ticker ARKK) was the star fund of 2020, gaining about 152.5% as investors piled into bets on disruptive technology. Then the bets turned: the fund lost about 23.4% in 2021 and about 67.0% in 2022, when rising interest rates hammered growth stocks. Add the three years and divide by three and its average annual return looks healthy: +20.7%.
story.puzzle: Someone who put $10,000 in at the start of 2020 and held for three years ended with about $6,383 (using the rounded yearly returns), a loss of about 36%. How can an 'average' of +20.7% a year lose money — and which average tells the truth?
story.payoff: The arithmetic mean, (152.5 − 23.4 − 67.0)/3 = 20.70%, answers 'what was a typical single year?'. Wealth compounds, so 'what constant yearly return gives the same ending value?' needs the geometric mean: (2.525 × 0.766 × 0.330)^(1/3) − 1 = 0.6383^(1/3) − 1 = −13.90% a year. Three years at −13.90% turn $10,000 into $6,383, the same ending value as the three actual years. The gap between the two means is the cost of volatility: the bigger the swings, the further the geometric mean sits below the arithmetic one.
sources: Morningstar, 'ARK Innovation ETF has likely been a disappointment for most investors' (ARKK gained 152.5% in 2020): https://www.morningstar.com.au/etfs/ark-innovation-etf-has-likely-been-a-disappointment-for-most-investors

days.module: LM3 Benchmarking Returns
days.title: Money-weighted vs time-weighted returns
days.concept: The money-weighted return is the IRR of the investor's own cash flows and so rewards or punishes the timing of deposits and withdrawals, while the time-weighted return chain-links sub-period returns and so measures the manager regardless of those flows.
los: Money-weighted return = IRR of contributions (−), withdrawals and ending value (+)
Time-weighted return: HPRs between external cash flows, chain-linked, then annualized geometrically
Why MWR > TWR when money arrives before good periods (and < when before bad ones)
TWR is the standard for evaluating managers; MWR fits investor experience

calculator.task: An investor buys one share at 100, buys a second at 120 a year later, receives dividends and sells both at the end of year 2: MWR by IRR and TWR by chain-linking

calculator.ti: irr(CF0, {CF1, CF2}); home-screen product and square root

memorize.back: The IRR of the investor's cash flows: Σ CF_t / (1 + MWR)^t = 0
TWR = (1 + HPR_1)(1 + HPR_2)…(1 + HPR_n) − 1, annualized geometrically

memorize.front: When is TWR the right measure?
memorize.back: When the manager does not control the timing of external cash flows (manager evaluation)
MWR > TWR if more money is invested just before strong returns; MWR < TWR if before weak returns

traps: Treating deposits as returns in the TWR (sub-periods must break at each cash flow)
Getting the investor-perspective signs wrong in the IRR
Annualizing a multi-year TWR arithmetically instead of geometrically

story_idea.candidate: On 31 December 2009 the Wall Street Journal named Ken Heebner's CGM Focus Fund the best US stock fund of the decade (about 18% a year over the ten years to November 2009), while Morningstar estimated that its typical shareholder lost about 11% a year over the same period: investors poured about $2.6 billion in during 2008, after an 80% gain in 2007, just before the fund fell about 48%.
story_idea.why: Same fund, same ten years — how can the fund earn about +18% a year while the people who owned it lost about 11% a year?

days.headline_hint: The decade's best fund made 18% a year; its typical investor lost 11% a year. Both numbers are true

story.title: The best fund of the decade, and its losing investors
story.hook: On 31 December 2009 the Wall Street Journal named CGM Focus, run by the stock-picker Ken Heebner, the best-performing US stock fund of the decade: it had returned about 18% a year over the ten years to late November 2009. In the same breath the paper reported Morningstar's estimate for the fund's typical shareholder over that decade: a loss of about 11% a year. Much of the money had arrived at the wrong moment. After the fund gained about 80% in 2007, investors poured about $2.6 billion into it in 2008 — the year it fell about 48%.
story.puzzle: Same fund, same ten years. How can the fund earn about +18% a year while the people who owned it lost about 11% a year?
story.payoff: They are two different returns. The fund's +18% is a time-weighted return: sub-period returns are chain-linked whatever money flows in or out, so it measures the manager. The shareholders' −11% is a money-weighted return: the IRR of their own purchases and sales, so it counts how much money was in the fund each year. Take a hypothetical investor who put $10,000 in at the start of 2007 (+80%) and added $20,000 at the start of 2008 (−48%): she ends with $19,760. The fund's time-weighted return over the two years is 1.80 × 0.52 − 1 = −6.40%, or −3.25% a year; her money-weighted return, the IRR of −10,000, −20,000 and +19,760, is −27.49% a year. Two-thirds of her money arrived just before the bad year.
sources: Eleanor Laise, 'Best Stock Fund of the Decade: CGM Focus', The Wall Street Journal, 31 Dec 2009 (as excerpted and cited by GuruFocus): https://gurufocus.com/news/80345/wsj-best-stock-fund-of-the-decade-cgm-focus

steps: Sub-period 2 starts after the withdrawal at 750,000: HPR_2 = 690,000/750,000 − 1 = −8.00%
MWR = 1/v − 1 = 5.44% — above the TWR, because money was taken out just before the bad year

days.concept: A bond's price is the PV of its coupons (an annuity) plus the PV of its principal (a single sum), all discounted at the market yield, so the price falls when the yield rises and sits above par when the coupon rate exceeds the yield.

Zero-coupon bond price PV = FV/(1 + r)^N
Semiannual bonds: PMT/2, r/2, 2N periods
Premium (coupon > yield), discount (coupon < yield), par (coupon = yield)
Constant-yield price trajectory: prices pull to par as maturity approaches

days.headline_hint: Disney borrowed for 100 years — and the $100 it promised to repay in 2093 was worth six cents

story.title: Sleeping Beauty's hundred-year promise
story.hook: In July 1993 the Walt Disney Company sold $300 million of bonds that would not mature until 15 July 2093. The coupon was 7.55% and the bonds were sold at par, so buyers were promised 7.55% a year for up to a century. Wall Street nicknamed them 'Sleeping Beauty' bonds, after the princess who slept for a hundred years; they were the first 100-year bonds sold by an American company since 1954. Within days Coca-Cola sold century bonds of its own.
story.puzzle: What is a century of coupons plus $100 repaid in 2093 worth today — and how much of that value comes from the final repayment?
story.payoff: A bond is an annuity (the coupons) plus a single sum (the principal), both discounted at the market yield. Per $100 of par, assuming semiannual coupons (the US corporate norm): at Disney's own 7.55% the price is exactly 100.00, and the $100 repaid in 2093 is worth only 100/1.03775^200 = $0.06 of it — the coupons are almost all of the value. At a 9% yield the price falls to 83.89 (the final $100 worth $0.015); at 4% it rises to 187.06. A century bond is nearly a perpetuity: 7.55/0.09 = 83.89. Coda: Disney never had to repay in 2093. It redeemed the remaining $201 million of the bonds on their first call date, 15 July 2023.

days.concept: The yield to maturity is the IRR of buying a bond at its price and holding it to maturity; current yield, yield-to-call and yield-to-worst answer narrower questions, and yields can be compared only after converting them to the same periodicity.

Current yield = annual coupon / flat price
Yield to call: N to the call date, FV = call price; yield-to-worst = lowest of YTM and all YTCs
Periodicity conversion: (1 + APR_m/m)^m = (1 + APR_n/n)^n, e.g. (1 + r_s/2)^2 = 1 + r_annual
Street convention vs true yield; simple yield = (annual coupon + straight-line amortization of the discount, or − of the premium) / flat price
YTM assumptions: held to maturity, all payments on time, coupons reinvested at the YTM

story_idea.why: The coupon said 7.125% but investors were promised 'about 7.9%'. Where does the extra yield come from when you pay 90 for a bond that repays 100?

days.headline_hint: Argentina, eight defaults behind it, borrowed for 100 years at 90 cents on the dollar. What did 7.917% mean?

story.title: Argentina's 100-year bond
story.hook: On 19 June 2017 Argentina — which had defaulted on its debts eight times since independence, most recently in 2014 — sold $2.75 billion of US-dollar bonds that would not mature until 2117. Investors put in about $9.75 billion of orders. The coupon was 7.125%, but buyers paid only 90 cents on the dollar, and Bloomberg reported the yield as 7.917%. Less than three years later, in 2020, Argentina defaulted for a ninth time; in that year's restructuring the century bonds were swapped, at roughly 55 cents on the dollar by one estimate, for bonds due decades sooner.
story.puzzle: The coupon says 7.125%. Where does a 7.917% yield come from when you pay 90 for a bond that repays 100 — and can 7.917% be compared with the yield on a bond that pays once a year?
story.payoff: The YTM is the IRR of paying 90 for 200 semiannual coupons of 3.5625 plus 100 at the end: the calculator gives 3.9585% per half-year, and doubling it (the semiannual-bond basis) gives 7.917% — Bloomberg's number. Almost all of the extra yield is the coupon earned on a cheaper price: the current yield is 7.125/90 = 7.917% as well. Over a century the climb from 90 to 100 adds almost nothing — the final 100 is worth 4 cents today; on a 10-year bond at the same price it would lift the YTM to 8.64%. And 7.917% on a semiannual basis is 8.07% on an annual-pay basis, the number to compare with annual-pay bonds. A yield to maturity assumes the borrower pays every coupon on time for the whole life; Argentina defaulted within three years.

Accrued interest AI = (t/T) × PMT
Flat (quoted, clean) price = full price − AI

story_idea.candidate: In Greece's March 2012 debt exchange (the 'PSI') private holders of almost €200 billion of Greek government bonds received new Greek bonds and EFSF notes — and, separately, six-month EFSF zero-coupon notes (due 12 September 2012) covering the interest accrued on the old bonds up to 24 February 2012.
story_idea.why: No coupon was due on exchange day, so why did Greece owe bondholders interest — and how much is owed for part of a coupon period?

days.headline_hint: No coupon was due, yet Greece's 2012 debt swap paid bondholders for every day since the last one

story.title: Greece pays for the days, not the coupons
story.hook: In March 2012, in the private-sector involvement deal known as the PSI, private holders of almost €200 billion (face value) of Greek government bonds handed them in. For every €100 of face value they received €31.50 of new Greek bonds and €15 of short-term notes from the eurozone's rescue fund, the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF), plus GDP-linked warrants: €46.50 of new debt for every €100 of old bonds, a 53.5% cut in face value. One item was settled separately: the interest that had built up on each old bond since its last coupon date, up to 24 February 2012, was paid with six-month EFSF zero-coupon notes.
story.puzzle: No coupon was due on the day the old bonds were cancelled. Why did Greece owe bondholders any interest at all — and how much is owed for part of a coupon period?
story.payoff: A coupon is earned day by day by whoever holds the bond. Between coupon dates the bond's value is its PV at the last coupon date carried forward, PV × (1 + r)^(t/T); the slice of that full price which is the holder's share of the next coupon is accrued interest, AI = (t/T) × coupon. Greece was ending the old bonds partway through their coupon periods, so it paid holders what they had already earned. Illustration (not an actual Greek bond): €100,000 of a bond paying a 4.5% coupon once a year, last paid on 20 August 2011, had run 188 of the period's 366 days by 24 February 2012 (actual/actual), so AI = 4,500 × 188/366 = €2,311.48.

days.title: Money-market yields and repos
days.concept: Money-market rates are quoted on a discount basis (on face value) or an add-on basis (on price) over 360- or 365-day years, so they must be converted to a common basis such as the 365-day add-on bond-equivalent yield before they are compared.
los: Discount basis: PV = FV × [1 − (Days/Year) × DR]
Add-on basis: PV = FV / [1 + (Days/Year) × AOR]
Discount rate → add-on rate: AOR = (Year/Days) × (FV − PV)/PV
Bond-equivalent yield = 365-day add-on rate
Repo interest = principal × repo rate × (days/360); haircut = 1 − loan/collateral value
Why a discount rate understates the return on money invested

calculator.task: A 4-week (28-day) T-bill quoted at a 0.000% and then a 5.25% discount rate: price per 100, then the 365-day bond-equivalent yield; then a repo's interest

memorize.front: Price of a money-market instrument quoted on a discount basis
memorize.back: PV = FV × [1 − (Days/Year) × DR]
PV = FV / [1 + (Days/Year) × AOR]
AOR = (Year / Days) × (FV − PV) / PV
A 365-day add-on rate: BEY = (365 / Days) × (FV − PV) / PV
Repo interest = principal × repo rate × (days / 360)
Haircut = 1 − loan / collateral value, so loan = collateral value × (1 − haircut)

traps: Using a 365-day year for a US T-bill discount rate (it is 360)
Treating a discount rate as the return on money invested (it is computed on face value)
Comparing a 360-day rate with a 365-day rate without converting

story_idea.candidate: On 9 December 2008, at the height of the financial crisis, the US Treasury sold about $30 billion of four-week bills at a discount rate of 0.000% — investors paid the full face value for the privilege of getting the same amount back a month later.
story_idea.why: Why would anyone lend money for nothing, and how does a T-bill's 'discount rate' turn into the price an investor pays?

days.headline_hint: December 2008: investors lent the US Treasury $30 billion for four weeks and asked for nothing

story.title: Lending to the Treasury for nothing
story.hook: On 9 December 2008, less than three months after Lehman Brothers collapsed, the US Treasury auctioned $30 billion of four-week bills at a rate of 0.000% — the first zero rate since it began selling four-week bills in 2001. Bids came to more than four times the amount on offer. A week earlier the same bills had sold at 0.04%, and the day before, three-month bills had sold at 0.005%, reportedly the lowest since the Treasury began auctioning bills in 1929.
story.puzzle: Why would anyone lend money for four weeks for nothing — and how does a T-bill's 'discount rate' become the price an investor pays?
story.payoff: T-bills pay no coupon: they are sold below face value, and the quoted discount rate sets that discount on a 360-day year, PV = 100 × [1 − (28/360) × DR]. At 0.000%, PV = 100.00: investors paid $100 to get $100 back. A week earlier, at 0.04%, a $100,000 bill cost $99,996.89 — $3.11 of interest for four weeks, a 0.0406% bond-equivalent yield. In December 2008 the return that mattered was getting the money back: next to a bank or fund that might fail, a Treasury bill paying nothing was still the safest place to wait.
sources: The Bond Buyer, 'Treasury 4-Weeks Auctioned at Zero High Yield', 9 Dec 2008: https://www.bondbuyer.com/news/treasury-4-weeks-auctioned-at-zero-high-yield-BB1072861

days.module: Equity Valuation: Concepts and Basic Tools
days.title: Constant-growth dividend discount model
days.concept: If dividends grow at a constant rate g forever, a share is a growing perpetuity worth V_0 = D_1/(r − g), and the same equation read backwards gives the market's implied required return r = D_1/P_0 + g or implied growth g = r − D_1/P_0.
los: Gordon growth model V_0 = D_1/(r − g) with D_1 = D_0(1 + g)
Requires r > g
Implied required return r = D_1/P_0 + g (dividend yield + growth)
Implied growth g = r − D_1/P_0
Preferred stock (non-callable, fixed dividend) as a perpetuity: V_0 = D_p/r_p
LM4 link: required return and implied growth of equity
Dividend chronology (Equities): declaration date → ex-dividend date (the share price drops by about the dividend) → holder-of-record date → payment date
Implied growth when only D_0 is given: from P_0 = D_0(1 + g)/(r − g), g = (r × P_0 − D_0)/(P_0 + D_0)

calculator.task: Shell's 2019 dividend D_0 = 4 × 0.47 = 1.88; with g = 3% and r = 8% find V_0; then the growth a hypothetical market price of 25 implies when D_1 = D_0(1 + g), g = (r × P_0 − D_0)/(P_0 + D_0); value a preferred paying 5 at r_p = 6%
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with parentheses and STO/RCL

memorize.front: Value of a non-callable, non-convertible preferred share
memorize.back: V_0 = D_p / r_p
Declaration date → ex-dividend date (shares bought on or after it do not get the dividend; price falls by about D) → holder-of-record date → payment date

memorize.front: Implied growth when only D_0 and P_0 are known

traps: Using D_0 instead of D_1 in the numerator
Applying the model when g ≥ r (it gives a meaningless value)
Using the common-equity required return to value a preferred share

story_idea.candidate: On 30 April 2020 Royal Dutch Shell cut its quarterly dividend by two-thirds, from $0.47 to $0.16 a share — its first cut since the Second World War. Its shares were about 7% lower in the first hour of London trading (and, by one report, its US-listed shares fell as much as 14% in the first half hour in New York).
story_idea.why: If a share is worth its future dividends, why didn't a two-thirds dividend cut take two-thirds off the price — and what growth had investors been assuming?

days.headline_hint: Shell cut its dividend by two-thirds, its first cut since WWII. Why didn't the shares fall two-thirds?

story.title: Shell's first dividend cut since the war
story.hook: On 30 April 2020, with oil demand collapsing in the pandemic, Royal Dutch Shell cut its quarterly dividend by two-thirds, from 47 US cents a share to 16 cents. It was the company's first dividend cut since the Second World War; it had avoided a cut even in the deep oil downturns of the 1980s. Its shares were about 7% lower within the first hour of trading in London and, by one report, its US-listed shares fell as much as 14% in the first half hour of New York trading.
story.puzzle: If a share is worth the dividends it will pay, cutting the dividend by two-thirds should cut the share's value by two-thirds. Why did the price fall by only a fraction of that?
story.payoff: With constant growth, V_0 = D_1/(r − g): value is proportional to next year's dividend. Take Shell's 2019 dividend, 4 × $0.47 = $1.88, with illustrative assumptions g = 3% and r = 8%: V_0 = $38.73. Cut D_0 to 4 × $0.16 = $0.64 with r and g unchanged and V_0 = $13.18, 66% lower. The shares fell far less, so before the announcement the price must already have sat far below the old-dividend value. Read the model backwards, g = r − D_1/P_0, and that price was already implying much lower growth than the old dividend promised. The likeliest reading: investors had largely priced in a cut before Shell announced it.
sources: Reuters, 30 Apr 2020, 'Shell cuts dividend for first time since World War Two' (two-thirds cut from 47 to 16 cents; first cut since the Second World War; London shares down about 7% by 07:53 GMT), via LSE.co.uk: https://lse.co.uk/news/BP./update-4-shell-cuts-dividend-for-first-time-since-world-war-two-jxdreyv72ck75h3.html?page=18

days.title: Two-stage dividend discount model
days.concept: When dividends grow fast for a few years and then settle into stable growth, value = PV of the explicit dividends + PV of a Gordon terminal value V_n = D_(n+1)/(r − g_L) placed at the start of stable growth.
los: Two-stage DDM: V_0 = Σ_(t=1..n) D_t/(1 + r)^t + V_n/(1 + r)^n
Terminal value V_n = D_(n+1)/(r − g_L)
Valuing with the CF worksheet: add V_n to the year-n dividend
Multistage logic reused later for FCFE/FCFF inputs

story_idea.candidate: On 16 January 2003 Microsoft, public since March 1986, declared its first-ever dividend — 8 cents a share for the year (after a 2-for-1 split), about $864 million in all; in July 2004 it announced a one-time $3-a-share special dividend of about $32 billion, paid on 2 December 2004. By September 2025 its quarterly dividend was 91 cents ($3.64 a year).
story_idea.why: How do you value a company whose dividends start small and grow fast for a while before slowing down — when no single growth rate fits?

days.headline_hint: Microsoft paid nothing for 17 years, then 8 cents. How do you value a dividend that sprints, then slows?

story.title: Microsoft's 8-cent starter dividend
story.hook: Microsoft went public in March 1986 and for almost 17 years paid no dividend at all, keeping its cash. On 16 January 2003 it declared its first: 8 cents a share for the year (after a 2-for-1 split announced the same day), about $864 million in all, described at the time as a 'starter' dividend. On 20 July 2004 it announced a one-time special dividend of $3 a share — about $32 billion — paid on 2 December 2004. By September 2025 its regular dividend had reached 91 cents a quarter, $3.64 a year.
story.puzzle: From 8 cents to $3.64 a year is about 18.5% growth a year for 22.5 years. A single growth rate that high breaks the Gordon model (g above r), yet it cannot last forever either. How do you value a dividend that grows fast for a while and then slows?
story.payoff: Split the future in two. Discount each high-growth dividend on its own; once growth settles at a rate g_L below r, the rest is a Gordon growing perpetuity, V_n = D_(n+1)/(r − g_L), a value at time n that is discounted n periods. In the walkthrough (0.50 growing 20% for three years, then 5%, r = 9%) the three explicit dividends are worth $1.82 today and the terminal value $17.51: about 91% of the $19.34 value. That is the point for a company like Microsoft in 2003: most of what the shares were worth lay in the stable-growth years after the sprint.

story_idea.candidate: Apple's shares closed at $499.23 on Friday 28 August 2020; its 4-for-1 split took effect for trading on Monday 31 August (about $124.81 a share). That morning the price-weighted Dow Jones Industrial Average swapped ExxonMobil, Pfizer and Raytheon Technologies for Salesforce, Amgen and Honeywell — changes S&P Dow Jones Indices said were prompted by Apple's split — and Apple's weight in the Dow fell from about 12% (estimates range from 10% to 12%) to about 3%, while the split left its weight in the cap-weighted S&P 500 unchanged.
story_idea.why: Apple's business was exactly the same before and after the split. How can one index say it became four times less important and another say nothing changed?

days.headline_hint: Apple split its stock 4-for-1 and lost three-quarters of its pull on the Dow. Nothing about Apple changed.

story.title: Apple's split and the Dow's reshuffle
story.hook: Apple's shares closed at $499.23 on Friday 28 August 2020. Its 4-for-1 stock split took effect over the weekend, so by Monday 31 August each old share had become four, and Friday's close was the same as about $124.81 a share. That same morning the Dow Jones Industrial Average swapped out ExxonMobil, Pfizer and Raytheon Technologies for Salesforce, Amgen and Honeywell, changes S&P Dow Jones Indices said were prompted by Apple's split. Apple had been the Dow's heaviest member, about 12% of the index by one estimate; after the split it was about 3%. In the S&P 500 the split left its weight exactly where it was.
story.puzzle: Apple's business, profits and total market value were the same on Monday as on Friday. How can one index decide Apple suddenly matters a quarter as much, while another says nothing changed?
story.payoff: The Dow is price-weighted: its value is the sum of its 30 share prices divided by a divisor, so each company counts in proportion to its share price, not its size. Cutting Apple's price from $499.23 to $124.81 cut its weight by three-quarters — the 12% became about 3%. With the divisor at about 0.15, every $1 move in any Dow stock moved the index by about 6.7 points, so a 1% move in Apple (about $5) had been worth roughly 33 Dow points before the split and only about 8 afterwards. The divisor was reset that morning so the Dow's level did not jump (the split and the three swaps went into the same reset). The S&P 500 weights each company by price × shares: the price fell to a quarter, the share count rose four times, and the product — Apple's market value — did not change, so neither did its weight.

worked_example.problem: Three stocks over one quarter. X: price 50 → 54, 200 million shares, 40 million closely held. Y: 20 → 19, 500 million shares, none closely held, pays a 0.40 dividend. Z: 80 → 86, 100 million shares, 50 million closely held. Find (a) the float-adjusted market-cap weights and the index's price return, (b) the price return with full-cap weights and with equal weights, (c) the float-adjusted total return.
steps: Free float = shares outstanding − closely held: X 160m, Y 500m, Z 50m
Float caps at the start: X 50 × 160 = 8,000; Y 20 × 500 = 10,000; Z 80 × 50 = 4,000; total 22,000 ($ millions)
worked_example.answer: (a) 36.36% / 45.45% / 18.18%, price return 2.00%; (b) full-cap 3.21%, equal-weighted 3.50%; (c) total return 2.91%

walkthrough.problem: A price-weighted index holds A (400), B (80) and C (120) with a divisor of 3. A splits 4-for-1. Find the index before the split and the new divisor; then, after prices move to A 110, B 76, C 126 and B and C pay dividends of 2 and 1, the index's price return and total return. Compare the price return of a cap-weighted index of the same stocks (40, 50 and 30 million shares after the split).

check_plan: c1 (num, chain arithmetic + Δ%): a price-weighted index of 90, 45 and 165 with divisor 2.5 (index 120.0000); the 165 stock splits 3-for-1 → new divisor (90 + 45 + 55)/120 = 1.5833; prices then move to 93, 44 and 58 → index 123.1579, price return 2.6316%. Ask the price return as a percent to two decimals (tolerance 0.01). Hint: the prices, the divisor and the split ratio change.

c2 (mc, why): a company in a cap-weighted index splits 2-for-1 — what happens to its weight? Right: nothing — the price halves and the share count doubles, so P × Q is unchanged. Distractors: 'it halves' (price-weighted thinking, where a company's weight follows its share price); 'it doubles, because the number of shares doubled' (forgets that the price halved).

c3 (num, twist — a substitution, like the Dow's 2020 swap): a 4-stock price-weighted index has prices summing to 260 and a divisor of 2.0 (index 130); a stock priced 30 is replaced by one priced 110 → new divisor = 340/130 = 2.6154 (it rises, so the index does not jump). Ask the new divisor to four decimals (tolerance 0.0001).

c4 (mc, exam): a price-weighted index of A (25 → 30), B (50 → 45) and C (100 → 110, which also paid a 2.00 dividend) — the index's price return? A 5.71% (correct: 185/175 − 1); B 6.67% (averaged the three returns: that is equal weighting); C 6.86% (added C's dividend: that is the total return).

c5 (explain): why a price-weighted index must change its divisor after a split, and why a cap-weighted index need not. Must contain: index = Σ prices / divisor; a split cuts the price but not the company's value, so without a new divisor the index would fall for no economic reason; in a cap-weighted index P falls and Q rises by the same factor, so value and weight are unchanged.

days.module: LM5 Statistical Characteristics of Asset Returns
days.title: Median, quantiles and trimmed means
days.concept: The median, quantiles and trimmed or winsorized means describe where returns sit without being dragged around by a few extreme values; the y-th percentile is found at position L_y = (n + 1)y/100 in the sorted data, interpolating between neighbours.
los: Median and mode
Quantile location L_y = (n + 1) × y/100 with linear interpolation
Quartiles, quintiles, deciles, percentiles; interquartile range; box plot
Trimmed mean: an x% trimmed mean discards the lowest x/2% and the highest x/2% of observations, then averages the rest
Winsorized mean: replace the extremes with the nearest retained values, then average (a 95% winsorized mean resets the bottom and top 2.5%)

calculator.task: Nine judges' scores for one skater: sort, find the median and the 25th and 75th percentiles with (n + 1)y/100, then the mean, the trimmed mean (drop highest and lowest) and the winsorized mean
calculator.ba: 2ND DATA / 2ND STAT 1-V for n and x̄; hand interpolation for quantiles
calculator.ti: STAT 1-Var Stats (shows Q1, Med, Q3 — the TI-84 takes the medians of the lower and upper halves, which gives the same quartiles as the CFA formula when n is odd, as for this nine-score panel, but different ones when n is even, e.g. n = 10 or 12; use (n + 1)y/100 by hand)

memorize.front: Location of the y-th percentile in n sorted observations
Interpolating a percentile at a non-integer location
memorize.back: P = X_(below) + (L_y − whole part) × (X_(above) − X_(below))
Discard a stated % of the lowest and highest observations, then average the rest (a 5% trimmed mean drops the lowest 2.5% and the highest 2.5%)
Replace the extreme observations with the nearest retained values, then average (a 95% winsorized mean resets the bottom and top 2.5%)
IQR = Q3 − Q1

traps: Using n × y/100 instead of (n + 1) × y/100
Forgetting to sort the data first
Trusting the TI-84's Q1/Q3, which use a different quartile method from the CFA formula (they agree only when n is odd)
Confusing trimmed (drop the extremes) with winsorized (replace them)
Misreading the naming: a 5% trimmed mean drops 2.5% at each end, and a 95% winsorized mean resets 2.5% at each end

story_idea.candidate: At the Salt Lake City Winter Olympics on 11 February 2002 the Russian pair Berezhnaya and Sikharulidze beat Canada's Salé and Pelletier 5–4 on the judges' cards despite a stepped-out landing; the French judge Marie-Reine Le Gougne was reported to have said she had been pressured to vote for the Russians (she later retracted), and on 15 February the Canadians received a second set of gold medals. The ISU's new judging system (from 2004) throws out the highest and lowest marks of up to nine judges and averages the other seven — a trimmed mean.
story_idea.why: If one judge can be bent, how should you average nine scores so that a single extreme mark cannot decide a gold medal?

days.headline_hint: One judge's vote moved an Olympic gold in 2002. Skating's fix was to throw out the highest and lowest marks.

story.title: The 5–4 vote at Salt Lake City
story.hook: On 11 February 2002, at the Salt Lake City Winter Olympics, Canada's Jamie Salé and David Pelletier skated what was widely described as a clean free program, while Russia's Elena Berezhnaya and Anton Sikharulidze made a visible error when Sikharulidze stepped out of a double Axel. The judges gave the gold to the Russians anyway, five votes to four. Within days the French judge, Marie-Reine Le Gougne, was reported to have said she had been pressured by her federation to vote for the Russians, a claim she later retracted. On 15 February the IOC and the International Skating Union gave Salé and Pelletier a second set of gold medals, the Russians keeping theirs, and in April the ISU suspended Le Gougne and the French federation's head, Didier Gailhaguet, for three years.
story.puzzle: One judge's vote was enough to move a gold medal. If any single judge might be leaning on the scale, how do you combine nine scores so that no one mark — however extreme — can decide the result?
story.payoff: The ISU's new judging system, which replaced the 6.0 system from 2004, uses a trimmed mean: a panel of up to nine judges scores each element, and the highest and lowest marks are thrown out before the rest are averaged — with nine judges, the middle seven (a 22% trimmed mean: one of nine from each end). In today's illustrative panel, one generous 9.75 and one harsh 6.50 pull the plain mean to 8.3889; the trimmed mean is 8.4643 and the median 8.50. Raise the top mark from 9.75 to 10.00 and the plain mean rises by 0.25/9 = 0.0278, while the trimmed mean does not move at all: the most extreme judge is always the one thrown away. (The 2002 event was judged on ordinal placings under the old 6.0 system, so these marks illustrate the method; they are not the real 2002 scores.)
sources: HISTORY.com, 'Canadian figure skaters awarded gold after judging scandal' (This Day in History, 15 February): https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-15/winter-olympics-scandals-figure-skating-2002

ESPN, 30 Apr 2002 (ISU suspends Le Gougne and Gailhaguet for three years): https://www.espn.com/oly/news/2002/0430/1376056.html

Wikipedia, '2002 Winter Olympics figure skating scandal' (Le Gougne's statement and retraction): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics_figure_skating_scandal

worked_example.problem: Twelve monthly fund returns (%): 2.1, −0.8, 1.5, 3.4, −4.6, 0.9, 1.2, −1.1, 2.6, 0.4, 7.9, −0.3. Find the median, Q1, Q3, the IQR and the 10th percentile with L_y = (n + 1)y/100; then the mean, the trimmed mean that drops one observation at each end, and the winsorized mean that replaces them.
steps: Check against the TI-84: its 1-Var Stats would show Q1 = −0.55 and Q3 = 2.35 (medians of each half), not the CFA values

walkthrough.problem: Nine judges' marks for one program (illustrative): 8.50, 8.25, 9.75, 8.75, 8.00, 8.50, 6.50, 8.75, 8.50. Get n, the mean and Σx from 1-V statistics; sort and find the median and the 25th and 75th percentiles with (n + 1)y/100; then the trimmed mean (drop the highest and lowest) and the winsorized mean.
walkthrough.display_ti: 1-Var Stats L1: x̄=8.3889, Σx=75.5000, n=9, Q1=8.1250, Med=8.5000, Q3=8.7500 (the same as the CFA values here because n is odd; with an even n they differ); (75.5−6.5−9.75)/7 → 8.4643; (75.5−6.5−9.75+8+8.75)/9 → 8.4444

check_plan: c1 (num, 1-V + chain arithmetic): another panel of nine — 8.00, 7.75, 8.25, 9.50, 8.00, 8.50, 7.50, 8.25, 5.75: Σx = 71.50, mean 7.9444; trimmed mean (drop 5.75 and 9.50) = 56.25/7 = 8.0357. Ask the trimmed mean to four decimals (tolerance 0.0001). Hint: new marks; drop one at each end.

c2 (mc, why): why does a trimmed mean resist one biased judge when the arithmetic mean does not? Right: the most extreme mark is discarded, so it has no effect, while in the plain mean every point it is out of line moves the average by 1/n of a point. Distractors: 'the trimmed mean replaces the extreme marks with the nearest remaining marks' (that is the winsorized mean); 'the trimmed mean is the middle score of the nine' (that is the median).

c3 (num, twist — a percentile at a fractional location, n = 10): returns 4.2, −2.5, 1.8, 6.1, −0.7, 3.3, 0.9, −5.4, 2.6, 7.4 → sorted −5.4, −2.5, −0.7, 0.9, 1.8, 2.6, 3.3, 4.2, 6.1, 7.4; 30th percentile at L = 11 × 0.30 = 3.3 → −0.7 + 0.3 × (0.9 − (−0.7)) = −0.22%. Ask as a percent to two decimals (tolerance 0.01). (Here the CFA Q1 is −1.15% at L = 2.75, but the TI-84 shows Q1 = −0.70 — the quartile-rule trap.)

c4 (mc, exam): eight returns, as reported — 2.0, −1.5, 6.5, 0.5, 4.0, −3.0, 2.5, 1.0 — the 75th percentile? A 2.500% (location n × y/100 = 6 → 6th sorted value); B 1.125% (location 6.75 interpolated in the unsorted list); C 3.625% (correct: L = 9 × 0.75 = 6.75 in the sorted list: 2.5 + 0.75 × (4.0 − 2.5)).

c5 (explain): the difference between a trimmed and a winsorized mean, and why skating uses one. Must contain: both limit the pull of extreme values; trimmed drops a set share of observations at each end, winsorized replaces them with the nearest retained values; with the top and bottom marks dropped, no single judge's extreme mark can move the score.

days.module: LM5 Statistical Characteristics of Asset Returns
days.title: Dispersion: variance, SD and downside risk
days.concept: Variance and standard deviation measure how far returns typically stray from their mean (the sample version divides by n − 1), the coefficient of variation scales that risk per unit of mean return, and target downside deviation counts only the shortfalls below a chosen target.
los: Range; mean absolute deviation MAD = Σ|X_i − X̄|/n
Sample variance s² = Σ(X_i − X̄)²/(n − 1); sample SD s = √s²
Population variance σ² = Σ(X_i − μ)²/N
Coefficient of variation CV = s/X̄
Target downside deviation s_Target = √[Σ_(X_i ≤ B)(X_i − B)²/(n − 1)]

calculator.task: Six annual returns: Sx and σx from 1-V statistics, the CV, then the target downside deviation for a target B = 0% by hand
calculator.ba: 2ND DATA, 2ND STAT 1-V: x̄, Sx (sample), σx (population); chain arithmetic for downside deviation
calculator.ti: 1-Var Stats L1: x̄, Sx, σx; list arithmetic for the squared shortfalls

memorize.back: s² = Σ (X_i − X̄)² / (n − 1)
σ² = Σ (X_i − μ)² / N
MAD = Σ |X_i − X̄| / n
CV = s / X̄ (risk per unit of mean return)
s_Target = √[ Σ_(X_i ≤ B) (X_i − B)² / (n − 1) ] — sum over observations at or below the target B, divide by n − 1 using all n

traps: Dividing by n when the sample variance is asked
Reading σx (population) instead of Sx (sample) on either calculator
In downside deviation, dividing by the number of below-target observations instead of n − 1
Reporting variance in %² as if it were a percentage

story_idea.candidate: Around 1950 Lt. Gilbert S. Daniels, a young physical anthropologist working at the Air Force's Aero Medical Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio, checked how many of 4,063 measured pilots were 'approximately average' on ten body dimensions used in cockpit design. Height alone left 1,055; adding chest circumference left 302, sleeve length 143, crotch height 73, torso circumference 28 — and by the tenth dimension none. He published 'The "Average Man"?' in December 1952. (Replaces the Trial of the Pyx idea.)
story_idea.why: Every average in the cockpit was a perfectly good number. Why did a cockpit built to the average pilot fit nobody — and what number was missing?

days.headline_hint: The Air Force measured 4,063 pilots to design for the average one. Not a single pilot was average.

story.title: The pilot who wasn't there
story.hook: Around 1950 Lieutenant Gilbert S. Daniels, a young physical anthropologist at the Air Force's Aero Medical Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio, had body measurements for 4,063 pilots. Cockpits were built to fit the 'average' pilot, so he asked how many pilots actually were average. He took ten dimensions that matter in a cockpit, such as height, chest circumference and sleeve length, and kept only the men within a narrow 'approximately average' band on each. Height alone left 1,055; adding chest circumference left 302; sleeve length, 143; crotch height, 73; torso circumference, 28 — and by the tenth dimension, nobody. He published the result in December 1952 under the title 'The "Average Man"?'.
story.puzzle: The average height, the average chest and the average reach were all perfectly good numbers. Why did a cockpit built to them fit no one — and what number was missing?
story.payoff: The missing number is the spread. On height alone only 1,055 of the 4,063 pilots — 26% — fell inside Daniels's 'average' band, because real people scatter widely around the mean, and each extra dimension cut the group again. Variance and standard deviation measure that scatter: the typical distance of an observation from its mean. Returns behave the same way. Today's fund averages 5% a year, yet no year came closer than 2 points to 5%: its sample standard deviation of 13.18% says a typical year misses the average by about 13 points, and its downside deviation of 6.45% measures only the shortfalls below 0%. An average return, like the average pilot, describes almost no actual year.
sources: Gilbert S. Daniels, 'The "Average Man"?', Aero Medical Laboratory technical note, Wright Air Development Center, Wright-Patterson AFB, Ohio, December 1952 (DTIC AD0010203): https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/tr/pdf/AD0010203.pdf

Full text (OCR) of the same report — 4,063 men; 1,055 after stature, 302 after chest circumference, 143 after sleeve length, 73 after crotch height, 28 after torso circumference: https://archive.org/stream/DTIC_AD0010203/DTIC_AD0010203_djvu.txt

Punya Mishra, 'Opinion: Gilbert Daniels, the gardener who changed our world', Arizona State University (retelling of the 4,063-pilot study and its ten dimensions): https://education.asu.edu/about/news/opinion-gilbert-daniels-gardener-who-changed-our-world

University of Minnesota, 'A contemporary investigation into anthropometric dimensions and a…' (re-applies Daniels's method to modern data): https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/a-contemporary-investigation-into-anthropometric-dimensions-and-a/

worked_example.problem: Five annual returns: 6%, −2%, 10%, 3%, 8%. Find the range, the mean absolute deviation, the sample variance and standard deviation (and the population versions), the coefficient of variation, and the target downside deviation for a target B = 4%.
steps: Downside deviation, B = 4%: returns at or below 4% are −2 (−2 − 4 = −6) and 3 (3 − 4 = −1); (36 + 1)/(5 − 1) = 9.25; √9.25 = 3.0414%

walkthrough.problem: A fund's six annual returns: 14%, −8%, 22%, 3%, −12%, 11%. Find the mean and the sample and population standard deviations with 1-V statistics, the coefficient of variation, and then the target downside deviation for B = 0% by hand.

check_plan: c1 (num, 1-V): five annual returns 11%, −6%, 15%, 2%, −4% — mean 3.60%, Sx = 9.1815% (σx = 8.2122% is the trap). Ask Sx as a percent to two decimals (tolerance 0.01). Hint: new data; read Sx, not σx.

c2 (mc, why): why does the sample variance divide by n − 1 rather than n? Right: the deviations are measured from the sample's own mean, which sits closer to the data than the true mean does, so Σ(X − X̄)² runs too small; dividing by n − 1 corrects it (one degree of freedom is used up by X̄). Distractors: 'to add a safety margin, since risk should be overstated'; 'because the first observation has no deviation from itself'.

c3 (num, twist — target downside deviation with B = 3% on c1's returns): returns at or below 3%: −6, 2, −4 → (−9)² + (−1)² + (−7)² = 131; 131/(5 − 1) = 32.75; s_Target = 5.7228% (dividing by the 3 shortfalls instead gives 6.6081% — the trap).

c4 (mc, exam): the sample standard deviation of 8%, −4%, 12% and 0%? A 6.32% (divided by n: the population SD); B 7.30% (correct: √(160/3)); C 53.33% (the sample variance, in %², reported as if it were the SD).

c5 (explain): what a fund's standard deviation of returns tells you, and how the target downside deviation differs. Must contain: the typical distance of returns from their mean (squared so signs cannot cancel, then square-rooted back to %); the sample version divides by n − 1; downside deviation counts only returns at or below the target B (still dividing by n − 1), so upside surprises are not counted as risk.

days.module: LM5 Statistical Characteristics of Asset Returns
days.title: Covariance and correlation
days.concept: Covariance measures whether two return series move together, and correlation rescales it to lie between −1 and +1 (r = s_XY/(s_X s_Y)) so that the strength of the co-movement can be compared across pairs.
los: Sample covariance s_XY = Σ(X_i − X̄)(Y_i − Ȳ)/(n − 1)
Correlation r_XY = s_XY/(s_X s_Y), −1 ≤ r ≤ +1
BA II Plus has no covariance key: s_XY = r × Sx × Sy from LIN statistics
Scatter plots; limits: outliers, nonlinearity, spurious correlation; correlation ≠ causation

Spearman rank correlation r_s = 1 − 6Σd_i²/[n(n² − 1)], computed on ranks so outliers and nonlinear but monotonic relations matter less (2027 coverage uncertain — insurance; its significance test is on Day 50)

calculator.task: Five years of stock and bond index returns: r, Sx and Sy from two-variable statistics, then the sample covariance r × Sx × Sy
calculator.ba: 2ND DATA (X = stocks, Y = bonds), 2ND STAT, 2ND SET to LIN: Sx, Sy, r
calculator.ti: First time only: 2nd 0 (CATALOG) DiagnosticOn ENTER ENTER so r is shown. Then 2-Var Stats L1,L2 for Sx and Sy, and 8:LinReg(a+bx) L1,L2 for r (2-Var Stats does not show r)

memorize.back: s_XY = Σ (X_i − X̄)(Y_i − Ȳ) / (n − 1)
r_XY = s_XY / (s_X × s_Y)

memorize.front: Covariance from correlation (BA II Plus route)
memorize.back: s_XY = r × s_X × s_Y
−1 ≤ r ≤ +1; 0 means no LINEAR relation, not no relation
r_s = 1 − 6 Σ d_i² / [n (n² − 1)], d_i = difference between the two ranks of observation i

traps: Mixing population SDs (σx) with a sample covariance
Reading a zero correlation as 'no relationship' when the relation is nonlinear
Treating a correlation as proof of causation (spurious correlation)
Comparing covariances across pairs with different volatilities (use correlation)

story_idea.candidate: On 13 September 2022 a hotter-than-expected inflation report (consumer prices up 8.3% on a year earlier) sent the S&P 500 down 4.32%, its worst day since June 2020, while the two-year Treasury yield jumped from about 3.57% to 3.74% — stocks and bonds fell together. For the year the S&P 500 lost 18.11% including dividends and the Bloomberg US Aggregate 13.01%, the only year in the Aggregate's history in which both fell by more than 10%.
story_idea.why: Bonds are supposed to rise when stocks fall. How do you measure whether two assets really move against each other, and what changed in 2022?

days.headline_hint: On 13 Sept 2022 stocks fell 4.3% and bonds fell with them. That year the 60/40 cushion vanished.

story.title: The year the cushion failed
story.hook: On the morning of Tuesday 13 September 2022 the US government reported that consumer prices were 8.3% higher than a year earlier, more than forecast. By the close the S&P 500 had fallen 4.32%, its worst day since June 2020, and bonds offered no shelter: the two-year Treasury yield jumped from about 3.57% to 3.74%, which meant bond prices fell too. The whole year went the same way. The S&P 500 lost 18.11% including dividends and the Bloomberg US Aggregate bond index lost 13.01% — the only year in the Aggregate's history in which both fell by more than 10%.
story.puzzle: The classic 60/40 portfolio rests on the idea that bonds rise when stocks fall. How do you measure whether two assets really move against each other — and what does that number say about the years leading up to 2022?
story.payoff: Covariance and correlation measure exactly that. Take 2018–2022, today's walkthrough: the S&P 500 returned −4.38%, 31.49%, 18.40%, 28.71% and −18.11%, the Aggregate 0.01%, 8.72%, 7.51%, −1.54% and −13.01%. Their sample covariance is +146.29 (%²) and their correlation +0.78: in those years the two mostly moved the same way, good years together and bad years together. A positive correlation means bonds tend to fall when stocks fall, so they cushion a stock-market drop less; 2022 was the extreme case, when bonds fell hard too and a 60/40 mix of the two lost about 0.6 × 18.11 + 0.4 × 13.01 = 16.07%. Five annual returns are a small sample, so the number describes those years; it is not a law.

YCharts, Bloomberg US Aggregate total return by year (2018 0.01%, 2019 8.72%, 2020 7.51%, 2021 −1.54%, 2022 −13.01%): https://ycharts.com/indices/%5EBBUSATR
S&P 500 total return by year: upmyinterest.com (2018 −4.38%, 2019 31.49%, 2020 18.40%): https://www.upmyinterest.com/sp500/ ; maisretorno.com (2021 28.71%): https://maisretorno.com/indice/sp500-tr

worked_example.problem: Four years of returns (%): stock fund X = 10, −5, 15, 0; bond fund Y = 2, 6, 1, 3. By hand, find the sample covariance, both sample standard deviations and the correlation; then the Spearman rank correlation.
steps: r = −18.3333/(9.1287 × 2.1602) = −0.9297: a strong negative linear relation
Spearman: ranks (1 = highest) X 2, 4, 1, 3 and Y 3, 1, 4, 2; d = −1, +3, −3, +1; Σd² = 20; r_s = 1 − 6 × 20/[4 × (16 − 1)] = 1 − 120/60 = −1: the rankings are exactly reversed

walkthrough.problem: S&P 500 total returns (X) and Bloomberg US Aggregate returns (Y), 2018–2022 (%): X = −4.38, 31.49, 18.40, 28.71, −18.11; Y = 0.01, 8.72, 7.51, −1.54, −13.01. Find Sx, Sy and r with two-variable statistics, then the sample covariance r × Sx × Sy.
walkthrough.display_ti: 2-Var Stats L1,L2: x̄=11.2220, Sx=21.6329, ȳ=.3380, Sy=8.7106; LinReg(a+bx) L1,L2: r=.7763; r*Sx*Sy (VARS 5:Statistics) → 146.2914

check_plan: c1 (num, LIN): five years X = 12, −3, 7, 20, −6 and Y = 4, 6, 3, −2, 7 — Sx = 10.7005, Sy = 3.5071, r = −0.9260; covariance = r × Sx × Sy = −34.75 (%²). Ask the covariance to two decimals (tolerance 0.01). Hint: new data; store r, Sx and Sy before multiplying.

c2 (mc, why): why compare pairs of assets by correlation rather than covariance? Right: covariance is in %² and grows with each asset's volatility; dividing by s_X × s_Y strips out the units and the scale, leaving a number between −1 and +1. Distractors: 'covariance cannot be negative' (it can); 'correlation uses the population formula and covariance the sample formula' (both can be sample statistics).

story_idea.candidate: In 1654 Blaise Pascal took up the 'problem of points', probably put to him by the Chevalier de Méré: how to split the stakes of a game stopped before anyone has won. In his letter to Pierre de Fermat of 29 July 1654 he works a game to three wins with 32 pistoles staked by each player: at 2–1 the leader should take 48 and the other 16 (Pacioli's 1494 rule of splitting by rounds won would have given about 42.67).
story_idea.why: If a game is interrupted with one player ahead, what is each player's share 'worth' — and how do you value outcomes that never happened?

days.headline_hint: In 1654 Pascal had to split a gambling pot for rounds never played. His answer founded probability.

story.title: Pascal, Fermat and the unfinished game
story.hook: In the summer of 1654 Blaise Pascal, in Paris, was trading letters with Pierre de Fermat in Toulouse about a gambling puzzle that had probably been put to Pascal by the Chevalier de Méré. Two equally skilled players each stake 32 pistoles, the first to win three rounds to take all 64 — but they have to stop early. The old answer, printed by Luca Pacioli in 1494, was to split the money in proportion to rounds already won. In his letter of 29 July 1654 Pascal gave a different answer: if one player leads two rounds to one, he should take 48 pistoles and the other 16.
story.puzzle: Pacioli's rule would give the leader two-thirds of 64, about 42.67 pistoles. Pascal said 48. Where does 48 come from — how do you put a value on rounds that were never played?
story.payoff: Pascal valued the game by what could happen next — the total probability rule for expected value. At 2–1 the next round goes one of two equally likely ways. If the leader wins it (probability ½) he has three wins and takes all 64; if he loses (½) the score is 2–2, an even game worth 32 to each. His share is ½ × 64 + ½ × 32 = 48, his opponent's 16. The same rule chains backwards: at 2–0 the leader's share is ½ × 64 + ½ × 48 = 56, and at 1–0 it is ½ × 56 + ½ × 32 = 44 — exactly the 44 pistoles Pascal gives in the same letter. A share of an unfinished game is the expected value of all the ways it could finish.
sources: Pascal to Fermat, 29 July 1654, English translation (University of York, history of statistics pages): https://www.york.ac.uk/depts/maths/histstat/pascal.htm
