story_idea.candidate: On 9 November 1999, at Chester Crown Court, the solicitor Sally Clark was convicted by a 10–2 majority of murdering her two baby sons after the paediatrician Sir Roy Meadow told the jury the chance of two cot deaths in such a family was about 1 in 73 million (1 in 8,543, squared). The Royal Statistical Society said in October 2001 that the figure had no statistical basis; her convictions were quashed on a second appeal in January 2003. Ray Hill (2004) estimated double cot death at about 4.5 to 9 times as likely as double murder.
story_idea.why: A 1-in-73-million coincidence sounds like proof of guilt. What is the right question to ask — and how does new evidence properly change a probability?

days.headline_hint: '1 in 73 million' helped convict Sally Clark of murder. Bayes' formula shows it answered the wrong question.

story.title: Sally Clark and the 1-in-73-million figure
story.hook: On 9 November 1999, at Chester Crown Court in England, the solicitor Sally Clark was convicted by a 10–2 majority of murdering her two baby sons, who had died suddenly in infancy. The paediatrician Sir Roy Meadow had told the jury that the chance of two cot deaths (sudden infant death syndrome, SIDS) in a family like hers was about 1 in 73 million: he had taken 1 in 8,543 for one such death and squared it. In October 2001 the Royal Statistical Society said publicly that the figure had 'no statistical basis', and in January 2002 it wrote to the Lord Chancellor that 'the calculation leading to 1 in 73 million is false'. Her convictions were quashed on a second appeal in January 2003, after she had spent about three years in prison.
story.puzzle: If the innocent explanation has a 1-in-73-million chance, isn't guilt all but certain? What question should the jury have been asking — and how should the evidence of two deaths change a probability?
story.payoff: Two errors. First, squaring (8,543² = 72,982,849) treats the deaths as independent, but a family that has lost one baby to SIDS is more likely to lose another: the mathematician Ray Hill later put that dependency factor at about 5 to 10. Second — the error Bayes' formula catches — 1 in 73 million is P(two deaths | innocent), not P(innocent | two deaths). Bayes puts the evidence in the denominator: P(two deaths) adds up every way two deaths can happen, and the double murder of babies is also extraordinarily rare. What matters is the ratio of the two explanations. Hill estimated double SIDS at roughly 4.5 to 9 times as likely as double murder, so on the deaths alone P(guilty | two deaths) = 1/(1 + 9) = 10% to 1/(1 + 4.5) = 18% — the opposite of the impression the jury was given. (Statistics alone cannot settle guilt, which rests on the medical and other evidence; the point is that the figure the jury heard answered the wrong question.)

days.headline_hint: Paul the octopus picked 8 World Cup winners out of 8. The binomial formula says how surprised to be.

story.title: Paul the octopus, 8 for 8
story.hook: Before each of Germany's seven matches at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, keepers at the Sea Life aquarium in Oberhausen, Germany, lowered two boxes into the tank of an octopus named Paul, each holding food and marked with one team's flag; the box he opened first was his 'pick'. He chose Germany to beat Australia, Ghana, England, Argentina and Uruguay, chose Serbia the day Germany lost to Serbia, and chose Spain for the semi-final that Germany lost to Spain. Then he picked Spain over the Netherlands for the final on 11 July 2010, and Spain won. Paul died that October, aged about two, with a perfect World Cup record: eight correct calls out of eight.
story.puzzle: Eight right in a row. Was Paul psychic — and if he was only guessing, how surprised should we be?
story.payoff: Treat each pick as a coin flip: n = 8 trials, p = 0.5. The binomial formula gives P(8 of 8) = 8C8 × 0.5⁸ = 1/256 = 0.39%: rare for one guesser. But Paul was far from the only animal, pundit or fan making picks, and nobody writes about the ones who failed. If 100 guessers each called the same eight matches by independent coin flips, the chance that at least one goes eight for eight is 1 − (255/256)¹⁰⁰ = 32.4%. Even 6 or more right out of 8 has probability (28 + 8 + 1)/256 = 14.45% for a pure guesser. A streak picked out after the fact is weak evidence of skill — the same trap as judging a fund manager by one lucky run.

days.module: LM6 Statistical Distributions for Financial Asset Prices and Returns
days.title: The normal curve and fat tails
days.concept: In a normal distribution the probability of an outcome depends only on how many standard deviations it lies from the mean, z = (X − μ)/σ, while real returns' skewness and excess kurtosis make extreme moves far more likely than the normal curve says.
los: Standardizing: z = (X − μ)/σ
Confidence bands: about 68% within ±1σ, 90% within ±1.645σ, 95% within ±1.96σ, 99% within ±2.58σ
Probabilities with normalcdf/invNorm (TI-84) or a z-table (exam, BA II Plus)
Skewness (an LM5 outcome, revisited here): positive skew → mean > median > mode; negative skew → mean < median < mode
Kurtosis (LM5): normal = 3; excess kurtosis = kurtosis − 3; leptokurtic = fat tails
Value at risk as a left-tail percentile (describe only)

calculator.task: Daily index returns with mean 0.05% and SD 1%: the z-score of a −22.6% day, P(return < −2%), and the return with only a 5% chance of being beaten on the downside
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic for z; then the z-table / memorized critical values (the BA II Plus has no distribution functions)
calculator.ti: 2nd VARS (DISTR) 2:normalcdf(lower, upper, μ, σ) and 3:invNorm(area, μ, σ); −1E99 for −∞

memorize.back: z = (X − μ) / σ
Positive skew (long right tail): mean > median > mode; negative skew (long left tail): mean < median < mode
Excess kurtosis = sample kurtosis − 3; > 0 (leptokurtic) means fatter tails than the normal
The minimum loss expected over a period a given small % of the time (e.g. on the worst 5% of days): a left-tail percentile of returns

traps: Using 1.96 for a one-tailed 5% test (it is 1.645)
Dividing by the variance instead of the standard deviation in z
Getting the mean–median order backwards for skewed data
Calling kurtosis of 3 'fat-tailed' (3 is normal; excess kurtosis is 0)

story_idea.candidate: On Monday 19 October 1987 the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 508 points, or 22.6%, from 2,246.74 to 1,738.74 — still its largest one-day percentage drop — on NYSE volume of about 604 million shares, roughly three times normal; the selling began in Asian markets.
story_idea.why: If daily returns were normal with a typical daily SD of about 1%, how many standard deviations was that day — and what does its happening at all tell you about the normal curve?

days.headline_hint: On 19 October 1987 the Dow fell 22.6% in a day. Under a normal curve, that was a 22-sigma day.

story.title: Black Monday, 1987
story.hook: On Friday 16 October 1987 the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 108.35 points, or 4.6%, to 2,246.74. On Monday 19 October the selling began in Asian markets, moved through Europe and reached New York. By the close the Dow had lost 508 points, or 22.6%, finishing at 1,738.74, and about 604 million shares had changed hands on the New York Stock Exchange, roughly three times a normal day. It is still the largest one-day percentage fall in the Dow's history.
story.puzzle: Suppose daily returns follow a normal curve with a mean of 0.05% and a standard deviation of about 1%. How many standard deviations was that day — and what does it mean that it happened at all?
story.payoff: Standardize it: z = (X − μ)/σ = (−22.6 − 0.05)/1 = −22.65. On that normal curve, a day at least that bad has a probability of about 7 × 10⁻¹¹⁴ (log₁₀ = −113.2). At 252 trading days a year you would expect to wait about 6 × 10¹¹⁰ years for one — the universe is about 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years old. Yet it happened. The lesson is not that 1987 was impossible but that the normal curve is the wrong model for the tails: real daily returns have excess kurtosis (fat tails) and negative skewness, so huge falls come far more often than a bell curve says. The normal curve is a fair guide to ordinary days and a dangerous one to extreme ones.
sources: CNN Money, 'Remembering the worst day in Wall Street history', 19 Oct 2017 (Dow −508 points, −22.6%): https://money.cnn.com/2017/10/19/investing/romans-numeral-black-monday
CNBC, 'Remembering the Crash of '87': https://www.cnbc.com/amp/id/100104087

RBC Wealth Management, 'The crash of 1987 by the numbers' (Friday 16 Oct close 2,246.74 after −108.35 points, 4.6%; about 604 million NYSE shares; began in Asia): https://ca.rbcwealthmanagement.com/william.vastis/blog/1294862-The-crash-of-1987-by-the-numbers
Stanford University CS201 project page on the 1987 crash (close of 1,738.74): https://cs.stanford.edu/people/eroberts/cs201/projects/financial-transactions/hist_motiv1.htm

worked_example.problem: Annual returns on an equity portfolio are normal with mean 8% and standard deviation 16%. (a) P(return < 0)? (b) The interval holding 95% of one year's outcomes? (c) A sample of daily returns has mean 0.04%, median 0.07% and kurtosis 5.1 — describe its skew and its tails.
steps: (a) z = (0 − 8)/16 = −0.50; z-table: P(Z < −0.50) = 0.3085 — about a 30.85% chance of a loss
(c) The mean (0.04%) is below the median (0.07%): negative skew, a longer left tail of large losses
Excess kurtosis = 5.1 − 3 = 2.1 > 0: leptokurtic — fatter tails than the normal, so extreme days happen more often than a z-table implies
worked_example.answer: (a) 30.85%; (b) −23.36% to 39.36%; (c) negatively skewed, excess kurtosis 2.1 (fat tails)

walkthrough.problem: Suppose daily index returns are normal with mean 0.05% and standard deviation 1%. Find (a) the z-score of a −22.6% day, (b) P(return < −2%), and (c) the daily return with only a 5% chance of a worse day.

check_plan: c1 (num, normalcdf( or z-table): monthly returns normal with mean 0.8% and SD 4.5% — P(month < −10%): z = (−10 − 0.8)/4.5 = −2.40, P = 0.0082 = 0.82%. Ask as a percent to two decimals (tolerance 0.01). Hint: new μ, σ and cutoff; z comes out round, so the table works on the BA II Plus.

c2 (mc, why): why can one z-table serve every normal distribution? Right: subtracting μ and dividing by σ turns any normal variable into the standard normal (mean 0, SD 1), and its probabilities depend only on how many SDs a value lies from the mean. Distractors: 'all normal distributions have the same standard deviation'; 'z divides by the variance, which removes the units'.

c3 (num, twist — solve for σ): the 5% left-tail cutoff of a normally distributed return is −10% and the mean is 1% → σ = (1 − (−10))/1.645 = 6.6869% (the exact z 1.6449 gives 6.6875%; tolerance 0.01).

c4 (mc, exam): annual returns normal with mean 7% and SD 15% — the interval holding 95% of outcomes? A −17.68% to 31.68% (1.645: the 90% band); B −31.70% to 45.70% (2.58: the 99% band); C −22.40% to 36.40% (correct: 7 ± 1.96 × 15).

c5 (explain): why Black Monday is evidence of fat tails. Must contain: under the normal model a −22σ day has essentially zero probability; it happened, so real returns have more extreme outcomes than the normal (excess kurtosis > 0, leptokurtic), often with negative skew; normal-based risk measures such as VaR understate tail risk.

days.module: LM9 Simulation of Financial Asset Prices and Returns
days.title: Lognormal prices and Monte Carlo simulation
days.concept: If continuously compounded returns are normal, prices are lognormal — never negative and skewed right — and Monte Carlo simulation draws many random returns from such a model to build the whole distribution of outcomes when no formula is handy.
los: Continuously compounded return r = ln(P_1/P_0) = ln(1 + HPR); multi-period r_(0,T) = sum of one-period log returns
Lognormal prices: P_T = P_0 e^(r_(0,T)) (LM6)
Monte Carlo steps: specify the model and distributions, draw random values, compute the outcome, repeat many times, summarize
Generating normal draws from uniform random numbers (inverse transform)
Historical simulation (sample actual past returns) and bootstrap resampling (random draws with replacement from the sample) vs Monte Carlo; strengths and limits
Lognormal moments (insurance): if ln P_T ~ N(μ, σ²), mean of P_T = e^(μ + σ²/2), above its median e^μ

calculator.task: Convert a 3-day price path to daily log returns and add them; then simulate one day of a price at 100 whose log return is μ + σz with μ = 0.05%, σ = 2% and z = 1.2816 (a 90th-percentile draw): P_1 = 100 × e^(μ + σz)
calculator.ba: LN and 2ND eˣ with STO/RCL; chain arithmetic
calculator.ti: LN( and e^( on the home screen; invNorm(rand) to draw a random z (rand is MATH ► PRB 1:rand)

memorize.front: Continuously compounded return over a period
memorize.back: r_cc = ln(P_1 / P_0) = ln(1 + HPR)

memorize.front: Price from a continuously compounded return

memorize.back: If ln(P_T) is normal, P_T is lognormal: bounded below by 0 and skewed right
Draw random samples WITH replacement from the observed data to simulate the sampling distribution

memorize.front: Monte Carlo simulation, step by step
memorize.back: Specify the model and the distribution of each random input → draw random values → compute the outcome → repeat many times → summarize the distribution of outcomes

traps: Adding simple returns across periods instead of log returns
Believing a lognormal price can go negative

Confusing Monte Carlo simulation (draws from an assumed distribution) with historical simulation and bootstrap resampling (both use the actual past returns; the bootstrap resamples them at random, with replacement)

story_idea.candidate: In 1946 the Polish-American mathematician Stanisław Ulam, recovering from an illness, wondered what the chance was that a game of Canfield solitaire would come out. Unable to work it out with combinatorics, he realised it would be easier to play many games and count — an idea he and John von Neumann turned into the Monte Carlo method at Los Alamos.
story_idea.why: When an outcome depends on so many random steps that no formula can handle it, how can you still find its probability?

days.headline_hint: A sick mathematician's 1946 solitaire game gave finance its way to simulate prices

story.title: Ulam's solitaire problem
story.hook: In 1946 the mathematician Stanisław Ulam, convalescing from an illness, passed the time with Canfield solitaire and asked what the chance was that a game laid out with 52 cards would come out. He spent a long time on pure combinatorics — a deck can be ordered in 52! ≈ 8.07 × 10^67 ways — and got nowhere. Then he wondered whether it would be more practical to lay the game out, say, one hundred times and simply count the successes. He took the idea to John von Neumann; at Los Alamos it became a way to model neutron diffusion in nuclear weapons, their colleague Nicholas Metropolis named it after the Monte Carlo casino, and Metropolis and Ulam published 'The Monte Carlo Method' in 1949.
story.puzzle: When an outcome depends on so many random steps that no formula can handle it — the cards in a deal, or a stock's price after a year of daily moves — how can you still find its probability?
story.payoff: Don't solve it: simulate it. Specify how each step is random — for a stock, a normal log return each period, so P_T = P_0 × e^(r_1 + … + r_T) is lognormal and can never fall below zero — draw random values, compute the outcome, repeat, and count. For a stock at 100 whose one-year log return is normal with mean 5% and SD 20%, the exact chance of ending below 80 is 8.60% (z = (ln 0.8 − 0.05)/0.20 = −1.3657). A seeded run of 100 simulated years gave 15% — Ulam's 100 deals would have been just as rough — while 10,000 runs gave 8.92%, closing in on the true value. Monte Carlo buys precision with repetitions, which is why it waited for computers.
sources: Roger Eckhardt, 'Stan Ulam, John von Neumann, and the Monte Carlo Method', Los Alamos Science no. 15 (1987), p. 131, quoting Ulam's own account of the 1946 Canfield solitaire question and laying it out 'one hundred times' (https://www.osti.gov/home/osti-collections-monte-carlo-methods.html; text at https://faculty.washington.edu/seattle/MC-2008/ulam-1.pdf)
Nicholas Metropolis and S. Ulam, 'The Monte Carlo Method', Journal of the American Statistical Association 44 (1949) — first open paper; Metropolis credited with the name
Los Alamos National Laboratory history 'Safety in numbers' (archived at webarchive.library.unt.edu) — Ulam idled by illness, playing solitaire

worked_example.problem: A stock closes at 50.00, then 55.00, then 49.50. Find each day's simple and continuously compounded (log) return, the 2-day log return, and show which kind of return adds up correctly.
steps: Simple returns: 55/50 − 1 = +10.00%; 49.50/55 − 1 = −10.00%. Adding them says 0%, but the price fell: 49.50/50 − 1 = −1.00%.
Check: ln(49.50/50) = ln 0.99 = −0.0101 — the same, because ln(a × b) = ln a + ln b.
worked_example.answer: 2-day continuously compounded return = −0.0101 (−1.01%); log returns add, simple returns do not.

walkthrough.problem: Part 1: closing prices are 80.00, 82.40, 79.93 and 81.50. Compute each day's log return, store and add them, and confirm the sum equals ln(81.50/80.00). Part 2: simulate tomorrow's price for a stock at 100 whose daily log return is μ + σz with μ = 0.05%, σ = 2% and the random draw z = 1.2816 (a 90th-percentile day): P_1 = 100 × e^(0.0005 + 0.02 × 1.2816). On the TI-84, invNorm(rand) gives a fresh random z each time you press ENTER — that is Monte Carlo by hand.

intermediate.what: invNorm(0.90) on the TI-84 (BA II Plus: the z is given in the question)

walkthrough.note: Typing z = 1.2816 gives 102.6476; using the TI-84's full invNorm(0.90) = 1.2815516 gives 102.6475 — say which on the page.

check_plan: c1 (num, calculator): a stock at 60 with daily log-return mean 0.04% and SD 1.5% gets the draw z = −1.6449 (a 5th-percentile day); simulated price P_1 = 60 × e^(0.0004 + 0.015 × (−1.6449)) = 58.56 (to the cent; tol 0.01). Hint: change S0, μ, σ, z.

c2 (mc, why; right = A): Why can you add daily log returns to get the week's return? A) ln(P_2/P_0) = ln(P_2/P_1 × P_1/P_0) = ln(P_2/P_1) + ln(P_1/P_0) — the log of a product is the sum of the logs (right); B) log returns are small, so the error from adding is negligible (wrong: the identity is exact, not an approximation); C) log returns assume prices are normally distributed (wrong: additivity holds for any prices; normality is a modelling choice).

c3 (num, twist): a stock at 40 has daily log returns 0.012, −0.008, 0.015, −0.020, 0.006 over a week; the sum is 0.005, so the price at the end is 40 × e^0.005 = 40.20 (to the cent; tol 0.01); the week's holding-period return is e^0.005 − 1 = 0.5013%.

c4 (mc, exam; right = B): a stock goes 50 → 60 → 45; its 2-period continuously compounded return is closest to: A) −5.00% (added the simple returns +20% and −25%); B) −10.54% = ln(45/50) (right); C) −10.00% (gave the holding-period return, not the continuously compounded one).

c5 (explain): In two or three sentences, how would you use Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the chance a stock ends the year below 80, and how does bootstrap resampling differ? Must contain: (1) assume a distribution for the random input (e.g. normal log returns) and draw from it; (2) compute the ending price for each draw, repeat thousands of times and count the share below 80; (3) bootstrap resampling instead draws at random, with replacement, from the actual past returns, so no distribution is assumed but only returns seen in the sample can appear (historical simulation also relies on the actual past record).
days.verification_note: Fact-check 2026-11-06 (WebSearch): Ulam's own account, as quoted by Eckhardt (Los Alamos Science 15, 1987), confirmed by search: the 1946 question came while he was convalescing from an illness (encephalitis, January 1946) and playing solitaire - 'what are the chances that a Canfield solitaire laid out with 52 cards will come out successfully?' - and his idea to 'lay it out say one hundred times and simply observe and count the number of successful plays' (the exact wording found quoted from George Dyson's Turing's Cathedral); later in 1946 he described the idea to von Neumann; Metropolis suggested the name; first open paper Metropolis & Ulam 1949. 52! = 8.0658e67 and the lognormal figures (z = -1.3657, 8.60%) recomputed in Python. The 15% (100 runs) and 8.92% (10,000 runs) come from the seeded simulation (random.Random(1946), gauss draws), not from a source. faculty.washington.edu and the LANL archive could not be fetched from this session, so the primary PDF was not read directly.

days.module: LM8 The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio
days.title: Two-asset portfolio return and risk
days.concept: A portfolio's expected return is the weighted average of its assets' expected returns, but its variance also depends on how the assets move together: σ_p² = w_1²σ_1² + w_2²σ_2² + 2w_1w_2ρ_12σ_1σ_2.
los: E(R_p) = Σ w_i E(R_i)
σ_p² = w_1²σ_1² + w_2²σ_2² + 2w_1w_2 Cov_12, with Cov_12 = ρ_12 σ_1 σ_2
Covariance from a joint probability table: Cov = Σ P(R_A, R_B)[R_A − E(R_A)][R_B − E(R_B)]
σ_p < weighted-average σ whenever ρ < 1

calculator.task: A 60/40 stock–bond portfolio with expected returns 9% and 4%, σ = 20% and 8% and ρ = 0.2: E(R_p) and σ_p, working in percent units (the covariance from a joint probability table is the worked example)
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL, x² and √x

memorize.back: E(R_p) = Σ w_i × E(R_i)
σ_p² = w_1²σ_1² + w_2²σ_2² + 2 w_1 w_2 ρ_12 σ_1 σ_2

memorize.front: Covariance from a joint probability table
memorize.back: Cov(R_A, R_B) = Σ P(R_A,i, R_B,j) × [R_A,i − E(R_A)] × [R_B,j − E(R_B)]

traps: Averaging the SDs as if the correlation were +1
Forgetting the 2 in the cross term
Mixing percentages and decimals when squaring (20² vs 0.20²)

story_idea.candidate: In March 1952 Harry Markowitz, a 24-year-old graduate student at the University of Chicago, published 'Portfolio Selection' in the Journal of Finance, arguing that investors should judge a portfolio by its overall risk and return, not stock by stock. The idea won him a share of the 1990 Nobel Prize in economics.
story_idea.why: Two risky assets put together can be less risky than either one alone. How can adding a risky asset reduce risk?

days.headline_hint: In 1952 a 24-year-old proved that adding a risky asset can make a portfolio safer

story.title: Markowitz in the library
story.hook: As a University of Chicago graduate student, Harry Markowitz was reading John Burr Williams's The Theory of Investment Value (1938) in the library when the problem struck him: Williams valued a stock as the present value of its expected dividends, but if investors cared only about expected value, they would put everything in the single best stock — and nobody does. In March 1952, aged 24, Markowitz published 'Portfolio Selection' in the Journal of Finance (pages 77–91), arguing that a portfolio must be judged by its overall expected return and variance. He later recalled Milton Friedman objecting at his dissertation defence that the work was not economics; in 1990 it won him a share of the Nobel prize in economics with Merton Miller and William Sharpe.
story.puzzle: If only expected return mattered you would own one stock. So what does diversifying buy — and how can adding a risky asset make a portfolio less risky?
story.payoff: Expected returns simply average, but risk does not: σ_p² = w_1²σ_1² + w_2²σ_2² + 2w_1w_2ρσ_1σ_2. For a 60/40 mix of stocks (expected 9%, σ = 20%) and bonds (expected 4%, σ = 8%) with ρ = 0.2, the expected return is the weighted average, 7.0%, but σ_p = 13.02% — well below the weighted-average SD of 15.2%. The gap exists because ρ < 1: the two don't always fall together, so part of their risk cancels. Markowitz's whole insight lives in that cross term.
sources: Harry Markowitz, 'Portfolio Selection', Journal of Finance 7(1), March 1952, pp. 77–91

Harry M. Markowitz, Autobiography, Les Prix Nobel 1990 (Nobel Foundation, nobelprize.org) — the idea came one afternoon in the library while reading John Burr Williams's Theory of Investment Value; an investor interested only in expected value would hold a single security; and his Nobel lecture 'Foundations of Portfolio Theory' (7 December 1990), which opens with Milton Friedman's objection at his dissertation defence that portfolio theory was not economics
Timothy Taylor, 'Harry Markowitz (1927–2023): Bringing Finance into Economics', Conversable Economist, 26 June 2023 — Friedman's 'not economics' remark as Markowitz recalled it
Wikipedia, 'Harry Markowitz' — born 24 August 1927; 1990 Nobel Memorial Prize shared with Merton Miller and William Sharpe

worked_example.problem: Stocks (A) and bonds (B) in three states — boom (probability 0.3): A = 25%, B = 4%; normal (0.5): A = 10%, B = 8%; recession (0.2): A = −15%, B = 5%. Find the covariance and correlation of their returns (work in percent).
worked_example.answer: Cov = −3.90 (%²), i.e. −0.00039; ρ = −0.1534 — the two tend to move in opposite directions, a little.

walkthrough.problem: A portfolio holds 60% stocks (E(R) = 9%, σ = 20%) and 40% bonds (E(R) = 4%, σ = 8%) with ρ = 0.2. Find E(R_p) and σ_p, working in percent units (variances in %²).

check_plan: c1 (num, calculator): 70% equities (E = 8%, σ = 18%) and 30% bonds (E = 3.5%, σ = 6%), ρ = −0.1: σ_p = 12.55% (percent to two decimals; tol 0.01); E(R_p) = 6.65% can be the hint's check. Hint: same keystrokes, new weights, SDs and ρ.

c2 (mc, why; right = B): two assets each with σ = 15%, held 50/50. When is σ_p exactly 15%? A) when ρ = 0 (wrong: that gives 10.61%); B) only when ρ = +1 — then σ_p is the weighted average of the SDs, 15%; any ρ below +1 makes it smaller (right); C) when ρ = −1 (wrong: that gives 0%).

c3 (num, twist — solve for ρ): a 50/50 portfolio of assets with σ = 20% and 10% has σ_p = 12%. Implied correlation: 0.0144 = 0.25 × 0.04 + 0.25 × 0.01 + 2 × 0.25 × ρ × 0.20 × 0.10 → ρ = 0.19 (two decimals; tol 0.005).

c4 (mc, exam; right = C): 40% in an asset with σ = 25% and 60% in one with σ = 10%, ρ = 0.3. σ_p is closest to: A) 16.00% (weighted average of SDs — assumes ρ = +1); B) 12.41% (forgot the 2 in the cross term); C) 13.11% (right).

c5 (explain): Why can adding a risky asset lower a portfolio's risk? Must contain: (1) portfolio variance includes a covariance (cross) term, not just each asset's own variance; (2) when ρ < +1 that term is smaller than for perfectly correlated assets, so σ_p is below the weighted-average σ; (3) the assets' ups and downs partly offset, while the expected return is still the weighted average.
days.verification_note: Fact-check 2026-11-06 (WebSearch): the library episode while reading John Burr Williams's The Theory of Investment Value (1938) is confirmed by Encyclopedia.com (citing Markowitz's Nobel Foundation autobiography) and a UC San Diego release ('an afternoon at the library'). Born 24 August 1927, so 24 in March 1952; 'Portfolio Selection', Journal of Finance 7(1), March 1952, pp. 77-91; 1990 prize shared with Merton Miller and William Sharpe (standard record, Wikipedia). Friedman's 'not economics' objection at the dissertation defence was found only in secondary sources in this pass (a Wikipedia mirror; Taylor 2023); it is from Markowitz's own Nobel lecture, which says he assumed Friedman was only half serious - the text attributes it to Markowitz's recollection, which is accurate. nobelprize.org could not be fetched. Portfolio numbers (7.0%, 13.02%, 15.2%) recomputed in Python.

days.module: LM8 The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio
days.title: Minimum-variance portfolio and efficient frontier
days.concept: The lower the correlation, the bigger the diversification benefit: the two-asset weight that minimizes variance is w_1 = (σ_2² − Cov_12)/(σ_1² + σ_2² − 2Cov_12), and the efficient frontier is the upper part of the minimum-variance frontier, above the global minimum-variance portfolio.
los: Minimum-variance weight w_1* = (σ_2² − Cov)/(σ_1² + σ_2² − 2Cov)
ρ = +1: no diversification (straight line); ρ = −1: a zero-risk portfolio with w_1 = σ_2/(σ_1 + σ_2)
Minimum-variance frontier, global minimum-variance portfolio, efficient frontier
Diversification benefit shrinks as correlations rise in a crisis

calculator.task: Two strategies with σ = 10% and 12%: the minimum-variance weights and the minimum σ_p at ρ = 0.1 and again at ρ = 0.7 (LTCM's models allowed for correlations up to about 0.3; in 1998 they reached about 0.7)
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.back: The part of the minimum-variance frontier above (higher return than) the global minimum-variance portfolio
Whenever ρ < +1; the lower ρ, the larger the reduction

traps: Treating the global minimum-variance portfolio as the best portfolio for every investor
Using ρ where the formula needs Cov (or the reverse)
Assuming diversification still works when correlations jump toward +1

story_idea.candidate: Long-Term Capital Management, the hedge fund run by John Meriwether with Nobel laureates Robert Merton and Myron Scholes, lost about $4.6 billion in under four months in 1998 after Russia defaulted on 17 August; trades that had seemed unrelated all lost at once, and the New York Fed organised a $3.6 billion rescue on 23 September.
story_idea.why: LTCM held dozens of 'independent' bets. Why did diversification fail just when it was needed — and how much does risk depend on correlation?

days.headline_hint: LTCM lost $553 million in one day in 1998 when its 'unrelated' bets all fell together

story.title: LTCM's worst day
story.hook: Long-Term Capital Management, the Greenwich, Connecticut hedge fund run by John Meriwether with the Nobel laureates Robert Merton and Myron Scholes among its partners, spread leveraged bets across markets around the world. By one later account, the correlations between its positions had historically been 10% or less, and its risk models allowed for up to 30%. After Russia devalued the rouble and defaulted on its domestic debt on 17 August 1998, investors everywhere fled to safety and correlations rose to about 70%. On Friday 21 August LTCM lost $553 million in a day — about 15% of its capital — when, by Roger Lowenstein's account, its models had judged a one-day loss above $35 million unlikely. On 23 September a group of 14 banks and securities firms, convened by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, agreed to put in about $3.6 billion; in under four months the fund had lost about $4.6 billion.
story.puzzle: LTCM's bets looked unrelated, so their risks should have largely cancelled. Why did diversification fail just when it was needed — and how much does a portfolio's risk depend on the correlation?
story.payoff: Find the lowest-risk mix of two strategies with σ = 10% and 12%. At ρ = 0.1 the minimum-variance portfolio puts 60% in the first and has σ_p = 8.05% — less than either alone. At ρ = 0.7 the best you can do is 9.83%, barely below the safer strategy's 10%. Spread across 100 equal bets of σ = 10% (the same formula, σ_p = σ√(1/n + (1 − 1/n)ρ)), the portfolio's σ is 3.30% at ρ = 0.1, 5.54% at 0.3 and 8.38% at 0.7 — two and a half times what a 0.1 correlation promised. Diversification is a bet on correlations, and in a crisis they jump toward +1.
sources: US General Accounting Office, 'Long-Term Capital Management: Regulators Need to Focus Greater Attention on Systemic Risk' (GGD-00-3, 1999) and letter GGD-00-67R (2000), https://www.gao.gov/assets/ggd-00-67r.pdf — 14 banks and securities firms agreed on 23 September 1998 to recapitalize LTCM, contributing about $3.6 billion on 28 September; Federal Reserve History, 'Near Failure of Long-Term Capital Management' — fourteen banks and brokerage firms put up $3.625 billion for 90% of the fund

Wikipedia, 'Long-Term Capital Management' — about $4.6 billion lost in less than four months in 1998; Russian default and devaluation of 17 August 1998

worked_example.problem: Asset 1 has σ = 20%, asset 2 has σ = 30%. Find the minimum-variance weight on asset 1 and the minimum σ_p when (a) ρ = 0 and (b) ρ = −1.
steps: σ_p = |0.60 × 20% − 0.40 × 30%| = |12% − 12%| = 0%: the two risks cancel exactly.

walkthrough.problem: Strategy 1 has σ = 10%, strategy 2 has σ = 12%. Find the minimum-variance weight w_1* and the minimum σ_p at ρ = 0.1; then repeat at ρ = 0.7. Work in percent units (variances in %²).
walkthrough.note: Why not ρ = 0.9 (the draft plan): then w_1* = 1.2857 > 1, a short position in strategy 2, which happens whenever ρ > σ_1/σ_2 = 0.8333 and is not taught yet.

check_plan: c1 (num, calculator): σ_1 = 15%, σ_2 = 25%, ρ = 0.2: w_1* = 0.7857 and minimum σ_p = 13.89% (ask for σ_p in percent to two decimals; tol 0.01). Hint: Cov = 0.2 × 15 × 25 = 75 (%²).

c2 (mc, why; right = C): as ρ falls from +1 to −1, what happens to the lowest attainable σ_p? A) nothing — the weights adjust so risk stays the same (wrong); B) it falls but can never reach zero because both assets are risky (wrong: at ρ = −1 it is exactly zero); C) it falls steadily, reaching zero at ρ = −1, because the cross term 2w_1w_2Cov turns negative and can cancel the two variances (right).

c3 (num, twist — ρ = −1): σ_1 = 12% (E = 6%) and σ_2 = 18% (E = 10%), ρ = −1. Zero-risk weight w_1 = 18/(12 + 18) = 0.60; that riskless portfolio's expected return = 0.6 × 6% + 0.4 × 10% = 7.60% (percent to two decimals; tol 0.01).

c4 (mc, exam; right = A): σ_1 = 20%, σ_2 = 15%, ρ = 0.25. The minimum-variance weight in asset 1 is closest to: A) 0.3158 (right: Cov = 0.0075); B) 0.4286 (used the ρ = −1 shortcut σ_2/(σ_1 + σ_2)); C) 0.3600 (ignored the covariance: σ_2²/(σ_1² + σ_2²)).

c5 (explain): What is the efficient frontier, and why isn't the global minimum-variance portfolio the best choice for everyone? Must contain: (1) the minimum-variance frontier gives the lowest σ for each expected return; (2) the efficient frontier is its upper part, above the global minimum-variance portfolio — points below it are dominated (same risk, less return); (3) which efficient portfolio is best depends on the investor's risk aversion (Day 34).

days.module: LM8 The Return and Risk of a Financial Portfolio
days.title: Risk aversion, utility and the capital allocation line
days.concept: A risk-averse investor scores a portfolio by utility U = E(r) − ½Aσ², and mixing the risk-free asset with the best risky portfolio gives a straight capital allocation line on which the highest-utility point depends on A; when the risky portfolio is the market, that line is the capital market line.
los: Utility U = E(r) − 0.5 A σ² (returns and SD as decimals)
Risk-averse (A > 0), risk-neutral (A = 0), risk-seeking (A < 0); indifference curves
Capital allocation line: E(R_p) = R_f + [(E(R_i) − R_f)/σ_i] σ_p; σ_p = w σ_i
Optimal weight in the risky portfolio: w* = [E(R_i) − R_f]/(A σ_i²)
CML with the market portfolio; lending (w < 1) and borrowing (w > 1) portfolios
Roy's safety-first ratio SFRatio = [E(R_p) − R_L]/σ_p (2027 coverage uncertain — insurance)

calculator.task: Risk aversion A = 4, risky portfolio with 10% expected return and 20% SD, R_f = 3%: the utility of holding all T-bills, all risky, and the optimal mix; the optimal risky weight w*; the CAL return at σ = 12%; and the safety-first ratio for a 2% threshold
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.back: U = E(r) − ½ × A × σ² (decimals)

memorize.front: Capital allocation line (and CML with the market portfolio)
memorize.back: E(R_p) = R_f + [(E(R_i) − R_f) / σ_i] × σ_p

memorize.back: w* = [E(R_i) − R_f] / (A × σ_i²)
SFRatio = [E(R_p) − R_L] / σ_p; choose the portfolio with the highest ratio

story_idea.candidate: In 1738 the Swiss mathematician Daniel Bernoulli published his answer to the 'St. Petersburg paradox' (posed by his cousin Nicolaus in 1713): a coin-flipping game with an infinite expected payout that nobody would pay more than a few ducats to play. His explanation — people value wealth by its usefulness to them, not its amount — is the root of utility theory.
story_idea.why: If a gamble's expected payoff is infinite, why will no sensible person pay much to play it, and how can you put a number on how much risk someone will accept?

days.headline_hint: A game with an infinite expected payout that nobody will pay 20 ducats for — and how to price risk

story.title: The game worth infinity that no one will buy
story.hook: On 9 September 1713 Nicolaus Bernoulli sent the French mathematician Pierre Rémond de Montmort a puzzle about a game with an infinite expected payout. His cousin Daniel Bernoulli published its best-known version in a paper written in St Petersburg and printed there in 1738: Peter tosses a coin until it lands heads and pays Paul 1 ducat if heads comes on the first toss, 2 on the second, 4 on the third, doubling each time. Every possible toss adds ½ ducat to the expected value — ½ × 1 + ¼ × 2 + ⅛ × 4 + … — so the expected payout is infinite. Yet, Daniel wrote, 'any fairly reasonable man would sell his chance, with great pleasure, for twenty ducats.'
story.puzzle: If a gamble's expected payoff is infinite, why won't a sensible person pay much to play it — and how can you put a number on how much risk someone will accept?
story.payoff: Bernoulli's answer: people value money by its usefulness to them, which grows more slowly than the amount (he used the logarithm). Scored that way, the chance to play is worth a sure 2 ducats to a player with nothing else and — by our computation with his rule — about 3.04 ducats to someone who already owns 10, 4.39 to someone who owns 100 and 5.97 to someone who owns 1,000: nowhere near twenty. The CFA's U = E(r) − ½Aσ² is the same idea for portfolios: U is the sure return the investor would swap the risky portfolio for. With A = 4, a portfolio with a 10% expected return and a 20% SD scores U = 0.10 − ½ × 4 × 0.20² = 2.00% — worse than a 3% T-bill — while the best mix on the capital allocation line, 43.75% in the risky portfolio, scores 4.53%.
sources: Daniel Bernoulli, 'Specimen theoriae novae de mensura sortis', Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Imperialis Petropolitanae 5 (1738); English translation by Louise Sommer, 'Exposition of a New Theory on the Measurement of Risk', Econometrica 22(1), January 1954, pp. 23–36 (the coin game and the 'twenty ducats' remark)

Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The St. Petersburg Paradox' (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/paradox-stpetersburg/) — Nicolaus Bernoulli's letter to Montmort of 9 September 1713 (originally framed with a die), Cramer's 1728 letter, Daniel's 1738 article
Wikipedia, 'St. Petersburg paradox' — quotes the 'twenty ducats' passage

worked_example.problem: An investor with A = 3 chooses between portfolio X (E = 8%, σ = 10%) and portfolio Y (E = 12%, σ = 20%). Which does she prefer, which would a risk-neutral investor prefer, and which wins on Roy's safety-first criterion with a 3% threshold?
steps: Risk-neutral (A = 0): U = E(r), so Y (12%) wins — risk no longer costs anything.
Safety-first, R_L = 3%: SF_X = (8 − 3)/10 = 0.50; SF_Y = (12 − 3)/20 = 0.45. X has the higher ratio, so X minimizes the chance of earning less than 3% (if returns are normal).

walkthrough.problem: A = 4; risky portfolio E(R) = 10%, σ = 20%; R_f = 3%. (1) Utility of all T-bills and of all risky. (2) The optimal weight w* = (E − R_f)/(Aσ²) and the utility of that mix. (3) The expected return on the CAL at σ_p = 12%. (4) Roy's safety-first ratio for the risky portfolio with R_L = 2%. Decimals throughout.

intermediate.what: U at w* = E − 0.5 × 4 × σ² at the w* mix

check_plan: c1 (num, calculator): A = 3, risky portfolio E = 9%, σ = 18%, R_f = 2.5%: w* = 0.065/(3 × 0.18²) = 0.6687 (four decimals; tol 0.0001; also accept 66.87% if asked in percent). Hint: change A, E, σ and R_f.

c2 (mc, why; right = A): an investor's A rises from 2 to 6 (same risky portfolio as the walkthrough). What happens to w*? A) it falls to one-third (0.8750 → 0.2917) because w* is inversely proportional to A (right); B) it rises, because A measures risk tolerance (wrong: larger A = more risk-averse); C) it stays the same, because everyone holds the same risky portfolio on the CML (wrong: they hold the same risky portfolio, but in different proportions).

c3 (num, twist — target return): with R_f = 3%, risky E = 10%, σ = 20%, what weight in the risky portfolio gives an expected return of 12%? w = (12 − 3)/(10 − 3) = 1.2857 (four decimals; tol 0.0001) — above 1, a borrowing portfolio with σ_p = 25.71%.
c4 (mc, exam; right = C): A = 2, E(r) = 11%, σ = 25%. The investor's utility is closest to: A) −14.00% (used σ instead of σ²); B) −1.50% (dropped the ½); C) 4.75% (right).

c5 (explain): Why do investors with different risk aversion all hold the same risky portfolio on the CML, yet different portfolios overall? Must contain: (1) the CAL/CML is a straight line from R_f through the optimal risky (market) portfolio, the best risk–return trade-off available; (2) each investor picks a point on that line by mixing it with the risk-free asset, w* = (E − R_f)/(Aσ²); (3) high A → more lending (w < 1), low A → borrowing (w > 1).
days.verification_note: Fact-check 2026-11-06 (WebSearch): Nicolaus Bernoulli's letter to Montmort of 9 September 1713 (framed with a die rolled until a six appears) and Cramer's 1728 letter are confirmed by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry (via search; plato.stanford.edu could not be fetched). Daniel's paper: Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Imperialis Petropolitanae, Tomus V, St Petersburg 1738, pp. 175-192; Sommer's translation, Econometrica 22(1), January 1954, pp. 23-36, whose game wording (one ducat on the first throw, two on the second, four on the third) is confirmed. The 'twenty ducats' sentence is the Sommer translation as quoted by Wikipedia; not re-read in the primary text. The 2, 3.04, 4.39 and 5.97 ducat figures are our computation with Bernoulli's log rule (recomputed in Python) and are labelled as such: they are certainty equivalents of a free ticket for wealth 0, 10, 100 and 1,000, which matches the text's 'worth a sure ... ducats' wording. (The issues file's 2.88 / 4.36 / 5.97 are the different quantity 'most a player would pay out of that wealth'; if a page uses that wording it must use those numbers.) Search did not confirm whether Bernoulli printed his own figures for 10, 100 and 1,000 ducats, so none are attributed to him. Utility numbers (2.00%, 43.75%, 4.53%) recomputed.

days.module: The Term Structure of Interest Rates: Spot, Par, and Forward Curves
days.title: Spot rates and bootstrapping
days.concept: Each cash flow should be discounted at the zero-coupon (spot) rate for its own date, and spot rates can be bootstrapped one maturity at a time from the yields of par bonds.
los: Price with spot rates: PV = PMT/(1 + Z_1)^1 + PMT/(1 + Z_2)^2 + … + (PMT + FV)/(1 + Z_N)^N
Discount factors DF_t = 1/(1 + Z_t)^t
Bootstrapping: solve 100 = c × DF_1 + … + (100 + c) × DF_N for the newest DF, then Z_N
The YTM as a single 'average' of the spot rates; zero-coupon (STRIPS) prices

Bootstrapping step for an N-year par bond with coupon c (per 100)

story_idea.candidate: In 1982 Merrill Lynch created 'TIGRs' (Treasury Investment Growth Receipts) by buying US Treasury bonds and selling separate claims to each coupon and the principal; in February 1985 the Treasury launched its own STRIPS program, letting each payment of a bond trade as a zero-coupon security.
story_idea.why: If a bond can be cut into a dozen separate payments, each with its own market price, what rate should each payment be discounted at?

days.headline_hint: In 1982 Wall Street cut Treasury bonds into pieces — and each piece needed its own interest rate

story.title: Cutting a Treasury bond into zeros
story.hook: In 1982 Merrill Lynch began buying long-term US Treasury bonds, placing them in a trust and selling separate receipts for each coupon and for the principal — Treasury Investment Growth Receipts, or TIGRs. Salomon Brothers answered with CATS. In January 1985 the Treasury announced its own program, STRIPS (Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities), and from February 1985 each coupon and the principal of eligible bonds could trade on their own as zero-coupon securities. That month a Christian Science Monitor headline called the private receipts 'the Treasury's feline menagerie' — fine for retirement accounts, not for short-term investing.
story.puzzle: Once a bond is cut into separate payments, each with its own market price, what rate should each payment be discounted at — and what does that say about the price of the whole bond?
story.payoff: Each strip is a zero-coupon bond, so its price reveals the spot rate for its own date. With 1-, 2- and 3-year par yields of 2.0%, 2.6% and 3.0%, bootstrapping gives spot rates of 2.0000%, 2.6078% and 3.0183%. A 3-year 6% bond is just three zeros: 5.8824 + 5.6989 + 96.9533 = 108.5346 per 100. If the bond sold for less than the sum of its strips, dealers would buy it, strip it and sell the pieces; if for more, they would buy the strips and put it back together. So the bond must equal the sum of its spot-discounted parts — and its YTM, 2.9837%, is just the single rate that reproduces that price.
sources: Christian Science Monitor, 'Beware the Treasury's feline menagerie. CATS and TIGRS fine for IRAs -- but they're not for short-term investing', 20 February 1985 (https://www.csmonitor.com/1985/0220/fwise70.html; headline and URL confirmed by search, date from the URL; the article text could not be fetched)

SuperMoney encyclopedia, 'Treasury Investment Growth Receipts (TIGRs)' — Merrill Lynch created special-purpose vehicles in 1982 to buy Treasuries and issue zero-coupon receipts; Salomon Brothers' CATS
Miles Livingston, 'Stripping of U.S. Treasury Securities' (University of Florida working paper) — private stripping began in 1982

TreasuryDirect, STRIPS history/timeline (https://www.treasurydirect.gov/research-center/timeline/strips); UN ESCWA glossary — program announced 15 January 1985; Benzinga, 'This Day In Market History: US Treasury Begins Issuing STRIPS' (15 February 1985)

steps: A 2-year par bond pays 5 and 105 and is priced at 100: 100 = 5 × DF_1 + 105 × DF_2.
Check: 5/1.04 + 105/1.050252² = 100.0000. The 2-year spot rate is above the 2-year par yield because the first coupon was discounted at the lower 1-year rate.

walkthrough.problem: Par yields (annual coupons) are 2.0% (1 year), 2.6% (2 years) and 3.0% (3 years). Bootstrap DF_1, DF_2, DF_3 and Z_2, Z_3; price a 3-year 6% annual-coupon bond at the spot rates; then find its YTM with TVM (N = 3, PV = −price, PMT = 6, FV = 100, CPT I/Y).

c2 (mc, why; right = B): with an upward-sloping curve, why is the 2-year spot rate above the 2-year par yield? A) spot rates include a liquidity premium that par yields do not (wrong); B) the par bond's first coupon is discounted at the lower 1-year rate, so the final payment must be discounted at a higher rate for the price to stay at 100 (right); C) par yields are semiannual and spot rates annual (wrong: both are on the same basis here).

c3 (num, twist — bootstrapping from a non-par bond): Z_1 = 2%; a 2-year 4% annual-coupon bond trades at 101.50. DF_2 = (101.50 − 4/1.02)/104 = 0.938254, so Z_2 = 3.2380% (percent to three decimals; tol 0.001).

c4 (mc, exam; right = A): spot rates are 2%, 3% and 4% for 1–3 years. A 3-year 5% annual-coupon bond is worth closest to: A) 102.96 (right); B) 102.78 (discounted every cash flow at the 3-year spot rate); C) 105.66 (discounted every cash flow at the average spot rate, 3%).

c5 (explain): Why should each cash flow of a bond be discounted at its own spot rate, and what is the YTM then? Must contain: (1) each payment is a separate zero-coupon claim with its own price and rate; (2) no-arbitrage — stripping and reconstitution force the bond's price to equal the sum of its strips' values; (3) the YTM is the single rate that gives that same price, a blend of the spot rates, not a rate for any one date.

days.module: The Term Structure of Interest Rates: Spot, Par, and Forward Curves
days.title: Forward rates and par rates
days.concept: An implied forward rate is the future one-period rate that makes investing for two periods equal to investing for one and rolling over — (1 + Z_2)² = (1 + Z_1)(1 + IFR_(1,1)) — and the par rate is the coupon that prices a bond at par given the spot curve.
los: Forward rate model: (1 + Z_A)^A × (1 + IFR_(A,B−A))^(B−A) = (1 + Z_B)^B
1y1y, 2y1y, 1y2y notation
Par rate: c_N = (1 − DF_N)/Σ DF_t
Upward-sloping spot curve → forward curve above it; inverted → below
No-arbitrage (LM4): cash-flow additivity gives implied forward rates

story_idea.candidate: On 22 March 2019 the yield on 3-month US Treasury bills rose above the 10-year Treasury yield for the first time since 2007. days.headline_hint: On 22 March 2019 the yield curve inverted — what bond prices were saying about rates to come

story.title: The day the curve inverted
story.hook: On Friday 22 March 2019 the yield on 3-month US Treasury bills, 2.46%, closed above the 10-year Treasury yield, 2.44% — the first such inversion since 2007. Campbell Harvey's 1986 University of Chicago dissertation had found that an inverted curve — 3-month yields above longer ones — came before US recessions; he has stressed that the signal counts only if it lasts about a quarter, and by the end of June 2019 it had. The Federal Reserve, which had been raising rates, cut them on 31 July 2019 for the first time since 2008, and cut twice more before the year was out. The NBER later dated the peak of the US expansion, and the start of a recession, to February 2020.
story.puzzle: When short-term rates sit above long-term rates, what is the bond market implying about where short-term rates will go?
story.payoff: A long spot rate is a geometric average of today's short rate and the forward rates that follow: (1 + Z_2)² = (1 + Z_1)(1 + 1y1y). If Z_2 is below Z_1, the forward rate must be lower still. On an inverted curve with Z_1 = 5% and Z_2 = 4.5%, the 1y1y forward is 1.045²/1.05 − 1 = 4.0024% — below both spot rates: the market is pricing short rates to fall. That is what happened in 2019. On 22 March 2019 itself the 1-year Treasury yielded 2.45% and the 2-year 2.31%; treated loosely as spot rates, they imply a 1y1y forward of about 2.17%, below the Fed's 2.25–2.50% target range at the time. (Forward rates are not pure forecasts — they can include risk premiums — but an inversion says rate cuts are being priced in.)
sources: Federal Reserve Board H.15 constant-maturity yields via FRED (DGS3MO, DGS1, DGS2, DGS10), fetched 2026-11-06 — 22 March 2019: 3-month 2.46%, 1-year 2.45%, 2-year 2.31%, 10-year 2.44%; the last earlier close with the 3-month above the 10-year was 27 August 2007. FRED DFEDTARU — target range upper bound 2.50% until the cuts effective 1 August, 19 September and 31 October 2019; no cut between 16 December 2008 and July 2019

DQYDJ, 'A Crucial Part of the Yield Curve Inverted 3/22/2019. What Does it Mean?' (https://dqydj.com/yield-curve-inversion-10year-3month/) and Pathstone Quarterly Flash Report, March 2019 — 10-year 2.44% vs 3-month 2.46% at the close

Research Affiliates, 'The Inverted Yield Curve' (interview with Campbell Harvey, 2019; https://www.researchaffiliates.com/documents/the-inverted-yield-curve.pdf) — last 10-year/3-month inversion in 2007; Harvey's 1986 dissertation; inversion must last about a quarter
Axios and Marketplace, 31 July 2019 — Fed cuts its target range to 2.00–2.25%, first cut since 2008; Dallas Morning News, 30 October 2019 — third cut of 2019 (after July and September), to 1.50–1.75%
NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee announcement, 8 June 2020 (https://www.nber.org/news/business-cycle-dating-committee-announcement-june-8-2020) — monthly peak in February 2020

c2 (mc, why; right = C): on an upward-sloping spot curve, why is the 1y1y forward above the 2-year spot rate? A) forward rates add a term premium on top of spot rates (wrong: the result follows from arithmetic alone); B) because forward rates are arithmetic averages of spot rates (wrong: it is the spot rate that is a geometric average of the short rate and the forwards); C) (1 + Z_2)² = (1 + Z_1)(1 + 1y1y) makes Z_2 a geometric average of Z_1 and the forward — for the average to sit above Z_1, the forward must sit above the average (right).
c3 (num, twist — build a spot rate from forwards): Z_1 = 3%, 1y1y = 4%, 2y1y = 5%: Z_3 = (1.03 × 1.04 × 1.05)^(1/3) − 1 = 3.9968% (percent to three decimals; tol 0.001).

c4 (mc, exam; right = B): Z_1 = 2.0%, Z_2 = 2.8%, Z_3 = 3.3%. The 1y2y rate is closest to: A) 4.31% (computed the 2y1y instead — one year starting in two); B) 3.96% (right: [(1.033³/1.02)^(1/2) − 1]); C) 8.07% (forgot the square root for a 2-year forward).

c5 (explain): What does an inverted spot curve say about forward rates, and why? Must contain: (1) a longer spot rate is a geometric average of the shorter spot rate and the forward rates after it; (2) if the longer rate is lower, the forwards must be lower than the spot rates; (3) so the market is pricing lower future short rates (with the caveat that forwards can contain risk premiums).

days.module: Yield and Yield Spread Measures for Fixed-Rate Bonds
days.title: Yield spreads and matrix pricing
days.concept: A yield spread is the extra yield over a benchmark — the G-spread over a government bond, the I-spread over swaps, the Z-spread added to every spot rate — and matrix pricing borrows the yields of comparable bonds to price one that rarely trades; for a floating-rate note the spread is a margin over the market reference rate — the quoted margin sets the coupon, the discount margin sets the required return.
los: G-spread = bond YTM − interpolated government YTM; I-spread = bond YTM − swap rate
Z-spread: PV = Σ CF_t/(1 + z_t + Z)^t
Option-adjusted spread = Z-spread − option value (concept)
Matrix pricing: interpolate the yield of comparable bonds (same rating, maturity), then price with TVM
Floating-rate notes: quoted margin vs discount margin; FRN priced with coupon (MRR + QM)/m and discount rate (MRR + DM)/m

calculator.task: Interpolate a 4-year yield from comparable 3-year (4.10%) and 5-year (4.70%) bonds, price an illiquid 4-year 5% annual-coupon bond with TVM, and find its G-spread over a 3.20% interpolated government yield
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic for the interpolation; TVM CPT PV
calculator.ti: Home screen for the interpolation; TVM Solver

memorize.back: G-spread = YTM of the bond − YTM of the (interpolated) government bond of the same maturity
The constant Z that makes PV = Σ CF_t / (1 + z_t + Z)^t equal the bond's price (z_t = the benchmark spot rate for date t — Day 36's Z_t)
OAS = Z-spread − option value (in bps): callable OAS < Z-spread
y = y_short + (T − T_short)/(T_long − T_short) × (y_long − y_short)
Coupon = (MRR + quoted margin)/m × 100; discount rate = (MRR + discount margin)/m
I-spread = YTM of the bond − swap rate of the same maturity (in the same currency)

traps: Using an unmatched benchmark maturity without interpolating
Confusing the Z-spread (added to each spot rate) with the G-spread (a single YTM difference)
Discounting an FRN at the quoted margin instead of the discount margin

story_idea.candidate: In March 2020 the iShares investment-grade corporate bond ETF (LQD) traded at about a 5% discount to its reported net asset value, because many of the bonds it held had not traded and were valued by matrix-style 'evaluated' prices while credit spreads blew out.
story_idea.why: If a bond hasn't traded for days, what is it worth — and how do you price it from bonds that did trade?

days.headline_hint: On 12 March 2020 a corporate bond ETF traded 5% below its own bonds' value — whose price was right?

story.title: When the ETF said one thing and its bonds another
story.hook: On Thursday 12 March 2020, as the pandemic tore through markets, shares of the iShares iBoxx $ Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF (LQD) closed at a 5.0% discount to the fund's net asset value; in 2018 and 2019 it had never closed more than 1% away from its NAV. Sellers got about 95 cents for each dollar the fund said its bonds were worth. That NAV rested on 'evaluated' prices, which pricing services estimate for the many bonds that had not traded, largely from the yields of comparable bonds that had. The gap shrank to 0.19% the next day and was back near 5% on 19 March; after the Federal Reserve announced on 23 March that it would buy corporate bonds and bond ETFs, it flipped, by Bloomberg's account, to a premium of about 5% on 25 March.
story.puzzle: If a bond hasn't traded for days, what is it worth — and how do you price it from bonds that did trade?
story.payoff: That is matrix pricing: take the yields of comparable bonds (same credit quality, nearby maturities), interpolate to your bond's maturity, and discount its cash flows at that yield. With comparable 3-year and 5-year yields of 4.10% and 4.70%, a 4-year bond gets 4.40%, so a 4-year 5% bond is worth 102.1576; over a 3.20% government yield its G-spread is 120 bp. The method is only as fresh as its comparables. In March 2020 the ETF traded live while evaluated prices lagged: for a 10-year 4% bond priced at par, a 5% price gap means a yield of 4.6361% — the market was demanding about 64 bp more spread than the evaluated price assumed.
sources: InvestmentNews, 'Fixed-income ETFs caught in bond market's liquidity trap' (March 2020), and Bloomberg, 'Fixed-Income ETFs Are Trapped in Bond Market's Liquidity Crunch', 13 March 2020 — LQD closed at a 5.0% discount to NAV on Thursday 12 March 2020 and 0.19% the next day; in 2018 and 2019 it never closed at more than a 1% discount or premium (the 'largest since 2008' line in that coverage referred to an aggregate-bond ETF's 4.4% discount, not to LQD)
CNBC, 'There's a discrepancy happening in bond ETFs. Here's what's behind it', 17 March 2020 — NAVs built from evaluated price estimates

Bloomberg (via Bloomberg Law / InvestmentNews), 'Fed's Ability to Buy ETFs May Help Ensure It Never Needs To', April 2020 — LQD 5% below NAV on 19 March, 5% premium on 25 March, after the Fed's 23 March 2020 announcement

Must contain: (1) used for a bond that trades rarely or not at all; (2) take the yields of comparable bonds — same credit quality, similar maturity and coupon — and interpolate to the bond's maturity (or add a spread to a benchmark); (3) discount the bond's cash flows at that yield to get its price.

days.module: Yield-Based Bond Duration Measures and Properties
days.title: Macaulay and modified duration
days.concept: Macaulay duration is the PV-weighted average time to a bond's cash flows, and modified duration = MacDur/(1 + r) turns it into the approximate percentage price fall for a 1-percentage-point rise in yield; MacDur is also the horizon at which price and reinvestment risk offset.
los: MacDur = Σ t × [PV(CF_t)/PV]
ModDur = MacDur/(1 + r) (r = yield per period; divide by periods per year to annualize)
%ΔPV ≈ −AnnModDur × ΔYield
Duration gap = MacDur − investment horizon (positive gap → price risk dominates; negative → reinvestment risk)
Properties: longer maturity, lower coupon, lower yield → higher duration; a zero's MacDur = its maturity

calculator.task: A 3-year 5% annual-coupon bond at a 4% yield: the PV of each cash flow, the price, the PV-weighted MacDur, ModDur, and the estimated % price change for +50 bp

memorize.back: MacDur = Σ t × [CF_t/(1 + r)^t] / PV
ModDur = MacDur / (1 + r)
%ΔPV ≈ −AnnModDur × ΔYield
Duration gap = Macaulay duration − investment horizon

memorize.front: Macaulay duration of a zero-coupon bond
memorize.back: Equal to its time to maturity
Compute in periods with r/2, then divide by 2 for years; AnnModDur = MacDur(periods) / (1 + r/2) / 2

traps: Dividing by (1 + annual yield) for a semiannual bond instead of (1 + periodic yield), then forgetting to annualize
Dropping the minus sign in the price-change estimate
Using Macaulay duration directly as the price sensitivity

story_idea.candidate: In September 2017 Austria sold €3.5 billion of 100-year bonds with a 2.1% coupon, maturing in 2117. As yields fell, the bond's price more than doubled by late 2020 — then, as rates rose in 2022, it lost more than half its value.
story_idea.why: A government bond with almost no default risk halved in price. What property of a 100-year, low-coupon bond makes it so sensitive to interest rates?

days.headline_hint: Austria's 100-year bond moved 0.4% for every basis point — then lost more than two-thirds of its value

story.title: Austria's century bond
story.hook: In September 2017 Austria sold €3.5 billion of 100-year bonds — the first century bond a euro-zone government had sold publicly by syndication (Belgium and Ireland had placed small ones privately) — with a 2.1% annual coupon, maturing on 20 September 2117 and priced to yield about 2.11%. Investors put in more than €11 billion of orders. Bloomberg's Gadfly columnists pointed out that a one-basis-point move in yield would shift its price by about 43 cents per 100 of face value. As euro yields sank, by 2020 the bond traded at more than twice its face value; as they climbed from 2022 it slid, and in 2026 it has traded between about 54 and 61 in Milan — 58.75 on 24 April, about 57 in October.
story.puzzle: Austria's credit hardly changed, yet its bond lost more than two-thirds of its value from the peak. What makes a 100-year, low-coupon bond so sensitive to interest rates — and how do you measure that sensitivity?
story.payoff: Macaulay duration: the PV-weighted average time until you are paid. Most of the century bond's value sits in small coupons decades away, so at issue its MacDur was 42.4 years and its modified duration 42.4/1.02112 = 41.5: each basis point moves the price about 0.415%, close to the 43 cents Bloomberg cited. At a price of 200 the yield was about 0.69% and ModDur about 57, so the rise in rates that followed hit it with enormous force. Compare the walkthrough's 3-year 5% bond: MacDur 2.86, ModDur 2.75. (Duration alone would have predicted a 171% loss for the rise from 0.69% to 3.67% — the yield at the April 2026 price of 58.75 — which is impossible; the real fall was 71%. That gap is Day 41's convexity.)
sources: Bloomberg, 'Austria Offers Europe's First Benchmark-Sized Century Bonds', 12 September 2017 — orders above €11 billion

GlobalCapital, 'Austria smashes expectations with century bond' (September 2017), and Bloomberg, 12 September 2017 — priced at 50 bp over Austria's 30-year benchmark against initial guidance of about 60; a 2.112% re-offer yield was reported by an earlier check but could not be re-confirmed by search on 2026-11-06, so the text says 'about 2.11%'

Business Recorder (Reuters), 2017 — Austria placed a 3.5 billion euro 100-year note, the first euro-zone country to sell 100-year bonds publicly via syndication; Belgium and Ireland had sold century bonds only by private placement, for 50–100 million euros each

Marcus Ashworth and Mark Gilbert, Bloomberg Gadfly, 'Austria Boldly Goes Into the 22nd Century With New Bond', 12 September 2017 — a one-basis-point change in yield moves the price by 43 cents, or 0.43%

MoneyWeek, 'Why would anyone ever buy a 100-year bond?' (David Stevenson, 2020) — the 2017 century bond trades for more than twice its face value; Bloomberg, June 2020 — by then buyers paid about 60% more than the issue price

Borsa Italiana MOT listing for AT0000A1XML2 (2.1% 20/09/2117) — 2026 reference prices 60.17 (2 March), 58.75 (24 April) and 56.91 (20 July); official price 56.98 on 13 October 2026; 2026 range 53.58–61.16; gross yield about 3.8%

days.module: Yield-Based Bond Duration Measures and Properties
days.title: Approximate duration, money duration and PVBP
days.concept: Price sensitivity can be measured by repricing the bond at yields a little higher and lower — ApproxModDur = (PV_− − PV_+)/(2 × ΔYield × PV_0) — and money duration and the price value of a basis point turn that sensitivity into currency.
los: ApproxModDur = (PV_− − PV_+)/(2 × ΔYield × PV_0); ApproxMacDur = ApproxModDur × (1 + r)
Money duration = AnnModDur × PV_full (× position size); ΔPV ≈ −MoneyDur × ΔYield
PVBP = (PV_− − PV_+)/2 for a 1 bp change
Portfolio duration ≈ Σ w_i D_i with market-value weights
Unrealized losses on a bond portfolio from a rate rise

MoneyDur = AnnModDur × PV_full of the position; ΔPV ≈ −MoneyDur × ΔYield

memorize.back: PVBP = (PV_− − PV_+) / 2, with yields ±1 bp

story_idea.candidate: Silicon Valley Bank failed on 10 March 2023. It had put much of a deposit surge into long-dated Treasuries and mortgage bonds — about $91 billion held to maturity — and by the end of 2022 rising rates had left those securities with roughly $15 billion of unrealized losses, close to the bank's entire equity.
story_idea.why: No borrower defaulted on SVB's bonds, yet the bank was wiped out. How do you turn 'rates went up 4%' into dollars lost?

days.headline_hint: No borrower defaulted on SVB's bonds, yet rising rates erased $15 billion: money duration shows how

story.title: Silicon Valley Bank's $15 billion hole
story.hook: Silicon Valley Bank was closed by regulators on 10 March 2023, a day after depositors tried to pull $42 billion. During the deposit boom of 2020–21 it had put much of its cash into long-dated bonds, mostly government-agency mortgage-backed securities; at the end of 2022 it carried $91.3 billion of securities as 'held to maturity', at amortized cost (roughly what it had paid). Their fair value was $76.2 billion — an unrealized loss of about $15 billion, close to the bank's roughly $16 billion of equity. The Federal Reserve's review put that portfolio's weighted-average duration at 6.2 years.
story.puzzle: No issuer defaulted on SVB's bonds, yet rising rates nearly wiped out its equity. How do you turn 'rates went up' into dollars lost?
story.payoff: Money duration: AnnModDur × market value. Run it backwards first. Treat the 6.2 years as a modified duration and the $91.3 billion cost as the starting value: the $15.1 billion loss is 16.54% of it, which implies a rise in yields of about 16.54%/6.2 = 2.67 percentage points — close to the 5-year Treasury yield's climb from about 1.37% to 3.99% during 2022 (2.62 points, which the same arithmetic turns into about $14.8 billion). Then forwards: at its $76.2 billion market value the portfolio's money duration was 6.2 × $76.2 billion = $472.44 billion, so every further 1-point rise would cost about $4.72 billion and every basis point about $47.2 million — its PVBP. (A rough check: the bonds were bought at different times, and mortgage bonds' duration lengthens as rates rise.) No borrower defaulted; duration alone turned a rate chart into a hole in the balance sheet.
sources: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 'Review of the Federal Reserve's Supervision and Regulation of Silicon Valley Bank' (Michael Barr), 28 April 2023, section 'Evolution of Silicon Valley Bank' (https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2023-April-SVB-Evolution-of-Silicon-Valley-Bank.htm) — at 31 December 2022 the HTM portfolio had a weighted-average duration of 6.2 years and was mostly agency MBS with maturities of 10 years or more; deposit outflow of over $40 billion on 9 March 2023 (page checked 2026-11-05; it does not give the dollar amounts below)

SVB Financial Group, Form 10-K for 2022 (sec.gov, sivb-20221231.htm and XBRL R3) — HTM securities $91.321 billion at amortized cost, fair value $76.2 billion (unrealized loss about $15.1–15.2 billion depending on rounding); total SVBFG stockholders' equity $16.0 billion ($16.3 billion including noncontrolling interests); summarized by The Rational Walk, 'The Fall of Silicon Valley Bank', March 2023

CNBC, 'SVB customers tried to withdraw nearly all the bank's deposits over two days, Fed's Barr testifies', 28 March 2023, and Bloomberg, 'SVB Depositors, Investors Tried to Pull $42 Billion Thursday', 11 March 2023 (from a California regulator's filing) — $42 billion of attempted withdrawals on 9 March; bank closed 10 March 2023

days.module: Yield-Based Bond Convexity and Portfolio Properties
days.title: Convexity: correcting the duration estimate
days.concept: Duration draws a straight line through a curved price–yield relation; adding ½ × convexity × (ΔYield)² corrects the estimate, so with positive convexity gains are larger and losses smaller than duration alone predicts — and the error grows with the size of the yield move.
los: ApproxCon = (PV_− + PV_+ − 2PV_0)/[(ΔYield)² × PV_0]
%ΔPV ≈ −AnnModDur × ΔYield + ½ × AnnConvexity × (ΔYield)²
Money convexity
Properties: longer maturity, lower coupon, lower yield → more convexity
Large yield shocks: duration-only vs duration + convexity vs full repricing

calculator.ba: TVM repricing (three yields for ApproxModDur and ApproxCon, then the new yield); chain arithmetic

memorize.back: ApproxCon = (PV_− + PV_+ − 2 × PV_0) / [(ΔYield)² × PV_0]

memorize.back: %ΔPV ≈ −AnnModDur × ΔYield + ½ × AnnConvexity × (ΔYield)²

memorize.front: Money convexity and the currency price change
memorize.back: MoneyCon = AnnConvexity × PV_full; ΔPV ≈ −MoneyDur × ΔYield + ½ × MoneyCon × (ΔYield)²

memorize.front: Sign of the convexity adjustment for an option-free bond
memorize.back: Always positive (adds to the estimate for yield rises and falls)

memorize.front: What gives a bond more convexity?
memorize.back: Longer maturity, lower coupon, lower yield, and (for the same duration) more dispersed cash flows

Giving the convexity term a negative sign when yields rise
Using ΔYield in percent so (ΔYield)² is 10,000 times too big

story_idea.candidate: After the UK 'mini-budget' of 23 September 2022, the yield on 30-year gilts jumped from about 3.7% to above 5% in a few trading days, forcing pension funds using liability-driven investment strategies to sell, until the Bank of England stepped in on 28 September.
story_idea.why: For a move that large, how badly does a straight-line duration estimate misjudge the price of a long, low-coupon gilt — and in which direction?

days.headline_hint: When gilts broke in 2022, a straight-line duration estimate got the damage wrong. Convexity fixes it

story.title: The week that broke the gilt market
story.hook: On Friday 23 September 2022 the UK government's "mini-budget" of tax cuts set off a sell-off in long-dated government bonds (gilts). The 30-year gilt yield, between about 3.5% and 3.7% on the eve of the statement (sources differ), rose about 1.2 percentage points in three trading days and touched about 5.1% early on Wednesday 28 September. Pension funds using liability-driven investment (LDI) strategies faced collateral calls and had to sell gilts into the falling market, pushing yields higher still. That day the Bank of England announced emergency purchases of long-dated gilts, and the 30-year yield fell more than a full percentage point, closing near 3.9% by Reuters' figures.
story.puzzle: Take a stylized long gilt: 30 years to maturity, a 0.5% annual coupon. Start it at 3.7%, the top of that eve-of-statement range: its modified duration is about 25.4, so duration says a 1.4-point jump in yield, to the 5.1% peak, costs about 25.4 x 1.4 = 35.6% of its value. Is that right, and if not, does a straight-line estimate overstate or understate the damage?
story.payoff: Repricing at 5.1% gives 30.0857 per 100 against 42.5929 at 3.7%: a fall of 29.36%, not 35.63%. Duration overstated the loss by about 6.3 percentage points because the price-yield curve bends upward, away from duration's straight line. Adding 1/2 x ApproxCon x (ΔYield)^2 = 1/2 x 731.34 x 0.014^2 = +7.17% brings the estimate to -28.46%, about 0.9 points from the exact change. Run the move in reverse (yield down 1.4 points) and the bond gains 43.92%, more than duration's +35.63%: positive convexity means smaller losses and bigger gains than the straight line predicts, and the gap grows with the square of the move.
sources: AJ Bell, "Three years after the mini-Budget, why isn't the market panicking about higher gilt yields?" (2025): 30-year gilt yield rose 1.2 percentage points in three trading days, 22-27 September 2022 - https://www.ajbell.co.uk/group/news/three-years-after-mini-budget-why-isnt-market-panicking-about-higher-gilt-yields

story_idea.candidate: In 1908 William Sealy Gosset, a chemist at the Guinness brewery in Dublin, published 'The Probable Error of a Mean' in Biometrika under the pen name 'Student', because Guinness did not let staff publish under their own names. story_idea.why: When you can afford only four or five samples, how far can you trust their average — and why isn't the normal curve good enough?

days.headline_hint: The Guinness brewer who could not sign his own name, and why four samples need wider error bands

story.title: The brewer who published as "Student"
story.hook: William Sealy Gosset left Oxford in 1899 to join the Guinness brewery in Dublin. His trials of barley and hops could seldom afford more than a handful of samples, while the statistical methods of the day assumed large ones. Guinness sent him to study in Karl Pearson's biometric laboratory at University College London in 1906-07 (two terms, by one account), and in 1908 he published "The Probable Error of a Mean" in Pearson's journal Biometrika. Because Guinness did not let its staff publish under their own names (reportedly after an earlier employee had given away trade secrets), the paper appeared under the pen name "Student".
story.puzzle: With only four or five measurements, how far can you trust their average, and why does the normal curve's "plus or minus 1.96 standard errors" promise more precision than a tiny sample can deliver?
story.payoff: The sample mean wanders around the true mean with standard error s/√n, but with tiny n the estimate s is itself shaky, so the right reliability factor comes from Student's t distribution, which has fatter tails. For 95% confidence with n = 4 (3 degrees of freedom) it is 3.182, not 1.96: an interval 62% wider. With n = 10 it is 2.262; by n = 30 it is 2.045, close to the normal's 1.96. That was Gosset's answer: small samples are usable, provided the error bands are honestly wider.
sources: The Irish Times, "How a student of Guinness became 'the Faraday of statistics'" (2014): Gosset at the Guinness brewery, a year in Karl Pearson's laboratory at University College London, pen name because Guinness barred staff from publishing - https://www.irishtimes.com/news/science/how-a-student-of-guinness-became-the-faraday-of-statistics-1.1779032

days.title: Hypothesis tests: testing a mean
days.concept: A hypothesis test asks whether a sample result is too far from the null hypothesis to be chance: compute test statistic = (sample statistic − hypothesized value)/standard error, compare it with the critical value or read its p-value, and know the two ways the decision can be wrong.

Significance level α; Type I error (reject a true H_0, probability α); Type II error (fail to reject a false H_0, β); power = 1 − β
p-value: reject H_0 if p-value < α
Six-step process; statistical vs economic significance; link to confidence intervals

story_idea.candidate: At Rothamsted Experimental Station in England in the 1920s, the algae scientist Muriel Bristol said she could tell whether milk had been poured into a cup before the tea or after. story_idea.why: How many cups must she get right before 'lucky guessing' stops being a believable explanation?

days.headline_hint: Milk first or tea first? The 1-in-70 tea test that shows exactly how a p-value works

story.title: The lady tasting tea
story.hook: At Rothamsted Experimental Station in Hertfordshire, England, where Ronald Fisher worked from 1919 to 1933, the algae scientist Muriel Bristol claimed she could taste whether the milk or the tea had been poured into her cup first. The story goes, in the account of Fisher's daughter and biographer Joan Fisher Box, that a test was arranged there and then. William Roach, who was present and later married her, said she got more than enough cups right to prove her case; later retellings say she named every one. In 1935 Fisher made the episode the first worked example of his book The Design of Experiments: eight cups, four milk-first and four tea-first, served in random order, and she must pick out the four milk-first cups.
story.puzzle: If she were only guessing, how often would she pick all four milk-first cups correctly, and how many right answers should it take before "lucky guess" stops being a believable explanation?
story.payoff: Under the null hypothesis "she is guessing", every choice of 4 cups out of 8 is equally likely, and there are 8C4 = 70 of them (Day 29's counting rule). So P(all correct | guessing) = 1/70 = 0.0143: that is the p-value. It is below a 5% significance level, so "guessing" is rejected. Had she found only three of the four, the chance of doing at least that well by luck is (16 + 1)/70 = 0.2429, and "guessing" would survive. A t-test of a fund's mean return asks the same question: if the null were true, how likely is a result at least this extreme?
sources: Wikipedia, "Muriel Bristol": the tea-tasting test at Rothamsted; William Roach's account that she "divined correctly more than enough" cups "to prove her case"; later accounts that she identified all eight - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muriel_Bristol
R. A. Fisher, The Design of Experiments (Oliver and Boyd, 1935), chapter 2: the lady tasting tea; 70 ways to choose 4 cups of 8
CUNY lecture notes, "Hypothesis Testing: Background, Error Types" (Fisher at Rothamsted 1919-1933; 1/70 = 0.0143) - https://www.math.csi.cuny.edu/~mvj/MTH410-S23/lectures/L09.html

days.title: Comparing two means: pooled and paired
days.concept: To compare two groups, test the difference in means with a pooled-variance t-statistic when the samples are independent, but test the mean of the differences when observations come in matched pairs.
los: Pooled variance s_p² = [(n_1 − 1)s_1² + (n_2 − 1)s_2²]/(n_1 + n_2 − 2)
Paired comparisons: t = d̄/(s_d/√n), df = n − 1
When to use which: independent vs dependent samples; equal-variance assumption

t = (d̄ − μ_d0) / s_d̄, with s_d̄ = s_d / √n, df = n − 1 (usually μ_d0 = 0)
