story_idea.candidate: From 27 March 2015 to 1 March 2016 the NASA astronaut Scott Kelly spent 340 days aboard the International Space Station while his identical twin, the retired astronaut Mark Kelly, stayed on Earth. NASA's Twins Study, published in Science on 12 April 2019 (Francine Garrett-Bakelman and colleagues), compared the brothers' measurements before, during and after the flight.
story_idea.why: Why compare Scott with his own twin, and with himself before launch, rather than with a crowd of other people — and when should two sets of numbers be tested as matched pairs instead of as two independent groups?

days.headline_hint: One twin in orbit for 340 days, one on the ground: why matched pairs see what crowds hide

story.title: One twin in space, one on Earth
story.hook: On 27 March 2015 the NASA astronaut Scott Kelly launched to the International Space Station, where he stayed 340 days, returning on 1 March 2016 (both dates in US time; at the launch and landing sites in Kazakhstan it was already the next day). His identical twin, the retired astronaut Mark Kelly, stayed on Earth. NASA ran the same battery of tests on both brothers before, during and after the flight, and published the results in Science on 12 April 2019 (Francine Garrett-Bakelman and colleagues). Among the findings: Scott's telomeres lengthened in space and shortened again after he came home, and, by NASA's count, 91.3% of his gene expression returned to its preflight baseline within six months of landing.
story.puzzle: People differ enormously from one another. Why measure Scott against his own twin and against his own pre-flight baseline, rather than against a crowd of strangers, and when should two sets of numbers be tested as matched pairs instead of as two independent groups?
story.payoff: Matching cancels whatever the pair shares (genes, upbringing, the person himself), so the comparison sees only the change. Today's walkthrough shows the same effect in returns: two strategies that ride the same market look indistinguishable when tested as independent samples (pooled t = 0.35), because month-to-month swings of about 2.4 percentage points swamp a 0.48-point edge. Test the six monthly differences instead and the shared swings cancel: s_d = 0.19, paired t = 6.10, far beyond the 5% critical value of 2.571 with 5 df. Same numbers, opposite verdict: the design of the data decides which test is right.
sources: Garrett-Bakelman, F. E. et al., "The NASA Twins Study: A multidimensional analysis of a year-long human spaceflight", Science 364(6436), eaau8650, 12 April 2019, doi:10.1126/science.aau8650

story_idea.candidate: On 5 February 2018 — 'Volmageddon' — the VIX volatility index more than doubled in one day, its biggest one-day percentage jump on record, and the exchange-traded note XIV, a bet that volatility would stay low, lost over 90% of its value after hours and was shut down.

days.headline_hint: Volmageddon: the day the fear gauge more than doubled, and how to test whether a variance really rose

story.title: Volmageddon: the day the fear gauge doubled
story.hook: On Friday 2 February 2018 the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX), the market's "fear gauge" computed from S&P 500 option prices, closed at 17.31. On Monday 5 February it closed at 37.32, up 115.6%, its largest one-day percentage rise on record. XIV, an exchange-traded note built to profit when volatility stayed low, lost more than 90% of its value. Because its indicative value had fallen to 20% or less of the previous day's close, an "acceleration event" under its terms, Credit Suisse announced on 6 February that it would redeem the note early. It expected trading to end on 20 February, but Nasdaq halted the note after the close on Thursday 15 February.
story.puzzle: Everyone could see that volatility had jumped. But a few wild days happen even in calm markets. How do you test, with numbers, whether one period's variance is really bigger than another's, or bigger than the value a risk model assumed, and not just noise?
story.payoff: The VIX is an annualized implied standard deviation, so dividing by √252 turns the move into implied daily SDs of about 1.09% before and 2.35% after. The F-test compares variances, not SDs: (37.32/17.31)^2 = 4.65. If a month of 21 trading days before and after had shown those SDs, an F of 4.65 with (20, 20) degrees of freedom would far exceed the 5% one-tailed critical value of 2.12: the rise is not noise. The χ² test answers the companion question, whether one period's variance fits a single assumed value, such as the calm-market volatility a note like XIV was in effect betting on.

story_idea.candidate: In 1886 Francis Galton published 'Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature', based on the heights of 928 adult children of 205 pairs of parents in England. Children of very tall parents were tall, but on average less extreme than their parents.
story_idea.why: Why do the children of exceptionally tall parents tend to be less exceptional — and how do you draw the one 'best' line through a cloud of points?

days.headline_hint: Galton's tall parents had not-quite-as-tall children. The best line through the cloud explains why

story.title: Galton and the not-quite-as-tall children
story.hook: In 1886 Francis Galton published "Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature" in the Journal of the Anthropological Institute, using the heights of 930 adult children of 205 sets of parents (928 in his summary table). To put men and women on one scale he multiplied every female height by 1.08, and he summarized each couple by their average, the "mid-parent". Children of unusually tall parents were tall, but on average less extreme than their parents, and children of short parents less short: the children's deviations from the average were about two-thirds of the mid-parents'.
story.puzzle: Why should the children of exceptional parents be less exceptional, and of all the lines you could draw through 928 scattered points, which one is the "best"?
story.payoff: Least squares chooses the line that makes the sum of squared vertical misses as small as possible, and the algebra gives slope = Cov(X, Y)/Var(X) = r × s_Y/s_X, with the line passing through the point of means. When parents and children vary about equally (s_Y ≈ s_X) the slope is just r, and because r < 1 every prediction sits closer to the average than the parent. Galton's two-thirds is his slope, not r: a mid-parent, being an average of two people, varies less than single children (s_Y > s_X), so his r was lower still. Either way, a slope of two-thirds means a mid-parent 3 inches above average predicts a child about 2 inches above. In today's five families the slope is 0.52, so a mid-parent of 75 inches (7 above the mean of 68) predicts a child of 71.54, only 3.64 above the children's mean.
sources: Galton, F., "Regression Towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature", Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland 15 (1886): 246-263 - https://zenodo.org/record/1449548/files/article.pdf

story_idea.candidate: In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe published four small datasets — now 'Anscombe's quartet' — with the same means, variances, correlation (about 0.816) and fitted line (Y = 3 + 0.5X), yet wildly different shapes when plotted.

days.headline_hint: Four datasets, one line, one R²: Anscombe's 1973 warning about what a good fit really means

story.title: Anscombe's quartet: four datasets, one line
story.hook: In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe published "Graphs in Statistical Analysis" in The American Statistician. He built four small datasets of 11 points each. All four have the same mean of X (9) and of Y (7.50), the same variance of X (11), almost the same variance of Y (4.12 to 4.13), the same correlation (0.816) and the same least-squares line, Y = 3.00 + 0.500X. Plotted, they look nothing alike: a fuzzy straight line, a smooth curve, a perfect line knocked off by one outlier, and a vertical stack of points whose slope is set entirely by a single far-off point.
story.puzzle: If all four have the same line and the same R², does the regression fit all four equally well, and what does R² actually measure?
story.payoff: Split the variation for set I: SST = 41.27, SSR = 27.51, SSE = 13.76, so R² = SSR/SST = 0.667, SEE = √(SSE/9) = 1.237 and F = 17.99 (5% critical value 5.12 with 1 and 9 df). Sets II, III and IV also give R² = 0.67, SEE = 1.24 and F ≈ 18. R² only reports the share of Y's variation the line accounts for; it cannot say whether a straight line is the right shape, whether one point is doing all the work, or whether the errors behave. That is why Anscombe insisted on plotting the data, and why regression's assumptions are checked with residual plots.
sources: Anscombe, F. J., "Graphs in Statistical Analysis", The American Statistician 27(1), 1973, pp. 17-21, doi:10.1080/00031305.1973.10478966

story_idea.candidate: In June 1992 Eugene Fama and Kenneth French published 'The Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns' in the Journal of Finance, finding that from 1963 to 1990 a stock's beta did little to explain its average return once size and book-to-market were considered — headlines declared 'beta is dead'.
story_idea.why: A fitted slope is never exactly zero. How do you decide whether beta really explains returns or the slope is just noise?

days.headline_hint: "Beta is dead"? Fama and French found a flat slope in 1992; Fischer Black said not so fast

story.title: "Beta is dead" - or just hard to measure?
story.hook: In June 1992 Eugene Fama and Kenneth French published "The Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns" in the Journal of Finance. Studying US stocks from 1963 to 1990, they found that, once beta was allowed to vary for reasons unrelated to size, the relation between market beta and average return was flat, even when beta was the only explanatory variable, while size and book-to-market explained a great deal. Earlier that year, as Black later cited it, The New York Times (Eric Berg, 18 February 1992) reported Fama as saying that beta as the sole variable explaining returns on stocks was dead. In 1993 Fischer Black, co-creator of the Black-Scholes model, answered in the Journal of Portfolio Management with "Beta and Return", arguing that announcements of beta's death were premature.
story.puzzle: A fitted slope is never exactly 0, or exactly 1. How do you decide whether beta really explains a stock's returns, and if a test cannot find the relation, does that prove it is not there?
story.payoff: Test the slope with t = (b̂_1 - B_1)/s_b̂1 and n - 2 degrees of freedom. Today's six months give β̂ = 1.27 with s_b = 0.22: t = 5.80 against β = 0 (clearly not zero; critical 2.776 with 4 df) but only 1.22 against β = 1, so six months cannot tell this stock's beta from 1, and the 95% interval runs from 0.66 to 1.87. The same logic sat under the 1992 quarrel: returns are so noisy that slopes come with wide standard errors, and "fail to reject" is not "proved zero". Black went further, arguing that Fama and French had misinterpreted their own data.
sources: Fama, E. F. and French, K. R., "The Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns", Journal of Finance 47(2), June 1992, pp. 427-465 (abstract: beta-return relation flat for 1963-1990, even with beta alone) - https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v47y1992i2p427-65.html

Black, F., "Beta and Return", Journal of Portfolio Management 20(1), Fall 1993, pp. 8-18, doi:10.3905/jpm.1993.409462 (quotes Fama via Eric Berg, The New York Times, 18 February 1992; subtitle: announcements of the death of beta seem premature)

story_idea.candidate: In the 19 April 1965 issue of Electronics, Gordon Moore (later a co-founder of Intel) predicted in 'Cramming more components onto integrated circuits' that the number of components on a chip would keep doubling about every year; in 1975 he revised it to about every two years.
story_idea.why: Growth that doubles on schedule is a curve, not a line. How can a straight-line regression measure it — and how sure can a forecast ten years out be?

days.headline_hint: Moore's 1965 straight line through doubling chips: how logs let a regression measure growth

story.title: Moore's line on semi-log paper
story.hook: In the 19 April 1965 issue of Electronics, Gordon Moore, director of research and development at Fairchild Semiconductor (he would later co-found Intel), published "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits". He plotted the number of components per integrated circuit year by year, starting in 1959 with a single component (2^0), on a vertical axis marked in the log, base 2, of the count. The points fell close to a straight line: a doubling every year, to around 2^6 = 64 components by 1965. Moore extended the line a decade and predicted that by 1975 one chip could hold as many as 65,000 components, a thousand-fold increase. In 1975 he revised the pace to a doubling about every two years.
story.puzzle: Growth that doubles every year is a curve, not a line: 1, 2, 4, 8 ... 64. How can a straight-line regression measure it, what does its slope mean, and how far should anyone trust a forecast pushed ten years past the last point?
story.payoff: Take logs and doubling becomes adding: ln Y rises by the same ln 2 = 0.6931 every year, so ln Y = b0 + b1X is a straight line whose slope is the continuous growth rate, and the doubling time is ln 2/b1: one year on Moore's 1965 line, which is why ten more years meant 2^10 = 1,024 times as many components (2^16 = 65,536). Today's walkthrough fits the same model to five Intel processors from 1971 to 2000: b1 = 0.3326 a year, a doubling every 2.08 years, close to Moore's 1975 revision. A forecast is honest only with its interval. For 2010, ten years past the data, the line says about 1,070 million transistors, but with five points (3 degrees of freedom, t = 3.182) the 95% prediction interval runs from about 513 million to 2,232 million: s_f = 0.2311 against an SEE of 0.1512, because (X_f - X̄)² is large far from the data. In logs the interval is symmetric; back in transistors its top is about 4.4 times its bottom.
sources: Moore, G. E., "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits", Electronics 38(8), 19 April 1965, pp. 114-117 (rate of roughly a factor of two per year; as many as 65,000 components on a single chip by 1975; log2 vertical axis) - americanradiohistory.com/Archive-Electronics/60s/65/Electronics-1965-04-19-Moore's-Law.pdf; IEEE Milestone 'Moore's Law - Predicts Integrated Circuit Complexity Growth, 1965' (ieeemilestones.ethw.org)

Computer History Museum, Silicon Engine timeline, '1965 - Moore's Law Predicts the Future of Integrated Circuits' (1975 IEDM paper 'Progress in Digital Integrated Electronics' revised the rate to a doubling every two years; the 18-month figure was David House's) - computerhistory.org/semiconductor/timeline/1965-Moore.html

Moore, 1995 SPIE speech (points from 1959 fell close to a straight line doubling every year to 1965; extrapolated a decade to a thousand-fold increase); Computer History Museum blog 'Madeleine Moment Connects Moore's Law Artifacts' (plot starts with a 1-component device in 1959)

Intel processor transistor counts used in the walkthrough (4004 1971: 2,300; 8086 1978: 29,000; 80386 1985: 275,000; Pentium 1993: 3.1 million; Pentium 4 2000: 42 million) - Intel's published figures (Intel chip-history timeline poster); confirmed by search on 2026-11-06: Computer History Museum 'Intel x86 family' (8086 29,000; 80386 275,000), Computerworld x86 timeline and PC Magazine 1996 (Pentium 3.1 million, 1993), Wikipedia 'Transistor count' table (4004 2,300, 1971; Pentium 4 Willamette 42 million, 2000)
Regression, forecast and interval: numbers computed in blocks/numbers-51-60.py

c2 (mc, why): why does the prediction interval get wider the farther X_f is from X̄? A (right): the slope is itself estimated with error, and a slope error moves the fitted line more the farther you go from the centre of the data - the (X_f - X̄)²/((n - 1)s_X²) term; B: the residuals get bigger at large X (that would be heteroskedasticity, which the model assumes away: SEE is one number for every X); C: fewer observations lie near X_f, so the degrees of freedom fall (df = n - 2 for every forecast); right answer at A

c5 (explain): in two sentences, why can a straight-line regression measure growth that doubles, and what must you do with its forecast? Must contain: take logs, so constant-percentage growth becomes a constant change in ln Y (log-lin model); the slope b1 is the continuous growth rate per period (doubling time ln 2/b1); the forecast comes out in logs and must be exponentiated, and its interval widens far from X̄

days.module: Portfolio Risk and Return: Part II
days.title: Beta, CAPM and the security market line
days.concept: Only systematic risk is rewarded, so an asset's expected return is E(R_i) = R_f + β_i[E(R_m) − R_f] with β_i = Cov(R_i, R_m)/σ_m² = ρ_im σ_i/σ_m; an asset that plots above the security market line is undervalued (positive alpha).
los: β_i = Cov(R_i, R_m)/σ_m² = ρ_im σ_i/σ_m
CAPM: E(R_i) = R_f + β_i[E(R_m) − R_f] (cost of equity, Equities)
Security market line (β on the x-axis) vs capital market line (σ on the x-axis)
Alpha = forecast return − CAPM required return; above SML → undervalued
Systematic vs unsystematic risk; market model R_i = α_i + β_iR_m + e_i
Multi-factor/APT: E(R) = R_f + Σ β_k λ_k (explain)

calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.back: β_i = Cov(R_i, R_m) / σ_m² = ρ_im × σ_i / σ_m
E(R_i) = R_f + β_i × [E(R_m) − R_f]
α = forecast (or actual) return − CAPM required return; α > 0 → undervalued
E(R_p) = R_F + λ_1 β_p,1 + … + λ_K β_p,K
CML: total risk σ (efficient portfolios); SML: beta (any asset or portfolio)

traps: Multiplying beta by the market return instead of the market risk premium
Using σ (CML) to price an individual stock

story_idea.candidate: On Monday 8 August 2011, the first trading day after Standard & Poor's cut the United States' credit rating from AAA to AA+, the S&P 500 fell about 6.7% while gold rose to a record above $1,700 an ounce; gold went on to peak near $1,900 in early September 2011. Over long periods gold's price swings have been roughly as large as stocks', yet it has earned far less.
story_idea.why: If gold is about as volatile as stocks, why do investors accept a much lower long-run return for holding it — which kind of risk does the market actually pay for?

days.headline_hint: 8 August 2011: stocks fell 6.66% and gold settled at a record $1,713 - why markets pay for beta, not volatility

story.title: The day gold went up
story.hook: After the close on Friday 5 August 2011, Standard & Poor's cut the United States' credit rating from AAA to AA+. On Monday 8 August the S&P 500 fell 79.92 points, or 6.66%, to 1,119.46, while December gold futures settled at a record $1,713.20 an ounce on Comex, up $61.40 or 3.7%; on 6 September spot gold touched a record above $1,920. Gold is no calmer than stocks: over the 30 years to 2019 State Street measured its annualized volatility at 15.44%, against 14.32% for the S&P 500. Yet over two centuries it has barely beaten inflation: Jeremy Siegel's figures for 1802-2012 give stocks a real return of about 6.6% a year and gold about 0.7%.
story.puzzle: If gold swings about as much as stocks, why have investors accepted roughly 6 percentage points a year less for holding it? Which kind of risk does the market actually pay for?
story.payoff: Only risk that cannot be diversified away earns a premium, and CAPM measures it with beta: β = ρ x σ_i/σ_m. Gold's volatility is high, but what counts is how it moves with the market, and on days like 8 August 2011 it moved the other way. Suppose, for illustration, gold's correlation with stocks is 0.1: with State Street's volatilities β = 0.1 x 15.44/14.32 = 0.108, and with R_f = 4% and an equity risk premium of 5.5% CAPM asks only 4.59% a year, little more than cash. A stock with the same 15.44% volatility but a correlation of 0.9 has β = 0.970 and must offer 9.34%. Same σ, very different required returns: the market pays for beta, not for σ.
sources: Reuters via Investing.com, 'US STOCKS-Wall St sinks as fear jumps after historic downgrade', 8 August 2011 (S&P 500 down 79.92 points, or 6.66%, to 1,119.46) - m.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/us-stocks-wall-st-sinks-as-fear-jumps-after-historic-downgrade-221360; Wikipedia, 'Black Monday (2011)'

days.module: Portfolio Risk and Return: Part II
days.title: Risk-adjusted performance measures
days.concept: Risk-adjusted measures compare excess return with the risk that matters: the Sharpe ratio uses total risk σ, Treynor and Jensen's alpha use beta, M² restates the Sharpe ratio as a return at the market's risk, and Sortino and Calmar look at downside risk and drawdowns.
los: Sharpe = (R_p − R_f)/σ_p
Treynor = (R_p − R_f)/β_p
M² = (R_p − R_f) × σ_m/σ_p − (R_m − R_f)
Jensen's alpha α_p = R_p − [R_f + β_p(R_m − R_f)]

story_idea.candidate: In a November 2005 memo to the SEC titled 'The World's Largest Hedge Fund is a Fraud', the analyst Harry Markopolos argued that Bernard Madoff's steady returns of about 1% a month, with almost no losing months, were mathematically implausible. Madoff was arrested on 11 December 2008.
story_idea.why: How can returns be too good — and what single number would have flagged Madoff's record as suspicious?

days.headline_hint: Madoff's feeder fund printed a Sharpe ratio of 2.75 for sixteen years - the number that was too good

story.title: A Sharpe ratio too good to be true
story.hook: On Monday 7 November 2005 the financial analyst Harry Markopolos sent the SEC a revised version of his memo, later known as "The World's Largest Hedge Fund is a Fraud", arguing that Bernard Madoff's firm was most likely a Ponzi scheme; he wrote that the entire report tied into Fairfield Sentry, a fund of funds with over $5 billion invested with Madoff. Three days later an SEC examiner who had read it wrote to a colleague that he felt "much better that he is incorrect". Fairfield kept marketing the fund. Its August 2007 sheet boasted a sixteen-year record with only 14 down months, a compound annual return of 10.85% and an annual standard deviation of just 2.50%, and printed its own Sharpe ratio: 2.75, against 0.51 for the S&P 100. On 11 December 2008 the FBI arrested Madoff.
story.puzzle: How can returns be too good - and which single number, printed on the fund's own sheet, should have made any analyst suspicious?
story.payoff: The Sharpe ratio: excess return per unit of total risk. The sheet's own ratios imply a risk-free rate of about 3.975% (10.85 - 2.75 x 2.50). Then the S&P 100 earned 7.24 points of excess return for 14.11 points of volatility, 0.51 per unit, while Sentry claimed 6.88 points for only 2.50: 2.75 per unit, 5.4 times the index, for sixteen years. M² turns that into a return: scaled up to the index's 14.11% risk, Sentry's record would have earned 3.975% + 6.875% x 14.11/2.50 = 42.78% a year, an M² of 31.57 percentage points over the index. Markopolos's argument was that numbers like these were not mathematically possible for the strategy Madoff described; they were the signature of invented returns.
sources: Markopolos e-mail to Meaghan Cheung (SEC), Monday 7 November 2005, 'Resubmitted Madoff SEC Meeting.doc' (the report ties into Fairfield Sentry Ltd., a fund of funds with over $5 billion invested in Madoff Investment Securities), and SEC examiner Peter Lamore's e-mail of 10 November 2005 ('after having just read the "informant's" analysis I feel much better that he is incorrect') - SEC Office of Inspector General, Report OIG-509 (2009), Exhibit 289: sec.gov/news/studies/2009/oig-509/exhibit-0289.pdf
Memo title 'The World's Largest Hedge Fund is a Fraud' (November 2005) - e.g. ProPublica's reproduction, propublica.org/article/the-worlds-largest-hedge-fund-is-a-fraud-1219

Fairfield Sentry marketing sheet dated August 2007, filed as Exhibit 29 in the Madoff trustee's litigation (sixteen-year track record; only 14 down months since inception; compound annual return 10.85%, annual standard deviation 2.50%, Sharpe ratio 2.75, worst drawdown -0.64%; S&P 100 11.21%, 14.11%, 0.51; Lehman Aggregate 6.96%, 3.73%, 0.80; fund assets $7.0 billion) - madofftrustee.com/images/upload/11-02910_Merrill_Lynch_Suisse_Longstaff_Declaration_in_Support_of_Trustee_Opp_to_MTD_Exh29_123-0029.pdf (confirmed from search-indexed OCR text of the exhibit, not a full read of the PDF; a 2008 Fairfield document gives 13 losing months)

days.title: Effective duration and negative convexity
days.concept: When cash flows change with interest rates — callable bonds and mortgage securities — sensitivity must be measured by repricing under shifts of the benchmark curve, EffDur = (PV_− − PV_+)/(2 × ΔCurve × PV_0), and prepayments give mortgage securities negative convexity.
los: Effective duration EffDur = (PV_− − PV_+)/(2 × ΔCurve × PV_0)
Effective convexity EffCon = [(PV_−) + (PV_+) − 2PV_0]/[(ΔCurve)² × PV_0]
Negative convexity of callable bonds and MBS
Key rate durations: sensitivity to one maturity's rate; they sum to effective duration
Mortgage prepayment: SMM and CPR = 1 − (1 − SMM)^12; PSA benchmark, WAM, WAC, WAL, LTV (describe)

memorize.back: Price rises less when rates fall than it falls when rates rise (callables, MBS)

Treating CPR as 12 × SMM

story_idea.candidate: In early 1994, after the Federal Reserve began raising rates on 4 February, David Askin's Granite funds — about $600 million invested in complex mortgage-backed securities marketed as market-neutral — collapsed within weeks as prepayments slowed and prices fell faster than his models predicted.
story_idea.why: Why can a mortgage bond lose more when rates rise than it gains when rates fall, and why does ordinary duration miss it?

days.headline_hint: February 1994: one Fed hike, and Askin's 'market-neutral' mortgage funds were bankrupt by April

story.title: The market-neutral funds that were not
story.hook: In February 1994 the Federal Reserve raised its federal funds target from 3% to 3.25%, and bond markets around the world sold off. In New York, Askin Capital Management's Granite funds had been presented as "market-neutral": a balanced mix of "bullish" and "bearish" mortgage-backed securities whose gains and losses should offset whichever way rates moved. The funds were highly leveraged. As prices fell, lenders made margin calls, forced sales showed the portfolio was worth far less than the "theoretical" values the firm had been reporting, and in April 1994 the funds, which had held about $600 million of investors' money, went into bankruptcy; by later accounts nearly all of it was lost.
story.puzzle: If part of the book gained when rates rose and part when they fell, how could one rate rise wipe it out - and why does ordinary duration, which treats a bond's cash flows as fixed, miss the danger?
story.payoff: Mortgage cash flows are not fixed. When rates rise, homeowners stop refinancing, prepayments slow and the securities' lives extend just when a longer life hurts most; when rates fall, prepayments speed up and cap the gain. So the risk has to be measured the way Askin's "theoretical" prices were made, by repricing with a prepayment model under a shifted benchmark curve, and it is only as good as that model. Today's callable bond shows the asymmetry: a 25 bp fall adds 0.84, a 25 bp rise takes away 0.86. Effective duration is 3.3966 and effective convexity -31.97, so a 100 bp rise costs about 3.56% while a 100 bp fall earns only about 3.24%. With borrowed money behind every position, an asymmetry like that turns a "neutral" book into a one-way bet.
sources: Wikipedia, '1994 bond market crisis' (FOMC raised the federal funds target from 3% to 3.25% in February 1994, setting off a worldwide bond sell-off)

Granite Funds described as intended to be 'market-neutral' through 'a balanced mix of "bullish" and "bearish" securities' - S.D.N.Y. opinions in the Askin litigation, e.g. ABF Capital Management v. Askin Capital Management, 957 F. Supp. 1308 (1997); Primavera Familienstifung v. Askin, 130 F. Supp. 2d 450 (2001)

Valuations kept at 'theoretical' levels above trading prices; forced liquidations; funds with over US$600 million in assets went bankrupt; high leverage and margin calls - Wikipedia, 'List of trading losses' (Askin Capital Management, about USD 0.6 bn, 1994) and secondary accounts found by search; debtors In re Granite Partners, L.P., Granite Corporation and Quartz Hedge Fund, Bankr. S.D.N.Y. Nos. 94 B 41683-41685

steps: EffCon = (100.10 + 96.60 - 2 x 98.50)/(0.005² x 98.50) = -0.30/0.0024625 = -121.83 (negative: the up-move loses 1.90, the down-move gains only 1.60)
Convexity term for a 100 bp move either way: ½ x (-121.83) x 0.01² = -0.61%
worked_example.answer: EffDur 3.5533; EffCon -121.83; about -4.16% for +100 bp and +2.94% for -100 bp; SMM 0.5143%

EffCon = (PV− + PV+ − 2PV0)/((ΔCurve)² × PV0)
CPR = 1 − (1 − SMM)^12, in percent

c2 (mc, why): why is effective duration, not modified duration, the right measure for a callable bond or an MBS? A: modified duration only works for zero-coupon bonds; B: effective duration is modified duration measured in basis points; C (right): their cash flows change when rates change (calls, prepayments), so sensitivity must come from repricing with a model under curve shifts, while modified duration assumes fixed cash flows and a change in the bond's own yield; right answer at C

c5 (explain): what is negative convexity, and why did it hurt funds like Askin's? Must contain: the price rises less when rates fall than it falls when rates rise (EffCon < 0); caused by the borrower's prepayment (or issuer's call) option: faster prepayment caps gains, slower prepayment extends life when rates rise; leverage magnifies the asymmetric losses

days.module: Credit Risk
days.title: Credit risk: expected loss and spreads
days.concept: Expected loss equals the probability of default times the loss given default (exposure × (1 − recovery rate)); the credit spread is roughly that annual expected loss, and a spread change moves a bond's price by about −ModDur × ΔSpread + ½ × Convexity × (ΔSpread)².
los: Expected loss = POD × LGD; LGD = exposure × (1 − recovery rate)
Yield spread ≈ POD × LGD (per year)
Price impact of a spread change: %ΔPV ≈ −ModDur × ΔSpread + ½ × Convexity × (ΔSpread)²
Credit ratios: EBITDA/interest, debt/EBITDA, FFO/debt, debt/capital (higher leverage → weaker credit)
Seniority ranking and recovery; credit migration

story_idea.candidate: On 10 October 2008, an auction to settle credit default swaps on Lehman Brothers — which had filed for bankruptcy on 15 September — set the value of its bonds at 8.625 cents on the dollar, so protection sellers paid out about 91.4 cents for every dollar insured.
story_idea.why: Lehman's bonds had been rated A just weeks earlier. What does a default actually cost a bondholder, and how should a yield spread price that risk in advance?

days.headline_hint: Lehman's bonds were rated A in September 2008; on 10 October an auction valued them at 8.625 cents

story.title: 8.625 cents on the dollar
story.hook: In the second week of September 2008 Lehman Brothers was still rated A by Standard & Poor's and A2 by Moody's, though both agencies had it under review. Early on Monday 15 September it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. On Friday 10 October 2008 an auction run by Creditex and Markit under an ISDA protocol set the price used to settle credit default swaps on Lehman: 8.625 per 100 of face value. Sellers of protection therefore paid buyers 91.375 for every 100 they had insured.
story.puzzle: What does a default actually cost a bondholder - and how big a yield spread should have paid for that risk in advance?
story.payoff: The cost is the loss given default: exposure x (1 - recovery) = 100 - 8.625 = 91.375 per 100. Spread ≈ POD x LGD prices that loss a year at a time: with Lehman's LGD, each 1% of annual default probability needs about 91 bp of spread, and a 3% chance needs 2.74%. The recovery assumption matters as much as the default probability. Read a 1% spread with the common modelling assumption of 40% recovery (LGD 60%) and it implies a 1.67% annual chance of default; with Lehman's actual LGD of 91.375% the same spread covered only a 1.09% chance. And a widening spread hurts before any default: for a bond with ModDur 6.5 and convexity 55, 300 bp of widening costs about 19.50% - 2.475% = 17.025% of its price.
sources: Risk.net, 'Lehman recovery rate set at 8.625%', October 2008 (final price 8.625 determined at 2 p.m. on Friday 10 October 2008; protection sellers pay 91.375% of par) - risk.net/derivatives/credit-derivatives/1502450/lehman-recovery-rate-set-8625

days.lm11_note: Quantitative Methods LM11, Introduction to Financial Data Science, has no calculations at Level I; know the ideas. Big data is described by its volume, velocity and variety (veracity is often added), and alternative data includes text, satellite images and sensor or transaction feeds. Machine learning is supervised (labelled data: regression and classification), unsupervised (no labels: clustering, dimension reduction) or deep learning (many-layered neural networks); overfitting means a model has learned the noise in its training data and fails on new data. Generative AI and large language models produce text from patterns learned on huge corpora and can state errors fluently, so their output is checked like any unverified source. 2027 detail is uncertain: treat this as describe-only.

days.module: Pricing and Valuation of Forward Contracts and for an Underlying with Varying Maturities
days.title: Forward prices and the cost of carry
days.concept: No-arbitrage forces a forward price to equal the spot price carried forward at the risk-free rate, adjusted for income forgone and costs paid — F_0(T) = [S_0 − PV(I) + PV(C)](1 + r)^T — and the forward's value later is the PV of the change in the forward price.
los: F_0(T) = S_0(1 + r)^T (no income or costs)
With carry: F_0(T) = [S_0 − PV_0(I) + PV_0(C)](1 + r)^T; continuous: F_0(T) = S_0 e^((r + c − i)T)
Value at inception = 0; value of a long forward at t: V_t(T) = [F_t(T) − F_0(T)]/(1 + r)^(T − t)
Contango (F > S) and backwardation (F < S); futures marked to market daily (gains and losses settled each day)
Commodity futures return = price (spot) return + roll return + collateral return (Alternatives)

story_idea.candidate: On 20 April 2020 the May contract for West Texas Intermediate crude oil settled at −$37.63 a barrel: with demand collapsed by the pandemic and storage at Cushing, Oklahoma, nearly full, holders of expiring futures paid others to take their oil.
story_idea.why: How can the price of something people normally pay for become negative — and what links today's spot price to the price for delivery next month?

days.headline_hint: 20 April 2020: May oil settled at -$37.63 while June was +$20.43 - the price of carrying a barrel

story.title: Minus $37.63 a barrel
story.hook: On Monday 20 April 2020, the day before it expired, NYMEX's May contract for West Texas Intermediate crude oil fell as low as -$40.32 and settled at -$37.63 a barrel, the first negative price in the contract's 37-year history. Demand had collapsed in the pandemic, and working storage at Cushing, Oklahoma, where the contract is delivered, was near capacity: anyone still long at expiry had to take barrels there. The same day the June contract settled at +$20.43, and the physical spot price at Cushing was -$36.98.
story.puzzle: How can oil for delivery in May be worth -$37.63 and oil for delivery a month later +$20.43? What ties today's price to the price for later delivery?
story.payoff: No arbitrage: buying oil now and storing it must cost the same as locking in a price for later, so F = [S - PV(income) + PV(costs)] x (1 + r)^T. Turn it round and the gap between the two contracts is the market's price of carry. With interest rates near zero, June minus May = 20.43 - (-37.63) = $58.06 a barrel (or 20.43 + 36.98 = $57.41 against spot) for holding a barrel for about a month. Storage, not oil, was the scarce good, so the near price had to fall until someone with tank space was paid to take the barrels. That is contango (F above S) in its most extreme form, and it is why an investor who keeps rolling into the next contract earns a negative roll return.
sources: CFTC, Interim Staff Report: Trading in NYMEX WTI Crude Oil Futures Contract Leading up to, on, and around April 20, 2020 (November 2020) (May contract settled at -$37.63, the first negative price since listing 37 years earlier; session low -$40.32; Cushing working storage near capacity) - cftc.gov/media/5296/InterimStaffReportNYMEX_WTICrudeOil/download

S&P Global Platts, 'NYMEX WTI falls below -$5/b to all-time record low', 20 April 2020, and Hart Energy, 20 April 2020 (June contract settled at $20.43, down $4.60) - spglobal.com/platts/en/market-insights/latest-news/oil/042020-oil-futures-nymex-wti-falls-below-5b-to-all-time-record-low

WTI Cushing spot price -$36.98 on 20 April 2020, the only negative value in the EIA's WTI and Brent spot series since 1986 (datahub.io analysis of the EIA series, datahub.io/datapressr/wti-went-negative); June contract settlement 20.43 against -37.63 also tabulated in an AEA 2023 conference deck (aeaweb.org)

days.module: Pricing and Valuation of Interest Rate and Other Swaps
days.title: FRAs and interest rate swaps
days.concept: A forward rate agreement locks in an implied forward rate, and an interest rate swap is a bundle of such forward agreements whose fixed rate is set so the PV of fixed payments equals the PV of floating ones: s_N = (1 − DF_N)/Σ DF_i.
los: FRA fixed rate = implied forward rate from spot rates
FRA settlement (paid at the start of the interest period): Notional × (MRR − FRA rate) × (days/360)/[1 + MRR × (days/360)]
Par swap rate s_N = (1 − DF_N)/Σ_(i=1..N) DF_i
A swap as a series of forwards; pay-fixed gains when rates rise
Swap value after rates change: PV of the difference between old and new fixed rates on the notional

Using spot rates instead of discount factors in the swap-rate formula
Getting the direction wrong: pay-fixed benefits from rising rates

story_idea.candidate: Between 1987 and 1989 the London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham built up interest rate swaps with a notional value of about £6 billion — many times its annual budget — largely betting that UK rates would fall. When rates rose, the losses mounted; in January 1991 the House of Lords ruled that councils had no power to make such deals, voiding the contracts.
story_idea.why: A swap costs nothing to enter. So where did the council's huge losses come from, and what makes a swap's fixed rate 'fair'?

days.headline_hint: Hammersmith and Fulham ran up £6 billion of swaps betting rates would fall; UK base rates went to 15%

story.title: The council that bet on falling rates
story.hook: In the late 1980s the London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham ran up interest rate swap deals with a total notional principal of £6,052 million, although its total borrowing was only about £390 million. Its positions were bets that interest rates would fall. Instead UK base rates rose from about 7.5% in May 1988 to 15% by October 1989. The district auditor, Hazell, went to court, and on 24 January 1991 the House of Lords ruled that councils had no power to enter into such swaps, making them void and setting off years of litigation over the money that had changed hands.
story.puzzle: A swap costs nothing to enter. So where did the council's losses come from, and what makes a swap's fixed rate "fair" on the day it is agreed?
story.payoff: The fixed rate is set so that the PV of the fixed payments equals the PV of the floating ones, s_N = (1 - DF_N)/ΣDF_i, so the swap is worth zero on day one. A swap is a bundle of forward contracts on the floating rate, and once rates move it is worth the PV of the gap between the old fixed rate and the new par rate. As an illustration (not the council's actual book): receive 9% fixed for five years on £100 million, then let the five-year rate rise to 12% on a flat curve. The receiver now gets 3 points a year less than the market rate, worth -0.03 x 3.6048 x £100 million = -£10.81 million. Hammersmith's notional was 15.5 times its debt, so its swaps were not hedges of its borrowing but a leveraged bet.
sources: Hazell v Hammersmith and Fulham LBC [1992] 2 AC 1 (HL), decided 24 January 1991 (interest rate swaps beyond local authorities' powers; aggregate notional principal £6,052 million against borrowings of about £390 million; in a fixed-to-variable swap the council lost if rates rose) - en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazell_v_Hammersmith_and_Fulham_LBC; vlex.co.uk/vid/hazell-v-hammersmith-and-794020865
Wikipedia, 'Local authorities swaps litigation' (all of Hammersmith's swap positions were bets on a fall in interest rates; the restitution litigation that followed)

UK base rates: 7½% from 18 May 1988 (Hansard written answer, 1989) and 15% from October 1989 (Channel 4 FactCheck, 'How high were interest rates in the eighties?'; Bank of England Annual Report 1989). The Bank of England's own historical Bank Rate series records these levels as 7.375% and 14.875%; 7.5% and 15% are the clearing banks' base rates, hence 'UK base rates' rather than 'the Bank of England's base rate'
The swap-valuation example is illustrative; numbers computed in blocks/numbers-51-60.py

worked_example.problem: Today 90-day MRR is 3.0% and 180-day MRR is 3.4% (annualized, 360-day year). Find the implied rate for a 3x6 FRA. A dealer quotes 3.77%. In three months 90-day MRR is 4.5%: what does the long side (receives MRR, pays the FRA rate) receive on $20 million notional, paid at settlement?
steps: Growth over 180 days: 1 + 0.034 x 180/360 = 1.017; over the first 90 days: 1 + 0.030 x 90/360 = 1.0075
Implied 90-day rate starting in 90 days: (1.017/1.0075 - 1) x 360/90 = 3.7717%, so the FRA is quoted at 3.77%
Interest difference for the period: 20,000,000 x (0.045 - 0.0377) x 90/360 = 36,500.00, which would fall due at the END of the 90-day period
An FRA settles at the START of the period, so discount at the new MRR: 36,500/(1 + 0.045 x 90/360) = 36,500/1.01125 = 36,093.94

days.module: Pricing and Valuation of Options
days.title: Option payoffs, profits and value
days.concept: At expiry a call pays max(0, S_T − X) and a put max(0, X − S_T); profit subtracts the premium, so breakevens are X + c_0 for a call and X − p_0 for a put; before expiry an option's price is its intrinsic value plus time value, bounded below by no-arbitrage.
los: Call payoff c_T = max(0, S_T − X); put payoff p_T = max(0, X − S_T)
Profit for long and short positions; maximum gain and loss
Breakeven: call X + c_0; put X − p_0
Moneyness (in/at/out of the money); intrinsic value and time value
Lower bounds (European): c_0 ≥ max[0, S_0 − X/(1 + r)^T]; p_0 ≥ max[0, X/(1 + r)^T − S_0]
Factors affecting option values (direction)

story_idea.candidate: In early 1995 Nick Leeson, a trader at Barings Bank in Singapore, had sold large numbers of Nikkei 225 straddles betting the index would stay calm. After the Kobe earthquake on 17 January 1995 the Nikkei fell sharply; his losses reached about £827 million and Barings, Britain's oldest merchant bank, collapsed on 26 February.
story_idea.why: Selling options earns premium every day the market is quiet. What does the payoff of a sold straddle look like when the market moves a lot — and where does it start losing?

days.headline_hint: Nick Leeson sold Nikkei straddles for their premium; after Kobe the index moved and Barings fell

story.title: Selling calm before the earthquake
story.hook: Over about fourteen months to early 1995, Nick Leeson, Barings' star derivatives trader in Singapore, sold, by one count, more than 37,000 straddles on the Nikkei 225 (each a put and a call with the same strike and expiry), collecting premium on a bet that the index, then trading around 19,000, would stay in a narrow range. At 5:46 a.m. on 17 January 1995 an earthquake struck Kobe. On Monday 23 January, six days later, the Nikkei fell more than 1,000 points, about 5.6%, in a single session, and Leeson answered by buying vast numbers of Nikkei futures. His losses reached £827 million, and on 26 February 1995 Barings, a 233-year-old merchant bank, collapsed.
story.puzzle: Selling straddles pays premium every quiet day. What does a sold straddle pay when the market moves a lot - where does it start losing, and how far can the loss go?
story.payoff: A short straddle's payoff is -max(0, S_T - X) - max(0, X - S_T): the seller owes the distance between the index and the strike, whichever way it moves, and keeps the premiums. Take today's numbers: strike 19,000 and premiums of 300 + 280 = 580. The position makes money only between the breakevens 18,420 and 19,580, and the most it can ever make is 580. At 18,000, a 1,000-point fall, the payoff is -1,000 and the profit -420; at 17,950 it is -470, and every further point costs one more. Below the strike the loss stops only when the index reaches zero; above it, the short call's loss has no limit. Multiply that by tens of thousands of contracts and a bet on calm becomes a bank-breaking one.
sources: Board of Banking Supervision, Report of the Board of Banking Supervision Inquiry into the Circumstances of the Collapse of Barings (HMSO, July 1995) - the official inquiry

'Not Just One Man - Barings' case study (Boğaziçi University course material), citing the Board of Banking Supervision report (Leeson sold puts and calls with the same strikes and maturities, well over 37,000 straddles over a fourteen-month period; 34,400 options in November-December 1994 alone) - web.bogazici.edu.tr/bulent.senver/doc/Barings%20Bank%20Case.doc; the figure was not seen in the report itself, hence 'by one count'

Losses of £827 million and the collapse on 26 February 1995 - Chancellor's statement, HC Deb 18 July 1995 vol 263 cc1454-73 (api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1995/jul/18/barings); MoneyWeek, '26 February 1995: Rogue trader Nick Leeson breaks Barings Bank'; Barings founded 1762 (233 years before 1995); Newsweek, 'Busted' (1995) (Leeson bought Nikkei futures after the quake); Learnsignal, 'Barings Bank collapse: how Nick Leeson destroyed a 233-year-old bank'

Kobe (Great Hanshin) earthquake, 05:46 JST, 17 January 1995 - USGS Historic Earthquakes; Motley Fool, 'Revisiting the 1995 Kobe earthquake' (15 March 2011) (Nikkei 225 closed at 17,785 on 23 January 1995, down 1,055 points or 5.6%); a Wikipedia-derived page gives a 1,025-point plunge, so the hook says 'more than 1,000 points'. Pre-quake level: a slide-deck source puts the Nikkei at about 19,000-19,500 in late 1994 to January 1995 (sources differ on the band, so the hook says only 'around 19,000')

worked_example.problem: Options on a stock expire today. You bought a call (X = 50) for 3.00 and a put (X = 45) for 2.00. The stock closes at 41. Find each option's payoff and profit, and the two breakevens. Earlier, with the stock at 52, the call traded at 3.40: split that into intrinsic value and time value.
steps: Call payoff = max(0, 41 - 50) = 0; profit = 0 - 3.00 = -3.00 (a long call can lose at most its premium)
Breakevens: call X + c0 = 50 + 3 = 53; put X - p0 = 45 - 2 = 43
At S = 52: call intrinsic value = max(0, 52 - 50) = 2.00; time value = 3.40 - 2.00 = 1.40 (time value shrinks to zero by expiry)
worked_example.answer: Call profit -3.00, put profit +2.00; breakevens 53 and 43; intrinsic value 2.00 and time value 1.40

days.module: Option Replication Using Put-Call Parity
days.title: Put-call parity and synthetic positions
days.concept: A call plus a risk-free bond paying the strike (a fiduciary call) has the same payoff as a put plus the stock (a protective put), so S_0 + p_0 = c_0 + X/(1 + r)^T, any one price follows from the others, and with a forward F_0/(1 + r)^T + p_0 = c_0 + X/(1 + r)^T.
los: Put-call parity S_0 + p_0 = c_0 + X/(1 + r)^T (European options, same X and T)
Fiduciary call and protective put
Synthetic positions: synthetic call = S_0 + p_0 − X/(1 + r)^T; synthetic put = c_0 − S_0 + X/(1 + r)^T
Put-call-forward parity F_0(T)/(1 + r)^T + p_0 = c_0 + X/(1 + r)^T
Arbitrage when parity is violated

calculator.task: A stock at 50, 6-month European options with X = 50, r = 4% and a call at 4.20: the put price from parity; then the put from put-call-forward parity given a forward price of 51
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with yˣ (T = 0.5)

memorize.back: c_0 + X / (1 + r)^T (call + bond paying X) = p_0 + S_0 (put + stock)

traps: Discounting the stock price instead of the strike
Sign errors when building a synthetic position
Using T in months instead of years

story_idea.candidate: On 2 March 2000 3Com sold about 5% of its Palm subsidiary to the public. Palm's shares soared so high that 3Com's 95% stake was worth far more than all of 3Com — and, as Owen Lamont and Richard Thaler later documented, Palm's options showed puts priced far above what put-call parity allowed, because Palm shares were nearly impossible to borrow and short.
story_idea.why: If a put, a call, the stock and a bond are tied together by arbitrage, what should a Palm put have cost — and what stopped traders from forcing the price back?

days.headline_hint: 2 March 2000: 3Com's Palm stake was worth more than all of 3Com, and Palm's puts broke put-call parity

story.title: Palm, 3Com and the parity that broke
story.hook: On 2 March 2000 3Com sold about 5% of its handheld-computer subsidiary Palm to the public and said it would hand the rest to its own shareholders later that year, about 1.5 Palm shares (1.525, to be exact) for every 3Com share. Palm, sold at $38 a share in the offering, closed its first day at $95.06, while 3Com fell 21% to $81.81, so a 3Com share, carrying a claim to 1.525 Palm shares worth about $145, was priced about $63 below the Palm stock it contained, as if the rest of 3Com were worth about minus $22 billion. The economists Owen Lamont and Richard Thaler later documented the case and showed that Palm's options were out of line too: puts cost far more than put-call parity allowed, because Palm shares were very hard to borrow and sell short.
story.puzzle: If a put, a call, the stock and a bond are tied together by arbitrage, what should a Palm put have cost - and what stopped traders from forcing the price back into line?
story.payoff: Put-call parity, S0 + p0 = c0 + X/(1 + r)^T, means the options imply a stock price c0 - p0 + X/(1 + r)^T. Use today's numbers as an illustration: S0 = 50, X = 50, r = 4%, six months and a call at 4.20 give a parity put of 3.2290. If the put traded at 8.00 instead, the options would be pricing the stock at 4.20 - 8.00 + 49.0290 = 45.2290, 9.5% below the 50 on the exchange. The arbitrage is to sell what is dear and buy what is cheap: short the stock and buy a synthetic stock (buy the call, sell the put, lend PV(X)). But shorting needs borrowed shares, and Palm's were scarce and costly to borrow, so the trade could not be done at scale and the gap stayed open. Parity holds only when every leg can actually be traded.
sources: Lamont, O. A. and Thaler, R. H., 'Can the Market Add and Subtract? Mispricing in Tech Stock Carve-outs', Journal of Political Economy 111(2), April 2003, pp. 227-268 (NBER w8302): 3Com/Palm carve-out of 2 March 2000; 3Com kept about 95% of Palm and planned to distribute it, 1.525 Palm shares per 3Com share; options on Palm showed large violations of put-call parity, puts about twice as expensive as calls, because Palm shares were hard and costly to short. Ratio, -$63 stub (about -$22 billion in all) and the put-call parity finding confirmed by search on 2026-11-06 via Chicago Booth Review, 'Can the market add and subtract?' (chicagobooth.edu/review/can-market-add-and-subtract), Spatt's critique (memento.epfl.ch) and J. R. Varma's blog (jrvarma.in/blog/Y2012/Palm-3Com-puzzle.html); the paper's PDF itself could not be fetched

Closing prices on 2 March 2000: Palm $95.0625 after an IPO price of $38 (market value $53.4 billion), 3Com down $22.3125 or 21% to $81.8125 - Wall Street Journal, 3 March 2000 (reproduced at users.business.uconn.edu/jgolec/invwsj/6palm.htm); Wired, 'Palm soars in IPO'; CNNMoney, 2 March 2000 (money.cnn.com/2000/03/02/technology/palm/). WSJ and Time put 3Com's retained stake at 94%, the paper at 95%, hence 'about 5%' sold
Thaler, R. H., Misbehaving: The Making of Behavioral Economics (2015), retelling of the 3Com/Palm case (not separately checked)
Option prices are illustrative; numbers computed in blocks/numbers-51-60.py

worked_example.problem: A stock trades at 80. A one-year European put with X = 85 costs 7.50, and r = 5%. Find the call price that put-call parity requires. If the call actually trades at 7.50, show the arbitrage.
steps: The call at 7.50 is 0.9524 too dear: sell it and buy the synthetic call - buy the stock (-80), buy the put (-7.50), borrow PV(X) (+80.9524)

At expiry: if S_T > 85 the stock covers the call you sold plus the 85 you owe; if S_T < 85 the put sells the stock for 85 to repay the loan and the call expires worthless. The position nets zero in every state, so the 0.9524 is a riskless profit
worked_example.answer: Parity call = 6.55; selling the call at 7.50 against a synthetic call locks in 0.95 today

walkthrough.problem: A stock trades at 50. Six-month European options have X = 50, r = 4% a year, and the call costs 4.20. Find the put price from put-call parity. Then find it from put-call-forward parity when the 6-month forward price is 51.
walkthrough.display_ba: 49.0290 (PV of X, STO 1); 3.2290 (put); 3.2194 (put from the forward)

keys.what: PV of the strike X/(1 + r)^T, T = 0.5
Put from parity p0 = c0 − S0 + X/(1 + r)^T
Put from put-call-forward parity p0 = c0 + (X − F0)/(1 + r)^T

walkthrough.note: The two puts differ slightly because a forward price of 51 is a little above the no-carry value 50 x 1.04^0.5 = 50.9902; at that forward they would match. T = 0.5, not 6.

check_plan: c2 (mc, why): why is the strike discounted in put-call parity but the stock price is not? A: because the stock pays dividends; B: because the stock is riskier than the strike; C (right): the stock is worth S0 today, while the strike is paid only at expiry, so the bond that pays X at T costs X/(1 + r)^T today; right answer at C
c3 (num, twist - put-call-forward parity, solve for the call): F0 = 62, X = 60, r = 5%, T = 0.5, put 2.10: call = 2.10 + (62 - 60)/1.05^0.5 = 4.0518; tol 0.01

c4 (mc, exam): S0 = 40, X = 42, T = 9 months, r = 6%, call 3.10: the parity put price is closest to: A 5.10 (did not discount the strike); B 6.81 (discounted the stock instead of the strike); C 3.30 (right: 3.10 - 40 + 42/1.06^0.75); right answer at C

c5 (explain): why could Palm's puts break parity, and what normally stops that? Must contain: parity follows from a fiduciary call and a protective put having the same payoffs, so they must cost the same; a violation is closed by selling the dear side and buying the cheap side (here short the stock, buy the synthetic); short-sale constraints (hard-to-borrow Palm shares) blocked that leg, so the mispricing lasted
days.verification_note: Fact-checked 2026-11-06 by WebSearch (nber.org could not be fetched). Verified: 2 March 2000 carve-out; Palm priced at $38 and closed at $95.0625; 3Com fell 21% to $81.8125 (WSJ, Wired, CNNMoney; The Register's $83.81 is a typo); 1.525 Palm shares per 3Com share; stub value about -$63 a share, about -$22 billion in all; Palm puts about twice as expensive as calls, violating put-call parity, with shorting hard and costly (Chicago Booth Review, Spatt, Varma, citing Lamont & Thaler). Recomputed in Python: 1.525 x 95.0625 = 144.97 and 81.8125 - 144.97 = -63.16, so the hook now gives the exact ratio, 'about $145' and 'about $63 below' instead of the looser 'over $140' / 'more than $60', and adds the $38 IPO price and the 21% fall. Stake sold: sources give 5% or 6% (retained 95% or 94%), so 'about 5%' stays. Headline hint reworded to say 3Com's Palm stake (not Palm's shares in general) was worth more than all of 3Com. Payoff numbers are illustrative and unchanged.

days.module: Valuing a Derivative Using a One-Period Binomial Model
days.title: One-period binomial option pricing
days.concept: In a one-period binomial model an option is priced by building a riskless hedge of stock and option, which yields the risk-neutral probability π = (1 + r − d)/(u − d) and the option value c_0 = [π c_u + (1 − π) c_d]/(1 + r) — real-world probabilities never enter.
los: Up and down factors u = S_u/S_0, d = S_d/S_0 (some CFA readings write these gross returns as R^u and R^d, and the up-state values as S_1^u, c_1^u); no-arbitrage requires d < 1 + r < u
Risk-neutral probability π = (1 + r − d)/(u − d)
c_0 = [π c_u + (1 − π) c_d]/(1 + r); same for puts
Hedge ratio h = (c_u − c_d)/(S_u − S_d); the replicating portfolio
Checking the put value with put-call parity

calculator.task: S_0 = 100, u = 1.2, d = 0.85, r = 3% for one period, X = 100: π, the call value, the hedge ratio, and the put value checked against put-call parity
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.front: Risk-neutral probability of an up move
memorize.back: π = (1 + r − d) / (u − d), where u = S_u/S_0 and d = S_d/S_0 (also written R^u and R^d)
h = (c_u − c_d) / (S_u − S_d)

memorize.front: No-arbitrage condition for the binomial model
memorize.back: d < 1 + r < u

traps: Using real-world probabilities instead of π
Discounting at the stock's expected return instead of the risk-free rate
Getting the hedge ratio upside down

story_idea.candidate: On 26 April 1973 the Chicago Board Options Exchange opened for business, trading call options on 16 stocks — 911 contracts on the first day. Within weeks Fischer Black and Myron Scholes published their option-pricing formula, and traders were soon using it on hand-held calculators.
story_idea.why: An option's payoff depends on where the stock goes, yet nobody knows the odds. How can there be one correct price for it?

days.headline_hint: Chicago, 1973: how to put one price on a bet when nobody knows the odds

story.title: The exchange that opened before anyone knew the price
story.hook: On 26 April 1973 the Chicago Board Options Exchange opened, the first exchange for listed stock options. Only calls were traded, on 16 stocks, and 911 contracts changed hands that first day (puts did not arrive until 1977). That spring the Journal of Political Economy's May-June issue carried Fischer Black and Myron Scholes's 'The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities', and before long traders were pricing options with Texas Instruments calculators programmed with their formula. In September 1979 John Cox, Stephen Ross and Mark Rubinstein showed the same logic with nothing harder than a stock that can only go up or down in one step.
story.puzzle: A call pays off only if the stock rises, and nobody knows the odds of that. How can there be one correct price for it, the same for an optimist and a pessimist?
story.payoff: Take today's stock: S_0 = 100, up to 120 or down to 85, call strike 100, r = 3%. Buy h = 0.5714 of a share for each call you sell: the position is worth 48.5714 if the stock rises and 48.5714 if it falls. A position with no risk must earn the risk-free rate, so it is worth 47.1567 today, which pins the call at 57.1429 - 47.1567 = 9.9861. The chance of an up move never entered. The pi = 0.5143 that falls out of the formula is a pricing weight, not anyone's forecast: that is why one price can satisfy everyone.
sources: Cboe Holdings, 2012 Annual Report (first day: 911 contracts on 16 underlying stocks) — cdn.cboe.com/resources/annual_reports/annualreport2012.pdf
IBKR Campus / Cboe history pieces (calls only at launch; puts introduced 1977) — ibkrcampus.com/?p=189476; optionstrategist.com 'Happy 40th Birthday, CBOE'
Black, F. and Scholes, M. (1973), 'The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities', Journal of Political Economy 81(3), May-June 1973, pp. 637-654

Harvard Business School Baker Library exhibit 'Option Pricing in Theory & Practice: The Nobel Prize Research of Robert C. Merton' (formula spread to CBOE traders; TI handheld preprogrammed for Black-Scholes values and hedge ratios) — library.hbs.edu/hc/exhibits/merton
Wally Rhines, '20 Questions with Wally Rhines: Black-Scholes and IC design', SemiWiki (TI's options program for its programmable calculators)

Cox, J.C., Ross, S.A. and Rubinstein, M. (1979), 'Option pricing: A simplified approach', Journal of Financial Economics 7(3), September 1979, pp. 229-263 (credits William Sharpe's 1978 textbook Investments)

worked_example.problem: A stock trades at 50 and in one year will be either 62.50 (u = 1.25) or 40 (d = 0.80). The risk-free rate is 5%. Value a one-year European call with X = 50 by building a riskless hedge, then check with the risk-neutral probability.
steps: Hedge ratio: h = (c_u - c_d)/(S_u - S_d) = 12.50/22.50 = 5/9 = 0.5556 shares per call
Hold h = 5/9 share and sell 1 call. Up: (5/9) x 62.50 - 12.50 = 22.2222. Down: (5/9) x 40 - 0 = 22.2222. Same either way: riskless
A riskless position earns 5%: its value today = 22.2222/1.05 = 21.1640
Today the position costs h x S_0 - c_0 = 27.7778 - c_0, so c_0 = 27.7778 - 21.1640 = 6.6138

walkthrough.problem: S_0 = 100, u = 1.2, d = 0.85, r = 3% for one period, X = 100. Find pi, the call value, the hedge ratio, and the put value, then check the put with put-call parity.

keys.what: Risk-neutral probability pi = (1 + r - d)/(u - d)
Call value c_0 = [pi x 20 + (1 - pi) x 0]/1.03
Hedge ratio h = (20 - 0)/(120 - 85)
Put value p_0 = [pi x 0 + (1 - pi) x 15]/1.03
Parity check p_0 = c_0 - S_0 + X/(1 + r)

check_plan: c1 (num, calculator): S_0 = 80, u = 1.10, d = 0.90, r = 2%, X = 78: the call value = 5.8824 (pi = 0.6000; c_u = 10, c_d = 0); tol 0.01; solution with both keystroke lines

c2 (mc, why): Why do the real-world probabilities of up and down not appear in c_0? Right: the hedged position (h shares short one call) pays the same in both states, so it must earn the risk-free rate whatever the odds. Wrong: 'because investors are assumed to be risk-neutral in reality' (the model assumes no such thing); 'because the real probability of an up move always equals pi' (pi is a pricing weight, not a forecast)

c3 (num, twist): same stock as c1 — value the put with X = 78 (p_u = 0, p_d = 6): p_0 = 0.4 x 6/1.02 = 2.3529; solution confirms it with parity c_0 - S_0 + X/1.02 = 2.3529 and notes h = 0.625, i.e. 625 shares hedge 1,000 written calls

c4 (mc, exam): S_0 = 40, u = 1.30, d = 0.80, r = 4%, X = 42; analysts put the chance of an up move at 65%. The call's value is closest to: 4.62 (right: pi = 0.48); 6.25 (used the 65% real-world probability); 4.80 (forgot to discount by 1.04)

c5 (explain, say it back): In two sentences, why is pi called a 'risk-neutral' probability? Points: (1) a stock-and-option hedge is riskless so it earns r; (2) pi is the weight that makes the stock's expected return equal r; (3) it is used for pricing, not as a forecast of what will happen
days.verification_note: Fact-check 2026-11-06 (WebSearch, plus WebFetch of sec.gov primary documents where noted): VERIFIED: CBOE opened 26 April 1973 with 911 contracts on 16 stocks, calls only; listed puts began in 1977 (Cboe 2012 annual report, Option Strategist, Mondo Visione/CBOE release via search; Cboe's 50th-anniversary page gives 19 April for the 16-stock listing, but 26 April is the opening day in every other source). HBS Baker Library Merton exhibit confirms that within about six months of publication the formula was so widely used at the CBOE that Texas Instruments made a handheld preprogrammed for Black-Scholes prices and hedge ratios; the story keeps the looser 'before long' because other accounts date wide adoption later. Black-Scholes (JPE 81(3), May-June 1973, pp. 637-654) and Cox-Ross-Rubinstein (JFE 7(3), September 1979, pp. 229-263) citations are standard bibliographic facts. NO CHANGES to the story. Not verified: the TI model number and exact launch date (not stated in the story).

days.module: Exchange Rate Calculations
days.title: Exchange rates and cross rates
days.concept: An exchange rate A/B is the price of one unit of the base currency B in units of the price currency A, cross rates follow by multiplying quotes so the common currency cancels, and one currency's percentage change against another is not the negative of the other's.
los: Quote convention: A/B = units of A (price currency) per one unit of B (base currency)
Cross rate: (A/B) × (B/C) = A/C; inverting a quote 1/(A/B) = B/A
Percentage change of the base currency = (new/old) − 1 for the A/B quote
Change of the price currency against the base = 1/(1 + %Δ) − 1
Nominal vs real exchange rate (concept)

calculator.task: In CFA notation (price currency/base currency) CHF/EUR, francs per euro, falls from the 1.2000 floor to 1.0400 (an illustrative level after the shock): the % change of the euro against the franc and of the franc against the euro; then, with CHF/USD at 0.8950 (illustrative), the cross rate USD/EUR

calculator.ti: Home screen: (new/old − 1) × 100; division for the cross rate

memorize.back: Units of currency A (price currency) per 1 unit of currency B (base currency)
(A/B) × (B/C) = A/C

memorize.front: Percentage change of the base currency in an A/B quote
memorize.back: %Δ_base = (A/B)_new / (A/B)_old − 1

memorize.front: Percentage change of the price currency against the base
memorize.back: %Δ_price = 1 / (1 + %Δ_base) − 1

Assuming the franc's % rise against the euro equals the euro's % fall against the franc

story_idea.candidate: At about 10:30 a.m. on 15 January 2015 the Swiss National Bank dropped its 1.20-francs-per-euro floor (in place since September 2011) and cut its deposit rate to −0.75%. Within minutes the euro traded as low as about 0.85 francs before steadying near parity; FXCM's clients ran up about $225 million of negative balances and Alpari UK became insolvent.
story_idea.why: Reports said the euro fell almost 30% while the franc jumped close to 40%. Same move — can both be right?

days.headline_hint: Swiss shock: the euro fell about 29% and the franc rose about 41%, in the same few minutes

story.title: The morning the Swiss let go
story.hook: From September 2011 the Swiss National Bank held a floor under the euro: one euro would always buy at least 1.20 Swiss francs. At about 10:30 a.m. Swiss time on 15 January 2015 it dropped the floor without warning and cut its deposit rate to −0.75%. Within minutes the euro was trading as low as about 0.85 francs (reported lows vary by venue), before steadying a little above one franc. The US broker FXCM said clients' losses had left about $225 million of negative balances owed to it, and the London broker Alpari UK announced the next day that it was insolvent.
story.puzzle: Reports that day said the euro had lost close to 30% against the franc; others said the franc had jumped by as much as about 40% against the euro. It was one move in one currency pair. Which number is right?
story.payoff: Both. In CFA notation the floor was CHF/EUR 1.20 (francs per euro; the euro is the base). At 0.85 the euro's change is 0.85/1.20 − 1 = −29.17%. Turn the quote over: EUR/CHF went from 1/1.20 = 0.8333 to 1/0.85 = 1.1765, so the franc's change is 1.20/0.85 − 1 = +41.18%. Same ratio, different base: 1/(1 − 0.2917) − 1 = 0.4118. A fall of x in one currency is a rise of 1/(1 − x) − 1 in the other, which is always bigger than x.
sources: b-sharpe.com, 'Swiss franc: a look back at the end of the EUR/CHF floor in 2015' (floor 1.20 introduced September 2011, removed 15 January 2015)
eToro blog 15 Jan 2015 and investing.com/CMC Markets 15 Jan 2015 (announcement about 10:30 CET / 9:30 GMT; deposit rate −0.75%)
DailyFX, 15 Jan 2015, 'EURCHF falls as much as 28% after SNB removes floor'; Finance Magnates, 'CHF Crisis Revisited' (low of about 0.85, then just above parity)
AP via HeraldNet, 'Switzerland stuns markets by giving up on currency peg' (franc up as much as 39% at one point)

swissinfo.ch, 'FXCM faces losses as Swiss shock leaves Alpari UK insolvent' (FXCM statement of 15 Jan: about $225 million of negative client equity); Pound Sterling Live / IBTimes / Sharecast / The Drum (Alpari UK announced its insolvency on 16 Jan 2015; KPMG special administrators were appointed by the High Court on 19 Jan 2015)

worked_example.problem: JPY/USD (yen per dollar) rises from 110.00 to 125.00. Find the % change of the dollar against the yen and of the yen against the dollar. Then, with USD/EUR at 1.1000, find the cross rate JPY/EUR.
steps: The quote is JPY/USD, so the dollar is the base: its change = 125.00/110.00 − 1 = 13.6364%
The yen is the price currency: invert both quotes (USD/JPY = 1/110 then 1/125), so its change = 110.00/125.00 − 1 = -12.0000%
Cross rate: (JPY/USD) × (USD/EUR) = 125.00 × 1.1000 = 137.50 JPY/EUR — the dollars cancel

story_idea.candidate: In 1970 Chrysler switched its inventory costing from LIFO to FIFO; by one account (Bhattacharya, citing the New York Times of 10 February 1971) this let it show a small fourth-quarter profit instead of a loss (the account's dollar figures are unconfirmed and not used). In 1973-74, with US inflation above 10%, the shift went the other way — primarily FIFO to LIFO — on a scale that Zarnowitz and Moore (1977) said distorted the Commerce Department's inventory statistics.
story_idea.why: Same goods, same cash: how can a costing rule turn a loss into a profit — and why would so many firms then pick the rule that shrinks profit?

days.headline_hint: Chrysler's loss became a profit — then America's companies chose smaller profits on purpose

story.title: One rule, two answers
story.hook: In 1970 Chrysler changed the way it costed its inventory, from LIFO to FIFO. By one account (a later academic history of Chrysler's accounts, citing the New York Times of 10 February 1971), the change let it report a small fourth-quarter profit where the old method would have shown a loss. Four years later, with US consumer prices rising more than 10% a year, companies rushed the other way. The 1973-74 switch, mainly from FIFO to LIFO, was so widespread that the economists Victor Zarnowitz and Geoffrey Moore later argued it had distorted the US Commerce Department's figures on business inventories. Those companies chose to report lower profits.
story.puzzle: Same factories, same goods, same cash paid to suppliers. How can picking an accounting rule turn a loss into a profit, and why would so many companies, a few years later, pick the rule that makes profit smaller?
story.payoff: When unit costs rise, FIFO sends the oldest, cheapest costs to COGS and LIFO the newest, dearest ones. In today's worked example (costs rising from $20 to $22 to $25, 120 units sold at $40), FIFO COGS is 2,540 and gross profit 2,260; LIFO COGS is 2,790 and gross profit 2,010. Chrysler's switch to FIFO lifted reported profit in exactly this way. The 1974 switchers accepted 250 less profit because, at a 25% tax rate, it saves 62.50 of tax in cash, and the US LIFO conformity rule meant that to use LIFO for taxes they had to report the lower LIFO profit to shareholders too.
sources: Keron Bhattacharya, chapter on Chrysler's accounting (Palgrave Macmillan), abstract on IDEAS/RePEc h/pal/palchp/978-1-349-12887-7_7, citing the New York Times, 10 February 1971 (the FIFO switch turned what would have been a Q4 1970 loss into a reported profit; the chapter's figures, a $7.6 million profit vs a $3.6 million loss, could not be confirmed against the NYT article or Chrysler's own reports and are deliberately not used on the page)

Biddle, G.C. (1980), 'Accounting Methods and Management Decisions: The Case of Inventory Costing and Inventory Policy', Journal of Accounting Research 18 (Supplement), pp. 235-280 — cites Zarnowitz and Moore (1977) on the 1973-74 shift 'primarily FIFO to LIFO'
Eastman Kodak annual report excerpt ('many U.S. corporations moved from ... FIFO ... to ... LIFO in 1974') — mcnygenealogy.com/book/kodak/highlights-v28-2.pdf
Haskins & Sells paper, November 1974 ('rapidly increasing prices will maximize the tax deferral in 1974'; several large companies changing to LIFO) — core.ac.uk

days.module: Analysis of Inventories
days.title: LIFO reserve, LIFO liquidation and NRV
days.concept: The LIFO reserve (FIFO inventory − LIFO inventory) lets an analyst restate a LIFO company as if it used FIFO — inventory + reserve, COGS − change in reserve, equity + reserve × (1 − t) — while a LIFO liquidation flatters profit with old, cheap costs and inventory is written down when it is worth less than cost.
los: Inventory_FIFO = Inventory_LIFO + LIFO reserve
COGS_FIFO = COGS_LIFO − (ending LIFO reserve − beginning LIFO reserve)
Balance-sheet restatement: equity + reserve × (1 − t); deferred taxes (or cash) + reserve × t
LIFO liquidation: old low costs flow into COGS, boosting margins temporarily

IFRS: lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV = estimated selling price − costs to complete and sell), reversals allowed; US GAAP: lower of cost and NRV for FIFO/average, lower of cost or market for LIFO, no reversals

story_idea.candidate: United States Steel's Form 10-K for 2022: current acquisition costs of its LIFO inventories exceeded their book value by $1,154 million at 31 December 2022 (up from $896 million), and liquidations of LIFO layers raised its EBIT by $44 million in 2022 ($11 million in 2021, $5 million in 2020).
story_idea.why: Part of U.S. Steel's inventory sits on its balance sheet at costs from decades ago. How do you compare it fairly with a rival using FIFO — and how much of a year's profit came simply from selling old, cheap layers?

days.headline_hint: U.S. Steel's $1.15 billion footnote: restating a LIFO company as if it used FIFO

story.title: U.S. Steel's $1,154 million footnote
story.hook: At the end of 2022 United States Steel valued 43% of its consolidated inventories on LIFO (the predominant method in its Flat-Rolled and Tubular segments), so part of its balance sheet carried raw materials and steel at costs from layers built up years ago. Its Form 10-K for 2022 says the current cost of those LIFO inventories exceeded their book value by $1,154 million at 31 December 2022, up from $896 million a year earlier. It also says that liquidations of LIFO layers lowered cost of sales and raised earnings before interest and income taxes by $44 million in 2022 (after $11 million in 2021 and $5 million in 2020). Total inventories on its balance sheet were $2,359 million.
story.puzzle: A rival on FIFO carries its inventory near today's cost. How do you put the two on the same footing (inventory, cost of sales, equity), and how much of 2022's profit came simply from selling old, cheap layers?
story.payoff: The $1,154 million is the LIFO reserve. Add it to the $2,359 million of inventory to see the balance sheet with those layers at current cost, as FIFO would show them: $3,513 million. The reserve rose by 1,154 − 896 = $258 million, so FIFO cost of sales would have been $258 million lower and pre-tax profit that much higher. Equity on a FIFO basis rises by the reserve after tax: at an illustrative 21% rate, 1,154 × 0.79 = $911.66 million, with $242.34 million to deferred taxes. And the $44 million from liquidated layers is a one-off: old costs flowing out, not better steelmaking.
sources: United States Steel Corporation, Form 10-K for fiscal year 2022, inventory note (LIFO reserve $1,154 million at 31 Dec 2022 and $896 million at 31 Dec 2021; LIFO liquidations raised EBIT by $44 million, $11 million and $5 million in 2022, 2021 and 2020; total inventories $2,359 million; LIFO used for 43% of consolidated inventories, predominantly Flat-Rolled and Tubular) — checked against the filing on EDGAR, 2026-11-05 — sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1163302/000116330223000016/x-20221231.htm

days.module: Analysis of Long-Term Assets
days.title: Capitalize or expense?
days.concept: Capitalizing a cost puts it on the balance sheet and spreads it over later years as depreciation, so it raises current profit, assets and equity and moves the cash outflow from operating to investing activities — and capitalized interest does the same with borrowing costs during construction.
los: Capitalize vs expense: effects on net income (first year and later), total assets, equity, CFO, CFI and ratios (ROA, ROE, interest coverage)
Total cash flow is unchanged; only its classification and timing of expense change
Capitalized interest: added to the asset, later depreciated; classified in CFI; interest coverage effects
Intangible assets: research expensed; development costs capitalized under IFRS when criteria are met (expensed under US GAAP, except software)

memorize.back: Higher net income, assets and equity; higher CFO and lower (more negative) CFI
Total expense and total cash flow are the same; capitalizing moves expense into later years (later-year NI is lower)
Added to the asset's cost (later depreciated); the cash paid is classified in CFI
Interest coverage = EBIT / interest expense (analysts add capitalized interest to the denominator)
IFRS: research expensed, development capitalized once criteria are met; US GAAP: both expensed (software development after technological feasibility is capitalized)
