Forgetting that the ratio effects reverse in later years

story_idea.candidate: In June 2002 WorldCom admitted that it had booked about $3.8 billion of ordinary 'line costs' — fees paid to other carriers — as capital investments, turning losses into profits. The fraud was uncovered by Cynthia Cooper, head of internal audit, and her team, working at night; WorldCom filed for bankruptcy weeks later.
story_idea.why: How can simply moving an expense onto the balance sheet turn a loss into a profit — and improve reported cash flow from operations too?

days.headline_hint: WorldCom's $3.8 billion trick: turning everyday bills into 'investments'

story.title: Cynthia Cooper's night shift
story.hook: In the spring of 2002 Cynthia Cooper, head of internal audit at WorldCom, set her small team to check the company's capital spending. Working often at night and in secret, they found entries that had moved 'line costs' (the access fees WorldCom paid other carriers to use their networks) into capital-expenditure accounts; Gene Morse searched the accounting system for them. On 25 June 2002 WorldCom announced that $3.055 billion of line costs in 2001 and $797 million in the first quarter of 2002 had been treated as capital spending, and that without the transfers it would have reported net losses for both periods. It filed for bankruptcy on 21 July 2002, and by November 2002 it expected its restatements to exceed $9 billion in all (later accounts put the total near $11 billion).
story.puzzle: Line costs were ordinary bills, paid in cash, month after month. How can moving them onto the balance sheet turn a loss into a profit and make operating cash flow look stronger too?
story.payoff: An expense hits this year's profit and CFO in full. A capitalized cost becomes an asset: only a slice (depreciation) reaches each year's income statement, and the cash paid is classified as investing. In today's walkthrough, capitalizing a 3 cost lifts year-1 net income from 3.75 to 5.55 and CFO from 3.75 to 6.15, while CFI goes from 0 to -3.00. WorldCom did this with $3.852 billion of costs that bought no long-lived asset at all, so they should never have been capitalized: reported EBITDA and CFO were inflated by the whole amount, and pre-tax profit by nearly as much.
sources: WorldCom press release and Form 8-K exhibit 99.1, 25 June 2002 ($3.055 billion in 2001, $797 million in Q1 2002; EBITDA would fall to $6.339 billion and $1.368 billion; net losses for both periods without the transfers) — checked against the exhibit on EDGAR, 2026-11-05 — sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000723527/000091205702025338/a2083227zex-99_1.txt; NANOG/MIT archive of the release

worked_example.problem: A 1.2 (millions) cost buys an asset with a 3-year life (straight-line, no salvage). Revenue is 10 and other cash expenses 6 each year; tax 30%, paid as expensed. Compare net income and cash flow over the 3 years if the cost is expensed in year 1 vs capitalized.

days.concept: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost minus salvage over its life — straight-line evenly, double-declining-balance at 2/n of each year's opening book value (front-loaded, stopping at salvage), units-of-production by use — and ratios of the accounts reveal an asset base's age and remaining life.

Amortization of finite-lived intangibles (no amortization for indefinite-lived/goodwill)
Estimated useful life = gross PPE/depreciation expense; average age = accumulated depreciation/depreciation expense; remaining life = net PPE/depreciation expense
Changes in estimates are prospective (no restatement)

story_idea.candidate: In February 1998 Waste Management restated its earnings for 1992-1997 by about $1.7 billion, then the largest restatement in US history. The SEC later charged that executives had inflated profits partly by stretching the useful lives of garbage trucks and raising their assumed salvage values.
story_idea.why: Nobody's trucks lasted any longer. How did changing two estimates in the depreciation formula add hundreds of millions to profit?

days.headline_hint: Waste Management's slow-aging trucks: two estimates inside a $1.7 billion restatement

story.title: Garbage trucks that aged slowly
story.hook: In February 1998 Waste Management, the US waste-hauling giant, filed restated financial statements for 1992 through the third quarter of 1997, admitting that pre-tax earnings had been overstated by about $1.7 billion — then the largest restatement in corporate history. In March 2002 the SEC sued its founder Dean Buntrock and five other former officers. Among the charges: they had avoided depreciation on the company's garbage trucks by stretching the trucks' estimated useful lives and giving them unsupported, inflated salvage values. The company's operating units depreciated each truck over eight years with no salvage value; in 1993, the SEC said, headquarters instead assumed 12 years and $30,000 of salvage, and booked the difference as a cut in expenses.
story.puzzle: Not one truck lasted a day longer. How could changing two estimates in a depreciation formula add hundreds of millions of dollars to profit?
story.payoff: Straight-line depreciation is (cost − salvage)/life, so both estimates sit inside the formula. Put the SEC's two sets of assumptions on a $100,000 truck like today's (the price is only an illustration): 8 years and no salvage give 100,000/8 = 12,500 a year; 12 years and $30,000 of salvage give (100,000 − 30,000)/12 = 5,833.33 a year — 6,666.67 (53.3%) less expense per truck, every year, with no change in the truck. Multiply by a fleet and the profit appears. Honest changes in estimates are made prospectively, with no restatement; Waste Management had to restate because its estimates were not supportable.
sources: US SEC, Litigation Release LR-17435 and complaint, SEC v. Dean L. Buntrock et al., filed 26 March 2002 (restatement filed February 1998 for 1992-Q3 1997; pre-tax earnings overstated about $1.7 billion; useful lives extended and salvage values inflated on garbage trucks; complaint para. 40: operating units used an eight-year life and no salvage, headquarters in 1993 assumed 12 years and $30,000) — checked against the SEC documents, 2026-11-05 — sec.gov/litigation/litreleases/lr17435.htm; sec.gov/litigation/complaints/complr17435.htm

days.module: Analysis of Long-Term Assets
days.title: Impairment, revaluation and disposal
days.concept: When an asset's carrying amount exceeds what it can recover, it is written down — under IFRS to the recoverable amount (higher of fair value less costs to sell and value in use), under US GAAP to fair value after a recoverability test on undiscounted cash flows — and selling an asset books a gain or loss of proceeds minus carrying amount.
los: IFRS: impaired if carrying amount > recoverable amount = max(fair value − costs to sell, value in use) (IAS 36 now says 'costs of disposal'; the curriculum uses 'costs to sell'); value in use = PV of future cash flows
US GAAP: step 1 — carrying amount > undiscounted future cash flows? step 2 — write down to fair value
Reversals: allowed under IFRS (up to the original carrying amount), not under US GAAP for assets held for use
Revaluation model (IFRS only): increases to revaluation surplus in OCI unless reversing an earlier loss
Derecognition: gain/loss = proceeds − carrying amount (non-cash; deducted from NI in indirect CFO)
Impairment is non-cash: CFO unaffected, ratios change

memorize.back: Higher of fair value less costs to sell and value in use (PV of expected future cash flows)

memorize.front: US GAAP impairment test (assets held for use)
memorize.back: Step 1: impaired if carrying amount > undiscounted expected future cash flows; step 2: loss = carrying amount − fair value
IFRS: allowed (up to the carrying amount there would have been without the impairment); US GAAP: not allowed for assets held for use
Increase: to revaluation surplus in OCI (to profit only if it reverses an earlier loss); decrease: to profit (to OCI only if it reverses an earlier surplus)
Gain (loss) = sale proceeds − carrying amount; non-cash, so removed from net income in indirect CFO; proceeds are in CFI

traps: Using discounted cash flows in the US GAAP recoverability test
Allowing impairment reversals under US GAAP
Treating an impairment as a cash outflow

days.headline_hint: Bought for $3.7 billion, sold for $50 million: Rio Tinto and the impairment test

story.title: Rio Tinto's $3.7 billion coal, sold for $50 million
story.hook: In 2011 the Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto paid about $3.7 billion for Riversdale Mining and its coal projects in Mozambique. The plan to move the coal by barge down the Zambezi River did not receive approval, and Rio said building the infrastructure had proved more challenging than it expected. On 17 January 2013 it said it would book about $14 billion of impairments in its 2012 results, about $3 billion of them on Rio Tinto Coal Mozambique, and chief executive Tom Albanese stepped down the same day. In July 2014 Rio agreed to sell the Mozambique coal business to India's International Coal Ventures for $50 million.
story.puzzle: Rio had paid real money for real coal in the ground. At what point does an accountant say an asset is no longer worth its balance-sheet figure, and how far down does it go?
story.payoff: Rio Tinto reports under IFRS, where an asset (or cash-generating unit) is impaired when its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount: the higher of fair value less costs to sell and value in use, the PV of the cash it is expected to produce. Rio measured Mozambique's recoverable amount as fair value less costs to sell, by discounting the expected cash flows. Without the barges, and with less recoverable coking coal than it had assumed, those cash flows shrank, the recoverable amount fell below the carrying amount, and Rio wrote off the difference: US$2.86 billion after tax in its final 2012 accounts, a non-cash charge (the cash had gone out in 2011). Today's walkthrough is the same test in miniature: carrying 500, value in use 397.46, fair value less costs to sell 400, so the loss is 100. The 2014 sale for $50 million then booked a gain or loss of proceeds minus the carrying amount left.

days.module: Topics in Long-Term Liabilities and Equity
days.title: Leases on the balance sheet
days.concept: A lessee records a right-of-use asset and a lease liability equal to the PV of the lease payments, and the liability then amortizes like a loan: each period interest accrues on the balance and the payment reduces it.
los: Lease liability = PV of the lease payments not yet paid at commencement, at the rate implicit in the lease (or the incremental borrowing rate); with payments in advance the first payment is made at commencement, so the liability is the PV of the remaining N − 1 payments and the annuity-due PV of all N equals the right-of-use asset
Right-of-use asset initially = lease liability (+ initial direct costs and prepayments)
IFRS 16 single model: depreciation of the ROU asset + interest on the liability (front-loaded expense)
US GAAP: finance lease like IFRS; operating lease — single straight-line lease cost, still on the balance sheet
Effects on ratios: higher debt-to-equity and assets; higher EBITDA under IFRS
Lessor accounting: finance (sales-type) vs operating lease (concept)

Lease liability + lease payments made at or before commencement + initial direct costs − lease incentives received
Interest = rate × opening liability; the payment reduces the liability by (payment − interest)
Depreciation of the ROU asset + interest on the lease liability (front-loaded; EBITDA rises because rent is no longer an operating expense)
On the balance sheet (ROU asset and lease liability); single straight-line lease cost in the income statement

story_idea.candidate: When the IASB issued IFRS 16 in January 2016, effective from 1 January 2019, it estimated that listed companies using IFRS or US GAAP had about US$3.3 trillion of lease commitments, more than 85% of them not shown on their balance sheets — airlines and retailers were among the most affected.
story_idea.why: If a company has signed contracts to pay rent for years, isn't that debt? How do you put a future stream of rent on today's balance sheet?

days.headline_hint: The rent is debt: how IFRS 16 put Tesco's £10.7 billion of lease liabilities on show

story.title: The £10.7 billion that came out of the shadows
story.hook: On 13 January 2016 the International Accounting Standards Board issued IFRS 16 Leases, effective from 1 January 2019. It estimated that listed companies using IFRS or US GAAP had about US$3.3 trillion of lease commitments, more than 85% of which did not appear on their balance sheets; its chairman Hans Hoogervorst said off-balance-sheet lease financing would no longer be 'lurking in the shadows'. On 15 February 2019 the British supermarket group Tesco showed investors its accounts on the new basis: total lease liabilities of £10,687 million at 25 August 2018, of which only £125 million (finance leases) had already been on its balance sheet as borrowings.
story.puzzle: A lease is a promise to pay rent for years. If you have signed it, isn't it debt? And how do you turn a future stream of rent into one number on today's balance sheet?
story.payoff: Discount it. The lessee records a lease liability equal to the PV of the payments still to be made and a right-of-use asset for the right to use the property. In today's walkthrough five advance payments of 10,000 at 6% are worth 44,651.06: that is the right-of-use asset. The first 10,000 is paid on day one, so the liability is 34,651.06. Then it behaves like a loan: interest of 2,079.06 accrues in year 1, and the next payment brings the balance down to 26,730.12. Tesco's £10.7 billion is that same calculation done for every lease it holds.
sources: IFRS Foundation press release, 13 January 2016, 'IASB shines light on leases by bringing them onto the balance sheet' (about US$3.3 trillion of lease commitments, over 85% off balance sheet; Hoogervorst's 'lurking in the shadows') — ifrs.org/news-and-events/news/2016/01/iasb-shines-light-on-leases-by-bringing-them-onto-the-balance-sheet/
IASB, IFRS 16 Effects Analysis, January 2016 — ifrs.org/-/media/project/leases/ifrs/published-documents/ifrs16-effects-analysis.pdf

Tesco PLC, 'Introducing IFRS 16' investor presentation, 15 February 2019 (total current and non-current lease liabilities £(10,687)m at 25 August 2018, including £125m of finance lease liabilities previously classified as borrowings; also RNS 'Introducing IFRS 16', 15 Feb 2019) — tescoplc.com/media/754270/tesco-plc-introducing-ifrs-16-presentation.pdf

days.title: Deferred taxes: DTL and DTA
days.concept: Income tax expense differs from taxes payable because accounting and tax rules recognise items at different times: a deferred tax liability arises when an asset's carrying amount exceeds its tax base, DTL = (carrying amount − tax base) × t, and income tax expense = taxes payable + ΔDTL − ΔDTA.
los: Accounting profit vs taxable income; income tax expense vs taxes payable
Carrying amount vs tax base of assets and liabilities
DTL = (carrying amount − tax base) × t for assets (and DTA when the tax base is higher)
Income tax expense = taxes payable + ΔDTL − ΔDTA
Temporary vs permanent differences (permanent: no deferred tax)
Valuation allowance (US GAAP) against DTAs unlikely to be realised

calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.front: Deferred tax liability on an asset
memorize.back: DTL = (carrying amount − tax base) × tax rate, when carrying amount > tax base

memorize.front: Deferred tax asset on an asset
memorize.back: DTA = (tax base − carrying amount) × tax rate, when tax base > carrying amount

memorize.front: Deferred tax on a liability (e.g. a warranty provision)
memorize.back: Signs flip: carrying amount > tax base gives a DTA; carrying amount < tax base gives a DTL
Income tax expense = taxes payable + ΔDTL − ΔDTA
Differences that never reverse (e.g. tax-exempt income, non-deductible fines): no deferred tax; they make the effective rate differ from the statutory rate
Reduces a DTA when it is more likely than not (over 50%) that some of it will not be realised; IFRS recognises a DTA only to the extent its use is probable

Recording deferred tax for a permanent difference
Using the current rate when a different enacted future rate applies

story_idea.candidate: In February 2019 the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy reported that Amazon had paid no US federal income tax on about $11.2 billion of US profit for 2018 — and expected a rebate of about $129 million — thanks largely to tax credits, stock-option deductions and accelerated depreciation.
story_idea.why: How can a company report billions of profit to shareholders and almost none to the tax authority — and where on its balance sheet does the difference show up?

days.headline_hint: Amazon made $11.2 billion in the US and owed no federal tax. The difference sits on its balance sheet

story.title: Amazon's federal tax bill: minus $129 million
story.hook: In February 2019 the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP), a Washington research group, went through Amazon's annual report for 2018. Amazon had made $11.2 billion of profit before tax in the United States, almost double the $5.6 billion of 2017, yet the current US federal tax line in its tax note was negative: a $129 million benefit, which ITEP called a rebate. ITEP pointed to tax credits, the deduction for pay handed out in stock, and fast ('accelerated') tax depreciation of equipment. But in the same note, current and deferred federal tax together came to a positive $436 million of federal tax expense charged against the profit Amazon reported to shareholders.
story.puzzle: How can a company owe the US government less than nothing for a year and still charge $436 million of federal tax against its profit for that year — and where does the $565 million difference go?
story.payoff: Amazon's tax depreciation ran ahead of its book depreciation, so the carrying amount (book value) of its equipment was above its tax base. That gap times the tax rate is a deferred tax liability: tax postponed, not forgiven, to be paid as the gap reverses. The identity income tax expense = taxes payable + ΔDTL − ΔDTA balances the two numbers: federal expense = −$129 million + $565 million of deferred federal tax = $436 million. On the balance sheet, Amazon's deferred tax liability for depreciation and amortization grew from $2,568 million at the end of 2017 to $3,579 million at the end of 2018, up $1,011 million across all its tax jurisdictions.
sources: ITEP, 'Amazon in Its Prime: Doubles Profits, Pays $0 in Federal Income Taxes', February 2019, https://itep.org/amazon-in-its-prime-doubles-profits-pays-0-in-federal-income-taxes/ ($11.2 billion of US profit, up from $5.6 billion; $129 million federal rebate; credits, stock-pay deduction, depreciation)

Amazon.com, Inc., Form 10-K for 2018 (SEC accession 0001018724-19-000004), Note — Income Taxes, read via the SEC XBRL API: current US federal −$129 million, deferred US federal +$565 million, total provision $1,197 million, US pre-tax income $11,157 million (2017: $5,630 million), deferred tax liability for depreciation and amortization $2,568 million (2017) and $3,579 million (2018), valuation allowance $4,950 million
story.verification: WebSearch 2026-11-06 plus the 2026-11-05 SEC EDGAR check: ITEP figures and the 10-K tax note (current federal −$129m, deferred federal +$565m, provision $1,197m, DTL for depreciation $2,568m → $3,579m, valuation allowance $4,950m) confirmed.

story_idea.candidate: After the US Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was signed on 22 December 2017, cutting the corporate rate from 35% to 21%, Citigroup reported a one-time charge of about $22 billion for the fourth quarter of 2017, mostly from writing down its deferred tax assets — producing a quarterly loss despite a strong business.
story_idea.why: A tax cut is supposed to help companies. Why did one of America's biggest banks take a $22 billion hit from it?

days.headline_hint: A tax cut that cost Citigroup $22 billion: what a lower rate does to deferred tax assets

story.title: The tax cut that cost Citigroup $22 billion
story.hook: On 22 December 2017 the US Tax Cuts and Jobs Act became law, cutting the federal corporate income tax rate from 35% to 21% from 1 January 2018. On 16 January 2018 Citigroup reported a fourth-quarter net loss of $18.3 billion, or $7.15 a share. The cause was a one-time, non-cash charge of about $22 billion, which Citi described that day as about $19 billion from remeasuring its deferred tax assets for the lower rate and the move to a territorial tax system, plus about $3 billion linked to the deemed repatriation of its foreign subsidiaries' earnings. Without the charge, Citi said, it earned $3.7 billion that quarter. Its annual report, filed a few weeks later, put the charge at $22.6 billion.
story.puzzle: A tax cut is supposed to help companies. Why did one of America's biggest banks book a $22 billion hit from one?
story.payoff: A deferred tax asset is a future tax saving — deductions or credits the company will use later — valued at the rate in force when they are used. At 35% a dollar of future deduction saves 35 cents; at 21% it saves 21 cents. So the same DTA is worth only 21/35 = 60% as much: a pure rate cut writes off 40% of it, and the write-down goes straight into income tax expense, though no cash changes hands. In Citi's final accounts that remeasurement, for the lower rate and the territorial switch together, came to $12.4 billion. Most of the rest was a $7.9 billion valuation allowance against foreign tax credits the new rules made harder to use, plus a $2.3 billion cut in those credits from the deemed repatriation: a DTA is worth only what the company expects to be able to use. Even after the charge, Citi still carried $22.5 billion of net DTAs at the end of 2017. Companies with net deferred tax liabilities saw the opposite: their postponed tax bills shrank and they booked one-time gains.
sources: Citigroup, Fourth Quarter 2017 Earnings Release, 16 January 2018, https://www.citigroup.com/rcs/citigpa/storage/public/qer417.pdf (net loss $18.3 billion, $7.15 a share; one-time, non-cash charge of about $22 billion, described as about $19 billion of DTA remeasurement for the lower rate and the territorial shift plus about $3 billion related to the deemed repatriation; $3.7 billion, $1.28 a share, excluding it)
Fox Business, 'Citigroup reports $18.3 billion loss, caused by new tax law', 16 January 2018 (the CFO: about $19 billion of DTAs written off, roughly $23 billion still on the balance sheet)

Citigroup 2017 Form 10-K (SEC accession 0000831001-18-000040), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000831001/000083100118000040/c-12312017x10k.htm: charge to continuing operations of $22.6 billion in Q4 2017 = $12.4 billion remeasurement (lower US rate and quasi-territorial system) + $7.9 billion valuation allowance against foreign tax credit carry-forwards and US residual DTAs of non-US branches + $2.3 billion reduction in FTC carry-forwards related to the deemed repatriation; net DTAs of $22.5 billion at 31 December 2017
Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, Public Law 115-97, signed 22 December 2017 (21% rate from 1 January 2018)

c2 (mc, why): a rate cut raises tax expense for a company with a net DTA but lowers it for one with a net DTL. Why? Right: both are measured at the enacted future rate — future deductions save less (DTA shrinks, a charge) and future tax bills are smaller (DTL shrinks, a gain). Wrong: 'taxes payable fall for both' (true but not why); 'the DTA is remeasured, the DTL is not' (both are).

days.verification_note: Fact-check 2026-11-06 (3 WebSearches). Verified: Q4 2017 net loss $18.3 billion ($7.15 a share), charge of about $22 billion ($8.43 a share) booked in the tax line, about $19 billion DTA remeasurement with the remainder tied to the deemed repatriation, and $3.7 billion ($1.28 a share) excluding it (Citi press release on citigroup.com; Asian Banker, investinglive coverage). days.module: Analyzing Income Statements
days.title: Basic and diluted EPS
days.concept: Basic EPS divides earnings available to common shareholders by the weighted-average shares outstanding; diluted EPS adds the extra shares that convertibles, options and warrants would create — and adds back what they cost — using the if-converted and treasury stock methods, and ignores anything antidilutive.
los: Basic EPS = (net income − preferred dividends)/weighted-average common shares
Weighted-average shares; stock splits and stock dividends applied retroactively
If-converted method: convertible preferred (add back preferred dividends) and convertible bonds (add back interest × (1 − t))
Treasury stock method: incremental shares = n − (n × X)/average market price
Antidilutive securities are excluded (they would raise EPS)
Equities link: effects of share repurchases and splits on shares and EPS

Share repurchases (Equities): bought-back shares leave the weighted average from the purchase date; a debt-funded buyback raises EPS only if the earnings yield (E/P) exceeds the after-tax cost of debt; buying back above book value per share lowers BVPS

(NI − preferred dividends + dividends on the convertible preferred) / (weighted-average shares + shares from conversion)
[NI − preferred dividends + convertible interest × (1 − t)] / (weighted-average shares + shares from conversion)
New shares = shares from exercise − (exercise proceeds / average market price)
Exclude any security whose inclusion would increase diluted EPS (or reduce a loss per share)

memorize.front: When does a debt-funded share buyback raise EPS?
memorize.back: When the earnings yield E/P exceeds the after-tax cost of debt r_d × (1 − t)

Adding back pre-tax rather than after-tax interest on convertible bonds

story_idea.candidate: In January 2018 Tesla's board granted Elon Musk an all-or-nothing performance award of options on about 20.3 million shares (before later stock splits) in 12 tranches, tied to market-value and operating milestones — one of the largest pay packages ever proposed.
story_idea.why: Shareholders didn't hand over any shares that day. Why does an option grant still reduce earnings per share — and by how much?

days.headline_hint: Tesla gave Musk options on 20 million shares. Shareholders handed over nothing that day — or did they?

story.title: Musk's 20,264,042 options
story.hook: On 21 January 2018 Tesla's board granted Elon Musk a 'CEO Performance Award': options to buy 20,264,042 Tesla shares at $350.02 each, the closing price before the grant. They came in 12 tranches of about 1.69 million shares — each 1% of the 168,867,016 shares then outstanding — and a tranche could vest only when Tesla's market value reached the next milestone, from $100 billion for the first in $50 billion steps to $650 billion, and a revenue or profit milestone was also met. At $350.02 a share, Tesla was then worth about $59 billion. Stockholders approved the award on 21 March 2018.
story.puzzle: Nobody handed Musk a single share that day. Why do options like these still shrink earnings per share — and why did Tesla's 2018 diluted loss per share come out exactly equal to its basic loss per share?
story.payoff: Diluted EPS asks 'what if every potential share existed?' The treasury stock method pretends the options are exercised and the exercise money buys shares back at the average market price, so only the shortfall is new: new shares = n − n × X / P. Suppose (an illustration only) all 20,264,042 options counted and the average price were $500: the $7.09 billion of exercise money buys back 14,185,640 shares, leaving 6,078,402 new ones. But in 2018 Tesla lost $976 million. Adding shares to a loss makes the loss per share smaller — antidilutive — so every option was left out and diluted EPS equalled basic EPS: −$5.72 on 170.5 million weighted shares. In 2020, its first profitable year (after a 5-for-1 split), options, warrants and convertible notes added 150 million shares — 933 million basic versus 1,083 million diluted — and EPS was $0.74 basic but $0.64 diluted.
sources: Tesla, Inc., Form 8-K, 23 January 2018 (SEC accession 0001193125-18-016648): grant on 21 January 2018 of a 100% performance-based option award, subject to a stockholder vote

Tesla, Inc., definitive proxy statement (DEF 14A) filed 8 February 2018 (SEC accession 0001193125-18-035345): 20,264,042 shares in 12 tranches, 1% of 168,867,016 shares outstanding on 19 January 2018 each; exercise price $350.02; market-capitalization milestones $100 billion to $650 billion in $50 billion steps; 16 operational milestones (Appendix A, Tables 1 and 2)
Tesla, Inc., Form 8-K, 21 March 2018 (SEC accession 0001564590-18-006479): stockholders approved the award on 21 March 2018

Tesla 2018 and 2020 Forms 10-K, read via the SEC XBRL API: 2018 net loss $976 million, basic and diluted EPS −$5.72, 170.525 million weighted shares; 2020 net income used in computing EPS $690 million (net income attributable to common stockholders was $721 million), 933 million basic and 1,083 million diluted weighted shares, EPS $0.74 basic and $0.64 diluted

days.module: Analyzing Statements of Cash Flows I
days.title: Cash from operations: indirect and direct
days.concept: Profit and cash differ: the indirect method starts with net income, adds back non-cash charges and losses, subtracts gains, and adjusts for working capital (an increase in an operating asset uses cash, an increase in an operating liability provides it), while the direct method rebuilds cash received and paid line by line.
los: Indirect CFO = NI + non-cash charges (depreciation, amortization, impairment) − gains + losses − Δoperating assets + Δoperating liabilities
Direct method: cash from customers = revenue − ΔAR; cash paid to suppliers = COGS + ΔInventory − ΔAP; cash paid for other items
Converting indirect to direct
Classification: interest and dividends paid/received under IFRS vs US GAAP
CFI and CFF items

calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.back: CFO = NI + non-cash charges − gains + losses − increases in operating assets + increases in operating liabilities
Revenue − increase in accounts receivable
COGS + increase in inventory − increase in accounts payable
US GAAP: CFO; IFRS: CFO or CFF
US GAAP: CFF; IFRS: CFO or CFF
US GAAP: CFO; IFRS: CFO or CFI

Getting the working-capital signs backwards
Putting interest paid in CFF under US GAAP

story_idea.candidate: W. T. Grant, one of the largest US retailers with over 1,000 stores, filed for bankruptcy on 2 October 1975. A 1980 study by James Largay and Clyde Stickney showed that, through 1973, its operations had been a net user of cash rather than a provider, even as it kept reporting profits.
story_idea.why: How can a company report a profit year after year and still run out of cash?

days.headline_hint: W. T. Grant reported profits for years and still went broke. Its cash flows had been warning all along

story.title: W. T. Grant: profits on paper, no cash in the till
story.hook: On 2 October 1975 the W. T. Grant Company, a US variety-store chain that had run more than 1,000 stores in the early 1970s, filed for bankruptcy protection; it was declared bankrupt in April 1976 and liquidated. At the time it was the second-largest bankruptcy in American history, after the Penn Central railroad's. In 1980 two accounting professors, James Largay and Clyde Stickney, rebuilt Grant's cash flows in the Financial Analysts Journal and found that through 1973, while Grant was still reporting profits, its operations had been a net user of cash, not a provider, as the money owed by customers buying on credit, and its inventories, kept growing; the popular shortcut 'cash flow = net income + depreciation', they warned, had hidden it.
story.puzzle: How can a company report a profit year after year and still run out of cash — and which line of its accounts would have warned you?
story.payoff: Net income counts a credit sale the day it is made; the cash arrives only when the customer pays. The indirect method starts from net income and corrects it to cash: add back non-cash charges such as depreciation, subtract gains, subtract increases in operating assets (receivables and inventory soak up cash) and add increases in operating liabilities (payables are cash not yet paid out). An illustration, not Grant's figures: net income 40, depreciation 10, receivables up 60, inventory up 50, payables up 20 gives CFO = 40 + 10 − 60 − 50 + 20 = −40. Profit of +40, cash of −40: that was Grant's pattern, with the gap filled largely by borrowing. 'Net income + depreciation' would have shown +50 and hidden the drain; only the working-capital lines reveal it.
sources: James A. Largay III and Clyde P. Stickney, 'Cash Flows, Ratio Analysis and the W. T. Grant Company Bankruptcy', Financial Analysts Journal 36(4), July–August 1980, pp. 51–54 (abstract, CFA Institute Research and Policy Center: through 1973 Grant's operations were a net user, rather than provider, of cash; net income plus depreciation can be a very poor indicator of the ability to generate cash), https://rpc.cfainstitute.org/research/financial-analysts-journal/1980/cash-flows-ratio-analysis-and-the-wt-grant-company-bankruptcy
US court decision on the Grant estate (reported at leagle.com, 1988): Grant filed a Chapter XI petition on 2 October 1975 and was adjudicated bankrupt by order of 13 April 1976

Store count (more than 1,000 in the early 1970s; sources give about 1,070 to 1,200 at the peak) and the 1976 liquidation: standard accounts of the case (e.g. the Wikipedia article 'W. T. Grant'); 'the second biggest bankruptcy (after the wreck of the Penn Central Transportation Co.) in U.S. history': Time, 'Retailing: Sale of the Century', https://time.com/archive/6845515/retailing-sale-of-the-century (seen via search summary)

Year-by-year cash figures not seen; the payoff's numbers are an illustration.

days.module: Analyzing Statements of Cash Flows II
days.title: Free cash flow: FCFF and FCFE
days.concept: Free cash flow is what is left after the business funds its investment: free cash flow to the firm, FCFF = CFO + Int(1 − t) − FCInv, belongs to all capital providers, and free cash flow to equity, FCFE = CFO − FCInv + net borrowing, belongs to shareholders.
los: FCFF = CFO + Int(1 − t) − FCInv
FCFE = CFO − FCInv + net borrowing
FCFF from net income: NI + NCC + Int(1 − t) − FCInv − WCInv
Cash-flow ratios: CFO/revenue, cash return on assets, debt coverage (CFO/total debt), interest coverage (CFO + interest + taxes)/interest, reinvestment (CFO/capex)
FCFE and FCFF as equity valuation inputs (Equities)

FCFF = NI + NCC + Int × (1 − t) − FCInv − WCInv

(CFO + interest paid + taxes paid) / interest paid

Subtracting working-capital investment again when starting from CFO
Using the wrong sign for net borrowing (borrowing adds to FCFE)

story_idea.candidate: Netflix reported net income of about $1.9 billion for 2019 but free cash flow of about −$3.3 billion, because it paid cash for new films and series much faster than it expensed them; it covered the gap by selling bonds (about $4.47 billion of proceeds from new debt in 2019), and in January 2021 it told shareholders it no longer expected to need external financing for day-to-day operations.
story_idea.why: A company reporting billions in profit was borrowing billions to keep going. How much cash is really left over for lenders and shareholders — and where does new borrowing fit in?

days.headline_hint: Netflix earned $1.9 billion and burned $3.3 billion. Free cash flow shows who paid for the shows

story.title: Netflix: $1.9 billion of profit, −$3.3 billion of free cash flow
story.hook: For 2019 Netflix reported net income of $1.87 billion on revenue of $20.2 billion. Its cash flow statement told a different story: operating activities used $2.89 billion of cash, because it paid for new films and series far faster than it expensed them, and its own free-cash-flow measure came to −$3.27 billion. It covered the gap by borrowing — $4.47 billion of proceeds from new debt in 2019, including $1.0 billion and €1.1 billion of senior notes due 2030 sold in the fourth quarter. On 19 January 2021, after free cash flow of +$1.9 billion in 2020, it told shareholders it believed it no longer needed to raise external financing for its day-to-day operations.
story.puzzle: How much cash did Netflix's business really leave for its lenders and for its shareholders — and why does new borrowing count for one group but not the other?
story.payoff: FCFF = CFO + Int(1 − t) − FCInv is the cash left for ALL capital providers before any financing. With CFO of −$2,887 million, interest paid of $599 million (after tax at the 21% US federal rate, an illustration: $473 million) and $253 million of capital spending, FCFF ≈ −2,887 + 473 − 253 = −$2,667 million: the business consumed cash. FCFE = CFO − FCInv + net borrowing ≈ −2,887 − 253 + 4,469 = +$1,329 million (treating the new debt as net borrowing): positive only because lenders put money in. The shareholders' cash was being supplied by the bondholders — which is why the January 2021 letter mattered.
sources: Netflix, Inc., Form 10-K for 2019, read via the SEC XBRL API: net income $1,866.9 million, revenue $20,156.4 million, net cash used in operating activities $2,887.3 million, purchases of property and equipment $253.0 million, interest paid $599.1 million, proceeds from issuance of debt $4,469.3 million

Netflix Q4 2019 letter to shareholders, Form 8-K exhibit 99.1, 21 January 2020 (SEC accession 0001065280-20-000035): free cash flow −$3,274.4 million (= CFO − property and equipment − change in other assets); Q4 2019 issue of $1.0 billion 4.875% and €1.1 billion 3.625% senior notes due 2030

Netflix Q4 2020 letter to shareholders, Form 8-K exhibit 99.1, 19 January 2021 (SEC accession 0001065280-21-000037): 2020 free cash flow +$1.9 billion vs −$3.3 billion in 2019; 'we believe we no longer have a need to raise external financing for our day-to-day operations'

days.module: Financial Analysis Techniques
days.title: Common-size, activity ratios and the CCC
days.concept: Dividing by sales turns statements into common-size percentages and balances into days — DSO, DOH and DPO — whose combination DOH + DSO − DPO, the cash conversion cycle, measures how long cash is tied up in operations, and a sales-based pro forma forecasts next year's statements from those same percentages and days.
los: Common-size (vertical) statements: income-statement items as % of revenue, balance-sheet items as % of total assets
Receivables turnover = revenue/average receivables; DSO = 365/receivables turnover
Inventory turnover = COGS/average inventory; DOH = 365/inventory turnover
Payables turnover = purchases/average payables; DPO = 365/payables turnover
Cash conversion cycle = DOH + DSO − DPO (negative = suppliers finance operations)
Sales-based pro forma: forecast revenue, then costs as % of revenue and working capital from DSO, DOH and DPO

calculator.task: Revenue 8,000, COGS 6,000, purchases 6,200, average receivables 400, inventory 300 and payables 900: DSO, DOH, DPO and the cash conversion cycle; then next year's pro forma receivables if revenue grows 10% and DSO is unchanged
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.back: DSO = 365 / (revenue / average receivables)
DOH = 365 / (COGS / average inventory)
DPO = 365 / (purchases / average payables)
CCC = DOH + DSO − DPO
Income statement: each item / revenue; balance sheet: each item / total assets
Receivables = DSO × forecast revenue / 365

Mixing year-end and average balances
Dividing balance-sheet items by revenue in a common-size balance sheet (use total assets)
Reading a negative cash conversion cycle as a warning sign (it means suppliers fund the business)

story_idea.candidate: Dell, which sold PCs directly and built each one to order, reported in its 10-K for the fiscal year ended 1 February 1998 7 days of inventory, 36 days of receivables and 51 days of payables — a cash conversion cycle of −8 days (+40 two years earlier) — while revenue more than doubled to $12.3 billion; later 10-Ks reported −12 and −18 days.
story_idea.why: How can a company grow fast without needing more cash — and what single number captures how long its cash is tied up?

days.headline_hint: Dell more than doubled its sales in two years and its suppliers paid for it: the negative cash cycle

story.title: Dell's negative eight days
story.hook: Dell sold PCs straight to customers — through account representatives, by telephone and over the Internet — and built each one to order, so it kept very little stock. Its annual report for the year to 1 February 1998 gave 7 days of supply in inventory, 36 days of sales in receivables and 51 days in accounts payable; two years earlier the figures had been 31, 42 and 33. Over those two years revenue more than doubled, from $5.3 billion to $12.3 billion (up 59% in the last year alone), while cash and marketable securities rose from $646 million to $1.84 billion. A year later Dell's 10-K reported its 'cash conversion cycle' as negative 12 days, and the year after that negative 18.
story.puzzle: Growth normally eats cash — more stock on the shelves, more customers owing you money. How did Dell grow this fast and still pile up cash, and what single number captures it?
story.payoff: Cash conversion cycle = DOH + DSO − DPO: days the cash sits in inventory, plus days waiting for customers to pay, minus days taken to pay suppliers. Fiscal 1998: 7 + 36 − 51 = −8 days; fiscal 1996: 31 + 42 − 33 = +40. A negative cycle means Dell collected from its customers before it paid for the parts, so its suppliers' credit financed both its inventory and its receivables, and growth released cash instead of consuming it. Very roughly, at fiscal-1998 sales of $12.3 billion one day was worth about $34 million, so the 48-day swing was worth on the order of $1.6 billion (rough, because inventory and payables days are measured on cost of sales, not revenue).
sources: Dell Computer Corporation, Form 10-K for fiscal 1998 (year ended 1 February 1998; SEC accession 0000950134-98-003218): days of sales in receivables 36/37/42, days of supply in inventory 7/13/31, days in accounts payable 51/54/33 for fiscal 1998/1997/1996; net revenue $12,327m/$7,759m/$5,296m (up 59% and 47%); cash and marketable securities $1,844m/$1,352m/$646m; CFO $1.6 billion; build-to-order and direct sales through account representatives, telephone and Internet
Dell, Form 10-K for fiscal 1999 (SEC accession 0000950134-99-003281): cash conversion cycle (12) days, (8) for fiscal 1998
Dell, Form 10-K for fiscal 2000 (SEC accession 0000950134-00-003430): cash conversion cycle (18) days
story.verification: SEC EDGAR check 2026-11-05 plus WebSearch 2026-11-06: fiscal 1998 days figures, revenue and the fiscal 1999 cycle confirmed from the 10-Ks; fiscal 2000's −18 from secondary sources citing the 10-K.

Wrong: 'it is losing money' (profitability is a different question); 'it pays suppliers before customers pay it' (that is a positive cycle).

Verified: Dell's fiscal 1998 10-K (year ended 1 February 1998; accession 0000950134-98-003218): receivables 36 days, inventory 7 days, payables 51 days (also in a 1998 424B2 prospectus); net revenue $12,327m / $7,759m / $5,296m, up 59% in fiscal 1998; direct, build-to-order model with low inventory. days.module: Financial Analysis Techniques
days.title: DuPont: what drives ROE
days.concept: Return on equity can be split to show why it is high or low — ROE = (NI/EBT)(EBT/EBIT)(EBIT/Revenue)(Revenue/Average assets)(Average assets/Average equity) — separating tax burden, interest burden, operating margin, asset turnover and financial leverage, and solvency ratios measure the risk behind the last two factors.
los: Profitability ratios: gross, operating, pre-tax and net margins (the common-size income statement), ROA, ROE, return on total capital
Three-step DuPont: ROE = net profit margin × total asset turnover × financial leverage
Five-step DuPont: tax burden × interest burden × EBIT margin × asset turnover × leverage
Solvency ratios: debt-to-assets, debt-to-capital, debt-to-equity, financial leverage = average assets/average equity
Coverage ratios: interest coverage = EBIT/interest (interest burden EBT/EBIT = 1 − 1/coverage); fixed-charge coverage = (EBIT + lease payments)/(interest + lease payments)

calculator.task: From an income statement and balance sheet (revenue 1,000, EBIT 150, interest 30, tax 30, average assets 1,250, average equity 500): the five DuPont factors, their product, and the three-step check
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.back: ROE = (NI / revenue) × (revenue / average total assets) × (average total assets / average equity)
ROE = (NI/EBT) × (EBT/EBIT) × (EBIT/revenue) × (revenue/average assets) × (average assets/average equity)
Average total assets / average total equity
EBIT / interest payments
(EBIT + lease payments) / (interest payments + lease payments)
Total debt / (total debt + total shareholders' equity)

traps: Inverting the interest burden (it is EBT/EBIT, at most 1)
Assuming higher leverage always raises ROE (only if returns on assets exceed the cost of debt)
Mixing ending and average balances

story_idea.candidate: In 1912 F. Donaldson Brown, an electrical engineer selling explosives for DuPont, wrote an internal efficiency report that got him pulled into the home office; by 1914, as assistant treasurer, he had combined earnings, working capital and plant investment into one measure, return on investment = profit margin × capital turnover. He took the formula to General Motors in 1921, where it became a standard tool for running a divisional company.
story_idea.why: Two companies earn the same return on equity — one a jeweller, one a supermarket. How can you tell what is really driving each one's returns?

days.headline_hint: Margin, turnover, leverage: the DuPont engineer who took return on investment apart

story.title: Donaldson Brown's formula
story.hook: In 1912 F. Donaldson Brown, a young electrical engineer selling explosives for the DuPont company, wrote an internal report on efficiency that caught the eye of John Raskob, Pierre du Pont's closest financial adviser, and was pulled into the home office. By 1914, as assistant treasurer, he had found a way to judge every part of the business with one measure, return on investment, and shown that it splits into two ratios multiplied together: profit as a share of sales (margin) times sales per dollar invested (turnover) — the DuPont formula. In 1921 Brown moved to General Motors, in which DuPont had bought a large stake, as its finance chief, and with Alfred Sloan used the same arithmetic to run GM's divisions.
story.puzzle: A jeweller and a supermarket both earn 18% on their shareholders' money. One keeps 12 cents of every sales dollar as profit, the other 2 cents. How can they land in the same place — and which one's 18% is riskier?
story.payoff: ROE = net profit margin × total asset turnover × financial leverage. Jeweller (illustrative numbers): 12% × 0.75 × 2.0 = 18%, from an ROA of 9% built on margin. Supermarket: 2% × 3.0 × 3.0 = 18%, from an ROA of only 6% built on turnover — plus more borrowing, with assets three times equity. Same ROE, different engines, and the supermarket's leans harder on debt. The five-step version splits the margin into tax burden × interest burden × EBIT margin, so you can see whether a high ROE comes from the operations or from the financing.
sources: Hagley Museum and Library, 'The Father of ROI: Donaldson Brown', https://www.hagley.org/librarynews/father-roi-donaldson-brown (joined DuPont's Explosives Department as a sales representative; 1912 internal efficiency report noticed by John J. Raskob; by 1914, as assistant treasurer, a formula combining earnings, working capital and plant investment into return on investment; known as the DuPont Method/Model) — content seen via WebSearch summary; the page itself could not be fetched from this session
H. Thomas Johnson and Robert S. Kaplan, Relevance Lost: The Rise and Fall of Management Accounting (Harvard Business School Press, 1987) — DuPont's return-on-investment formula and Brown's role

Hagley Museum and Library, finding aid for the Donaldson Brown papers, https://findingaids.hagley.org/repositories/3/resources/873 (DuPont treasurer 1918–1921; General Motors vice president in charge of finance 1921–1937); Alfred D. Chandler Jr., The Visible Hand (Harvard University Press, 1977) and Strategy and Structure (MIT Press, 1962) — Brown at DuPont and his move to General Motors
Alfred P. Sloan Jr., My Years with General Motors (Doubleday, 1964) — Brown's financial controls at GM

Brown's training: B.S. in electrical engineering, Virginia Polytechnic Institute, 1902, then graduate study at Cornell; joined DuPont in 1909 as an explosives salesman (Wikipedia, 'Donaldson Brown'; Virginia Tech Magazine retrospective, https://archive.vtmag.vt.edu/spring05/retrospect.html — seen via search summary)
story.verification: Checker 2026-11-06, four WebSearches in all: the 1912 report, the 1914 return-on-investment formula as assistant treasurer (Hagley; Business History Conference), Brown's electrical-engineering degree and 1909 start as an explosives salesman, and his 1921 move to GM as vice president in charge of finance (Hagley finding aid) confirmed. The jeweller and supermarket are illustrations, not real firms.

worked_example.problem: A jeweller has a net profit margin of 12%, total asset turnover of 0.75 and financial leverage (average assets / average equity) of 2.0. A supermarket has a margin of 2%, turnover of 3.0 and leverage of 3.0. Find each one's ROA and ROE with the three-step DuPont.
worked_example.answer: Both ROEs are 18%; the jeweller's comes from margin (ROA 9%), the supermarket's from turnover and leverage (ROA 6%).

walkthrough.problem: Revenue 1,000; EBIT 150; interest 30; income tax 30; average total assets 1,250; average equity 500. Find the five DuPont factors and ROE, then check with the three-step version.

check_plan: c1 (num, calculator): revenue 2,400; EBIT 288; interest 48; tax 60; average assets 1,600; average equity 800. ROE = 0.75 × 0.8333 × 0.12 × 1.5 × 2 = 0.225 (22.5%).

c2 (mc, why): when does adding debt raise ROE? Right: when the return on the assets it finances exceeds the after-tax cost of the debt — leverage magnifies ROA up or down. Wrong: 'always, because equity is smaller' (it can lower ROE through the interest burden); 'never, interest lowers net income' (ignores the leverage factor).
c3 (num, twist — solve for a factor): ROE 15%, net margin 5%, asset turnover 1.2. Financial leverage = 0.15 / (0.05 × 1.2) = 2.5.

c4 (mc, exam): EBIT 500, interest 100. Interest burden? Right 0.8 (EBT/EBIT). Distractors 1.25 (inverted, EBIT/EBT) and 0.2 (interest/EBIT). Could add: interest coverage 5, and interest burden = 1 − 1/5.

c5 (explain, say it back): how two firms with the same ROE can differ. Must contain: ROE = margin × turnover × leverage; high margin vs high turnover; leverage raises ROE and risk; five-step splits margin into tax, interest and operating parts.
days.verification_note: Fact-check 2026-11-06 (3 new WebSearches, after 1 by the earlier checker). Verified: Brown's B.S. in electrical engineering from Virginia Polytechnic Institute (1902) and his 1909 start at DuPont as an explosives salesman (Wikipedia; Virginia Tech Magazine); the 1912 internal efficiency report and the 1914 return-on-investment formula as assistant treasurer (Hagley 'The Father of ROI'; Business History Conference: 'developed the expanded ROI measure, or DuPont formula, in 1914'); DuPont treasurer 1918–1921 and GM vice president in charge of finance from 1921 (Hagley finding aid; Time) — the earlier open question on 1921 is closed, no hedge needed; DuPont's large GM stake (Brown helped arrange DuPont's 1918 purchase from William Durant); his GM work with Alfred Sloan. Raskob's noticing the 1912 report comes from the Hagley summary; one Russian-language source credits Hamilton Barksdale with the 1912 invitation, so the hook's 'caught the eye of John Raskob' rests on Hagley alone. No corrections to the story text; sources updated. Illustrations recomputed: 12% × 0.75 × 2.0 = 18%, 2% × 3.0 × 3.0 = 18%.

days.title: Sustainable growth and the justified P/E
days.concept: A firm that reinvests a fraction b of earnings at its return on equity can grow dividends at g = b × ROE, and putting that into the Gordon model gives the justified leading P/E = (1 − b)/(r − g), linking a fair multiple to payout, growth and risk.
los: Sustainable growth g = b × ROE, retention b = 1 − payout ratio
Justified leading P/E = P_0/E_1 = (D_1/E_1)/(r − g)
Justified trailing P/E = P_0/E_0 = (D_0/E_0)(1 + g)/(r − g)
Forecasted fundamentals vs comparables
Sensitivity: a P/E rises with growth and falls with r

calculator.task: ROE 15%, retention ratio 0.6, required return 10%: the sustainable growth rate and the justified leading and trailing P/E; then the growth rate the market must be assuming if the stock trades at 60 times forward earnings with the same payout and r
calculator.ba: Chain arithmetic with STO/RCL

memorize.back: g = b × ROE (b = retention ratio)
Payout = D / E = 1 − b

traps: Using the retention ratio b instead of the payout (1 − b) in the numerator
Mixing leading and trailing P/E
Applying the formula when g ≥ r

story_idea.candidate: At the end of 1972 the 'Nifty Fifty' — blue chips such as Polaroid, McDonald's and Avon — traded at far higher price-earnings ratios than the market (Polaroid 94.8, the S&P 500 18.9, by Jeremy Siegel's count) on the belief their growth would never stop. In the 1973-74 bear market many lost well over half their value; Polaroid fell about 90%.
story_idea.why: What P/E can a company's growth actually justify — and how much growth was the market assuming at 95 times earnings?

days.headline_hint: Polaroid at 95 times earnings: the growth a P/E quietly assumes, and what happens when it slips

story.title: The Nifty Fifty
story.hook: By the end of 1972 about fifty big American growth companies — Polaroid, McDonald's, Avon, Xerox, Disney and others — had become the 'Nifty Fifty', 'one-decision' stocks you bought and never sold. Investors paid prices that would take decades of earnings to repay: at the end of 1972 Polaroid traded at almost 95 times its earnings (94.8, by Jeremy Siegel's count), while the S&P 500 as a whole was at about 19 (18.9). In the 1973–74 bear market the group collapsed, and Polaroid's shares lost roughly 90% of their value.
story.puzzle: What growth rate was the market assuming when it paid 95 times earnings — and how much of that price depended on the growth lasting forever?
story.payoff: Justified leading P/E = (1 − b)/(r − g). Turn it round to read the growth inside a price: g = r − payout / (P/E). With a 30% payout and a 10% required return (illustrative numbers, not Polaroid's), and treating 95 as a P/E on next year's earnings, the price needs g = 10% − 0.30/95 = 9.68% a year forever — only about a third of a percentage point below r. Trim the growth belief to 8% and the same formula gives 0.30/0.02 = 15 times earnings: a price 84% lower. When g sits close to r, a small change in belief moves the price enormously — which is what 1973–74 did.
sources: Jeremy J. Siegel, 'The Nifty-Fifty Revisited: Do Growth Stocks Ultimately Justify Their Price?', Journal of Portfolio Management 21(4), Summer 1995 — December 1972 P/E ratios of the Nifty Fifty (Polaroid 94.8) vs the S&P 500 (18.9)

Jeremy J. Siegel, 'Valuing Growth Stocks: Revisiting the Nifty Fifty', AAII Journal, October 1998, https://www.aaii.com/journal/article/valuing-growth-stocks-revisiting-the-nifty-fifty (Nifty Fifty average P/E 41.9 in 1972 vs 18.9 for the S&P 500)
The Motley Fool, 'Sears and Avon circa 1972', 25 July 2000, reproducing Siegel's table: 1972 P/Es of Sears 29.2, Avon 61.2, Polaroid 94.8 vs 18.9 for the S&P 500 in December
Jeremy J. Siegel, Stocks for the Long Run (McGraw-Hill, various editions), chapter on the Nifty Fifty
Polaroid's 1973–74 decline of roughly 90% (one secondary source gives 91% in the two years after the 1972 peak): standard accounts of the bear market
story.verification: Checker 2026-11-06, three WebSearches in all: Polaroid's 94.8 and the S&P 500's 18.9 (Siegel's December 1972 table, reproduced by the Motley Fool), the 'one-decision' label and Polaroid's roughly 90% fall (several secondary sources give 90% or 91%) confirmed; Siegel's paper itself not read.

worked_example.problem: A company earns an ROE of 12% and pays out 40% of its earnings; the required return is 11%. Find the sustainable growth rate and the justified leading and trailing P/E.
worked_example.answer: g = 7.2%; justified leading P/E ≈ 10.53; justified trailing P/E ≈ 11.28.

walkthrough.problem: ROE 15%, retention ratio 0.6, required return 10%. Find the sustainable growth rate and the justified leading and trailing P/E; then the growth rate the market must be assuming if the stock trades at 60 times forward earnings with the same payout and required return.

check_plan: c1 (num, calculator): ROE 18%, payout 50%, required return 12%. g = 0.09; justified leading P/E = 0.5/0.03 = 16.6667 (trailing 18.1667).

c2 (mc, why): holding payout and g fixed, what does a rise in the required return do to the justified P/E, and why? Right: it falls — the denominator r − g widens, so each dollar of future dividends is worth less today. Wrong: 'it rises, investors demand more' (confuses return with price); 'no effect, P/E depends on growth only'.
c3 (num, twist — implied growth): a stock trades at 25 times forward earnings, payout 45%, required return 9%. Implied g = 0.09 − 0.45/25 = 0.072 (7.2%).
c4 (mc, exam): ROE 14%, retention 0.6, required return 10%. Justified TRAILING P/E? Right 27.1. Distractors 25 (leading P/E — forgot × (1 + g)) and 40.65 (retention b used in place of the payout).

c5 (explain, say it back): what growth Polaroid's P/E of about 95 implied. Must contain: g = r − payout/(P/E); the implied g sits just below r and must last forever; a small cut in g collapses the justified P/E.
days.verification_note: Fact-check 2026-11-06 (2 new WebSearches, after 1 by the earlier checker). Verified from secondary sources reproducing Siegel: Polaroid's December 1972 P/E 94.8, Avon 61.2, Sears 29.2, S&P 500 18.9, Nifty Fifty average 41.9 (Motley Fool 25 July 2000; AAII Journal; Morningstar, LGT); 'one-decision' stocks one never needed to sell; Polaroid's 1973–74 fall of about 90% (one source: about $150 to $14) or 91% (others), while the S&P 500 fell about 48%. Kept as 'roughly 90%'. Recomputed: g = 0.10 − 0.30/95 = 9.68%; 0.30/0.02 = 15×, 1 − 15/95 = 84% lower. Not verified: Siegel's 1995 JPM paper itself (figures seen only as reproduced). No corrections.

days.title: Multiples and enterprise value
days.concept: Multiples price a company relative to what it earns or owns, and EV/EBITDA uses enterprise value — equity value plus debt and preferred stock minus cash — so that companies with very different debt levels can be compared on their whole operating business.
los: Price multiples: P/E, P/B, P/S, P/CF (trailing and forward)
Enterprise value = market value of equity + market value of debt + preferred + non-controlling interest − cash and short-term investments
EV/EBITDA and EV/sales
Method of comparables: apply a peer median multiple; justify differences by growth, risk and payout
Residual income RI = NI − r × beginning book value (input concept for the residual income model)

memorize.back: EV = market value of equity + market value of debt + preferred stock + non-controlling interest − cash and short-term investments
Enterprise value / EBITDA (compares firms with different capital structures)
P/B = market price per share / book value per share
Trailing: price / last 12 months' EPS; forward (leading): price / next 12 months' expected EPS
RI_t = NI_t − r × B_(t−1)

story_idea.candidate: On 11 December 2019 Saudi Aramco listed on the Riyadh exchange after raising about $25.6 billion — then the biggest IPO ever — at a valuation of about $1.7 trillion; the next day its market value touched $2 trillion, more than Apple's at the time.
story_idea.why: Was Aramco 'worth' $1.7 trillion? How do you compare one company's price with others' when they carry very different debts and cash piles?

days.headline_hint: Aramco at $1.7 trillion, Apple at $1.2 trillion: comparing price tags when cash and debt differ

story.title: Aramco at $1.7 trillion
story.hook: On 11 December 2019 Saudi Aramco, the Saudi state oil company, began trading on the Saudi stock exchange (Tadawul) in Riyadh after selling 1.5% of its shares at 32 riyals each and raising about $25.6 billion — the largest initial public offering ever. The price valued the whole company at about $1.7 trillion; the shares rose 10%, the daily limit, on the first day, and on 12 December its market value touched $2 trillion. Apple was worth about $1.2 trillion at the time. Aramco had earned $111.1 billion in 2018, about twice Apple's $55.3 billion for its 2019 fiscal year.
story.puzzle: Was Aramco 'worth' $1.7 trillion — cheap or dear next to Apple? And how do you compare price tags when one company sits on a mountain of cash and another does not?
story.payoff: P/E first: Aramco ≈ 1,700 / 111.1 = 15.3 times 2018 earnings; Apple ≈ 1,200 / 55.3 = 21.7. But a market value buys only the shares. At 28 September 2019 Apple held $205.9 billion of cash and marketable securities against $108.0 billion of debt, so EV ≈ 1,200 + 108.0 − 205.9 = $1,102 billion (counting all its marketable securities as cash): its business cost about $98 billion less than its market value. With fiscal-2019 EBITDA of 63.9 + 12.5 = $76.5 billion (operating income plus depreciation and amortization), Apple's EV/EBITDA was about 14.4. EV/EBITDA puts companies with very different debt and cash on the same footing; a P/E does not.

days.module: Capital Investments and Capital Allocation
days.title: Capital budgeting: NPV, IRR and ROIC
days.concept: A company should accept a project when its NPV at the cost of capital is positive; the IRR agrees for a single conventional project but can mislead when ranking mutually exclusive projects of different size or timing, and sunk costs never enter the decision.
los: NPV rule: accept if NPV > 0
IRR rule: accept if IRR > cost of capital; multiple or no IRR with non-conventional cash flows
NPV vs IRR conflicts for mutually exclusive projects (scale and timing); crossover rate
Incremental cash flows: ignore sunk costs; include opportunity costs, externalities and cannibalization
ROIC = after-tax operating profit/average invested capital vs cost of capital
Real options (timing, abandonment, expansion, flexibility): describe

calculator.task: Two mutually exclusive projects — A: −1,000 then 600, 500, 300; B: −1,000 then 100, 400, 1,000: NPV at 8% and IRR of each (IRR prefers A, NPV prefers B), and the crossover rate (about 8.7%) as the IRR of the differences
calculator.ba: CF worksheet: NPV (I = 8) and IRR CPT for each project and for the difference
calculator.ti: npv( and irr( for each project and for the difference

memorize.back: Accept if NPV > 0; for mutually exclusive projects choose the highest NPV
Accept if IRR > required rate of return (cost of capital); for independent, conventional projects it agrees with NPV
The discount rate at which two projects' NPVs are equal (the IRR of the differences in their cash flows)
Ignore sunk costs; include opportunity costs, externalities and cannibalization
ROIC = after-tax operating profit / average book value of invested capital (value is created when ROIC > cost of capital)

traps: Including sunk costs in the analysis
Choosing between mutually exclusive projects by IRR instead of NPV
Ignoring opportunity costs (e.g. land already owned)

story_idea.candidate: Britain and France signed the treaty to build Concorde in 1962. As costs soared far beyond the original estimates, both governments kept funding it partly because so much had already been spent; it flew commercially from 1976 to 2003. The biologists Richard Dawkins and Tamsin Carlisle later coined the term 'Concorde fallacy' for throwing good money after bad.
story_idea.why: Billions had already been spent. Should that money count when deciding whether to keep going — and what rule makes the right call?

days.headline_hint: £1,070 million that would never come back: the rule that decides what happens next

story.title: Concorde and the money that was already gone
story.hook: On 29 November 1962 Britain and France signed a treaty to build a supersonic airliner together, with development then estimated at £150–170 million; the treaty had no break clause, so when Britain's new government tried to pull out in 1964 it had to back down. On 18 March 1974 the Industry Secretary, Tony Benn, told the House of Commons that the latest estimate of the total joint development cost was £1,070 million at January 1974 prices, that about £130 million of Britain's share was still to be spent, and that "none of these development costs will be recovered." That July the two governments agreed to finish the 16 production aircraft already authorized and to commit to nothing more. Concorde carried paying passengers from 21 January 1976 to 24 October 2003; 20 were built and only 14 ever entered airline service.
story.puzzle: By 1974 the development bill had passed a billion pounds and none of it would come back. Should the money already spent count when deciding whether to finish the job — and when two ways forward both look profitable, which rule picks the better one?
story.payoff: Whatever Britain chose in March 1974, the money already spent on development was gone in every case, so it could not change which choice was better: it is a sunk cost. An NPV counts only the cash that still differs between the options — the money still to be spent (Britain's remaining development share alone was about £130 million) against what finishing would bring in. Two years later the biologists Richard Dawkins and Tamsin Carlisle named the opposite instinct in Nature: the "Concorde fallacy", investing more because of what has already been invested. The same discipline settles today's ranking puzzle: at an 8% cost of capital project B adds 229.36 against A's 222.37, even though A's IRR (21.48%) beats B's (17.09%). Below the 8.74% crossover rate the two rules disagree, and the NPV is the one that measures the value added.

worked_example.problem: A company is deciding whether to launch a product. Last year it spent 50 (thousand) on a market study. The launch needs equipment costing 400 today and uses a plot of land the company owns that it could otherwise sell today for 100 after tax. The project's after-tax cash flows are 180, 200 and 220 at the end of years 1-3, and the cost of capital is 9%. Find the NPV and decide.
steps: Sunk cost: the 50 study has been spent whether or not the product launches, so it is left out
Opportunity cost: using the land gives up a sale worth 100 today, so it is part of the outlay: CF_0 = −400 − 100 = −500
The two traps: counting the study gives 3.3540 − 50 = −46.6460 (a wrong rejection); leaving out the land gives 103.3540 (value overstated by 100)

Find each project's NPV and IRR, then the crossover rate — the IRR of the differences B − A (0, −500, −100, 700) — and decide.

keys.ti: nothing to store: the cash flows go straight into npv( and irr(

keys.what: NPV of A at 8%
IRR of A
Project B: overwrite C01-C03, then NPV and IRR again
keys.ba: CF ↓ C01 = 100 ENTER ↓ ↓ C02 = 400 ENTER ↓ ↓ C03 = 1000 ENTER; NPV 8 ENTER ↓ CPT; IRR CPT

keys.what: Crossover rate = IRR of B − A (0, −500, −100, 700)
keys.ba: CF 2ND CLR WORK; CFo = 0 ENTER ↓; C01 = 500 +|− ENTER ↓ ↓; C02 = 100 +|− ENTER ↓ ↓; C03 = 700 ENTER; IRR CPT

keys.what: Decide
keys.ba: 8% < 8.7434%: below the crossover B has the higher NPV — choose B (IRR would wrongly pick A)
keys.ti: same; at the crossover both NPVs equal 207.8845

check_plan: c1 (num, calculator): projects C: −2,000, 1,400, 700, 400 and D: −2,000, 200, 800, 1,800 at a 9% cost of capital. The crossover rate = IRR of D − C (0, −1,200, 100, 1,400) = 12.2593%; percent to two decimals, tol 0.01; hint: only the cash flows change. Solution with both keystroke lines, and the decision: NPV_C = 182.45, NPV_D = 246.76, IRR_C = 15.37%, IRR_D = 14.13% → at 9% choose D

c2 (mc, why): projects A and B from the walkthrough at a 6% cost of capital: NPV_A = 262.92, NPV_B = 289.96, IRR_A = 21.48%, IRR_B = 17.09%. Which do you choose and why? Right: B — NPV measures the value added at the firm's actual cost of capital, and 6% is below the 8.74% crossover. Wrong: "A, because a higher IRR means more value" (an IRR is a rate, not an amount, and implicitly assumes reinvestment at the IRR); "either — both IRRs beat 6%" (that settles independent projects, not a choice between two)

c3 (num, twist — ROIC): EBIT 240, tax rate 25%, invested capital 1,400 at the start of the year and 1,600 at the end: ROIC = 180/1,500 = 12.00%; percent to two decimals, tol 0.01. Solution adds that against a 9% cost of capital the 3.00% spread means the firm is creating value (traps: pre-tax EBIT gives 16.00%; ending capital gives 11.25%)

c4 (mc, exam): a firm spent $40,000 last year on a feasibility study. The project needs $300,000 of equipment and land the firm owns that could be sold today for $60,000 after tax; after-tax cash flows are $120,000 a year for 4 years; cost of capital 10%. NPV closest to: A $20,384 (right: −360,000 + 380,383.85); B −$19,616 (included the sunk study — and wrongly rejects); C $80,384 (left out the land's opportunity cost)

c5 (explain, say it back): in two sentences, why does the money already spent on Concorde not belong in the decision to finish it, and which rule picks between two mutually exclusive projects? Points: (1) a sunk cost is the same whatever you choose, so it cannot change which option is better; (2) only incremental future cash flows count — including opportunity costs, externalities and cannibalization; (3) for mutually exclusive projects choose the higher NPV at the cost of capital, not the higher IRR

days.module: Capital Structure
days.title: The weighted average cost of capital
days.concept: The weighted average cost of capital blends the after-tax cost of debt, the cost of preferred stock and the cost of equity by target market-value weights, WACC = w_d r_d(1 − t) + w_p r_p + w_e r_e, and it is the hurdle rate for average-risk projects.
los: WACC = w_d r_d(1 − t) + w_p r_p + w_e r_e
Cost of debt = YTM on existing debt (after tax: × (1 − t)); cost of preferred r_p = D_p/P_p
Cost of equity by CAPM (r_e = R_f + β[E(R_m) − R_f]) or dividend discount (r_e = D_1/P_0 + g)
Target capital structure; market-value weights
Modigliani–Miller: without taxes capital structure is irrelevant; with taxes debt adds value through the interest tax shield (explain); factors affecting capital structure

calculator.task: A bond priced at 95 with a 6% annual coupon and 10 years left gives the pre-tax cost of debt (CPT I/Y); with t = 25%, β = 1.1, R_f = 4%, ERP = 5% and weights 30% debt / 70% equity, find the WACC
calculator.ba: TVM CPT I/Y; chain arithmetic with STO/RCL
calculator.ti: TVM Solver, solve I%; home screen

memorize.back: WACC = w_d × r_d × (1 − t) + w_p × r_p + w_e × r_e (target, market-value weights)
r_d × (1 − t), with r_d = YTM of the firm's debt (not the coupon rate)
r_p = D_p / P_p
r_e = R_f + β × [E(R_m) − R_f]

memorize.front: Cost of equity via dividend discount

memorize.back: V_L = V_U + t × D (value rises with debt via the tax shield)

traps: Using the coupon rate instead of the YTM as the cost of debt
Using book-value weights when market or target weights are available
Applying the tax shield to the cost of equity or preferred stock

story_idea.candidate: On 30 November 1988 the buyout firm Kohlberg Kravis Roberts won control of RJR Nabisco, the tobacco and food group, for about $25 billion — roughly $109 a share, against a share price in the mid-$50s before the bidding began that October — paid for overwhelmingly with borrowed money; it remained the largest leveraged buyout for nearly 18 years, until HCA in 2006.
story_idea.why: How could buyers pay almost twice the market price and still expect to profit — and how much does swapping equity for tax-deductible debt change a company's overall cost of capital?

days.headline_hint: KKR paid $109 for a share that had traded near $55: what borrowing does to a company's cost of capital

story.title: Barbarians at the gate, and the price of money
story.hook: On 20 October 1988 F. Ross Johnson, chief executive of the tobacco-and-biscuits group RJR Nabisco, proposed buying the company from its shareholders for $75 a share — a leveraged buyout of about $17 billion backed by Shearson Lehman Hutton — when the shares had been trading in the mid-$50s. The buyout firm Kohlberg Kravis Roberts bid against him, and after six weeks of bidding the board accepted KKR's $109 a share, about $25 billion, over management's $112, judging KKR's offer the more certain. Most of the price was paid with borrowed money. It stood as the largest leveraged buyout for nearly 18 years, until the 2006 buyout of the hospital chain HCA, and the fight became the book "Barbarians at the Gate".
story.puzzle: How could anyone pay about twice the market price and expect to come out ahead — and what happens to a company's overall cost of capital when most of its equity is swapped for debt?
story.payoff: Interest is paid before tax and dividends after it, so each dollar of debt costs the firm only r_d(1 − t): that is why the WACC formula multiplies only the debt term by (1 − t). Modigliani and Miller's version with taxes, V_L = V_U + tD, puts a price on the shield: at the 34% federal corporate rate of 1988, every $1 billion of permanent debt adds about $340 million of value, so an illustrative $20 billion of debt would be worth about $6.8 billion — roughly half the $12.4 billion premium implied by paying $109 rather than about $55 for some 229 million shares. The rest had to come from running the business better. The catch the formula hides: more debt also raises the cost of equity and the risk of financial distress, which is why the WACC does not keep falling as debt rises.

worked_example.problem: A company's target weights are 40% debt, 10% preferred stock and 50% common equity. Its bonds yield 7% to maturity and its tax rate is 30%. The preferred stock pays a $5 dividend and sells for $62.50. The common stock sells for $42, next year's dividend is expected to be $2.10, and dividends grow 5% a year. Find the WACC.
steps: Cost of equity (dividend discount): r_e = D_1/P_0 + g = 2.10/42 + 5% = 5.00% + 5.00% = 10.00%
Check: without the tax shield the debt term would be 2.80% and the WACC 8.60%

walkthrough.problem: A company's 10-year bonds pay a 6% annual coupon and trade at 95 (per 100 of par). The tax rate is 25%, its beta is 1.1, the risk-free rate is 4% and the equity risk premium is 5%. Target weights are 30% debt and 70% equity. Find the pre-tax cost of debt (the YTM), the after-tax cost of debt, the cost of equity and the WACC.

keys.ba: 2ND CLR TVM; 10 N; 95 +|− PV; 6 PMT; 100 FV; CPT I/Y
keys.ti: APPS 1:Finance 1:TVM Solver: N=10, I%=0, PV=(−)95, PMT=6, FV=100, P/Y=1, C/Y=1, END; cursor on I%, ALPHA ENTER

keys.what: After-tax cost of debt r_d(1 − t)
Cost of equity by CAPM: R_f + β × ERP
WACC = w_d × r_d(1 − t) + w_e × r_e
Trap check: the coupon instead of the YTM

check_plan: c1 (num, calculator): 8-year bonds with a 5% annual coupon trade at 102.50; t = 21%; β = 0.9, R_f = 3.5%, ERP = 5.5%; weights 40% debt / 60% equity: YTM 4.6191%, after tax 3.6491%, r_e = 8.45%, WACC = 6.5296%; percent to two decimals, tol 0.01; hint: price, coupon, years, tax rate, beta and weights change. Solution with both keystroke lines (trap: the coupon gives 6.65%)

c2 (mc, why): why is only the cost of debt multiplied by (1 − t)? Right: interest is deducted before tax is calculated, so the tax saved on each interest dollar lowers the firm's true cost; preferred and common dividends are paid out of after-tax profit. Wrong: "because debt is less risky than equity" (risk explains why r_d < r_e, not the tax factor); "because shareholders already pay personal tax on dividends" (personal taxes play no part in the WACC)

c3 (num, twist — cost of equity by dividend discount, then a three-part WACC): D_0 = 1.80, g = 4%, P_0 = 36 → D_1 = 1.872, r_e = 1.872/36 + 4% = 9.20%; preferred D_p = 4.50, P_p = 60 → r_p = 7.50%; r_d = 6%, t = 25%; weights 30% / 10% / 60%: WACC = 1.35% + 0.75% + 5.52% = 7.62%; percent to two decimals, tol 0.01 (trap: D_0 instead of D_1 gives 7.50%)

c4 (mc, exam): the firm's bonds carry a 5% coupon but trade to yield 6.2%; t = 25%; r_e = 11%; target weights 35% debt / 65% equity. WACC closest to: A 8.46% (used the coupon rate as the cost of debt); B 9.32% (forgot the tax shield); C 8.78% (right)

c5 (explain, say it back): in two sentences, what do Modigliani and Miller say about debt, without and with taxes? Points: (1) without taxes (perfect markets) capital structure does not change firm value or the WACC — cheaper debt is offset by a rising cost of equity; (2) with taxes the interest tax shield adds t × D, so V_L = V_U + tD; (3) in practice financial-distress costs limit how much debt is worth adding

days.module: Exchange Rate Calculations
days.title: Forward exchange rates and interest parity
days.concept: A forward exchange rate is the spot rate adjusted for the two currencies' interest rates, F_(A/B) = S_(A/B) × [1 + i_A(days/360)]/[1 + i_B(days/360)] with A the price currency and B the base currency, so the higher-interest currency trades at a forward discount and a hedged carry trade earns nothing extra.
los: Covered interest rate parity: F = S × (1 + i_price × days/360)/(1 + i_base × days/360)
Forward points: F = S + points/10,000 (points/100 for JPY-type quotes)
Forward premium/discount: F − S, and as an annualized % of spot
Higher-interest currency trades at a forward discount
Uncovered interest parity and the carry trade (concept); FX forwards in Derivatives use the same no-arbitrage logic
