story_idea.candidate: On 5 August 2024 Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 12.4% in a day, its biggest point drop ever, after the Bank of Japan had raised rates on 31 July and the yen surged — forcing traders to unwind 'carry trades' that borrowed yen near 0% to buy dollar assets yielding about 5%.
story_idea.why: If you can borrow yen at almost nothing and earn 5% in dollars, why isn't that free money — and what does the forward exchange rate say about it?

days.headline_hint: Borrow yen at 0.1%, earn 5.3% in dollars: why the forward rate takes the free lunch away

story.title: Black Monday in Tokyo
story.hook: On 31 July 2024 the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to about 0.25%, in a country where borrowing had cost almost nothing for years, while US dollar rates stood above 5%. Traders had been running "carry trades" — borrowing yen cheaply, selling them, and holding higher-yielding assets elsewhere — and the yen, which had touched a 38-year low of 161.96 per dollar on 3 July, was climbing. On Monday 5 August the Nikkei 225 fell 4,451.28 points, or 12.4%, to 31,458.42: its largest point fall ever, bigger even than the 3,836.48 points of October 1987. That day the yen strengthened as far as 141.675 per dollar as the trades were unwound.
story.puzzle: If you can borrow yen at almost nothing and earn more than 5% in dollars, why isn't that free money — and what does a bank's forward exchange rate say about it?
story.payoff: Covered interest parity. With JPY/USD at 157.00, a 90-day yen rate of 0.10% and a dollar rate of 5.30%, the 90-day forward rate is 157.00 × 1.00025/1.01325 = 154.9857 yen per dollar. Borrow ¥157 and you owe ¥157.0393 in 90 days; change it into $1, earn 90 days' interest at 5.30% to reach $1.01325, and sell those dollars forward at 154.9857: you get back exactly ¥157.0393. Hedged, the trade earns nothing — the dollar's forward discount (an annualized −5.13%) cancels the interest gap. The carry trader's profit came from leaving the currency unhedged, a bet that the yen would not rise; from 161.96 to 141.675 the dollar lost 12.52% against the yen, about 2.4 years' worth of a 5.2-point interest gap.

c2 (mc, why): why must the higher-interest currency trade at a forward discount? Right: otherwise you could borrow the low-rate currency, invest in the high-rate one and lock in the conversion back with a forward for a riskless profit; arbitrage moves F until hedged returns are equal. Wrong: "because high rates signal the currency will fall" (that is uncovered parity, an expectation, not a no-arbitrage result); "because the forward rate is the market's forecast of the future spot rate" (the forward is pinned by interest rates, not forecasts)

days.title: Liquidity ratios and the cost of trade credit
days.concept: Liquidity ratios — current, quick, cash and the defensive interval — measure whether near-term obligations can be met, and skipping a supplier's early-payment discount is borrowing at cost = [1 + d/(1 − d)]^(365/days beyond the discount period) − 1, to be compared with other short-term funding.
los: Current ratio = current assets/current liabilities; quick ratio = (cash + short-term marketable investments + receivables)/current liabilities; cash ratio = (cash + short-term marketable investments)/current liabilities
Defensive interval = (cash + short-term marketable investments + receivables)/daily cash expenditures
Cost of trade credit = [1 + d/(1 − d)]^(365/(days past discount)) − 1; take the discount if this exceeds the cost of short-term borrowing

Primary and secondary sources of liquidity; drags and pulls on liquidity (describe)

story_idea.candidate: Greensill Capital, the supply-chain finance firm founded by the Australian banker Lex Greensill, collapsed into insolvency in London in March 2021 after its credit insurance was not renewed, leaving Credit Suisse funds with about $10 billion of its notes frozen and companies such as steel-maker GFG Alliance scrambling for funding.
story_idea.why: Supply-chain finance lets suppliers get paid early for a small discount. What annual interest rate is hidden inside 'a 2% discount for paying 20 days sooner'?

days.headline_hint: Greensill's collapse and the 44.6% interest rate hiding inside "2/10, net 30"

story.title: The firm that paid suppliers early
story.hook: Greensill Capital, the London-based firm built by the Australian banker Lex Greensill, lived on supply-chain finance: paying a company's suppliers early, minus a small discount, collecting the full invoice from the company later, and selling those claims as notes to investors. About $10 billion of Credit Suisse supply-chain finance funds were invested mostly in Greensill-backed notes, and credit insurance — including, according to court filings, $4.6 billion of cover on Greensill's notes from a Tokio Marine unit — made them look safe. That cover was due to expire on 1 March 2021 and was not renewed. On 1 March Credit Suisse froze the funds, and on 8 March Greensill filed for insolvency in London and Australia.
story.puzzle: Getting paid a few weeks early for a 2% haircut sounds like a small courtesy. What annual interest rate is really hidden inside "2% off for paying 20 days sooner"?
story.payoff: Turn the terms into a loan. Under 2/10, net 30, a buyer that skips the discount keeps $98 for 20 more days and then pays $100: $2 of interest on $98, or 2.0408% per 20 days. A year holds 365/20 = 18.25 such periods, so the effective cost is 1.020408^18.25 − 1 = 44.59% — far more than the 36.50% you get by simply scaling 2% up. That is why a buyer with a 9% bank line should borrow to take the discount, and why a supplier that gives up 2% to be paid 20 days early is paying a high price for cash. Liquidity is not free, and the ratios that measure it — the quick ratio and the defensive interval — show how close a firm is to needing it.
sources: CNBC, 16 March 2021, "Credit Suisse flags possible charge from Greensill fallout" (supply-chain funds frozen on 1 March 2021) — cnbc.com/2021/03/16/credit-suisse-flags-possible-charge-from-greensill-fallout.html

days.title: Profit maximization, shutdown and concentration
days.concept: Every firm maximizes profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, breaks even where price equals average total cost, shuts down in the short run when price falls below average variable cost, and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (the sum of squared market shares) gauges how concentrated its market is.

story_idea.candidate: On 25 April 2019 the UK Competition and Markets Authority blocked the £7.3 billion merger of Sainsbury's and Asda, Britain's second- and third-largest supermarket chains, concluding that the combined group would hold close to 30% of the grocery market and that prices would rise.
story_idea.why: Two supermarkets merging leaves plenty of rivals. How do regulators put a single number on how concentrated a market is — and on how much one merger changes it?

days.headline_hint: Britain's No. 2 and No. 3 grocers tried to merge: the one number regulators use to size up a market

story.title: Sainsbury's, Asda and the 31% supermarket
story.hook: Sainsbury's planned £7.3 billion takeover of Walmart-owned Asda would have joined Britain's second- and third-largest supermarket chains: in Kantar's figures for the 12 weeks to 24 March 2019, Asda held 15.4% of the grocery market and Sainsbury's 15.3%, against Tesco's 27.4%. On 25 April 2019 the Competition and Markets Authority blocked the deal, finding that it would raise prices in stores, online and at petrol stations, with motorists paying more in over 125 places where the two chains' forecourts sat close together. The combined group would have held about 31% of the market, more than Tesco. Sainsbury's chief executive Mike Coupe said the regulator had ignored how competitive the market was.
story.puzzle: Even after the merger Britain would still have had Tesco, Morrisons, Aldi, Lidl and plenty more. How do regulators turn "how concentrated is this market?" into a single number — and how much did this one merger move it?
story.payoff: Square each firm's share and add: the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index. With Kantar's spring-2019 shares rounded to whole numbers — Tesco 27, Asda 15, Sainsbury's 15, Morrisons 10, Aldi 8, Co-op 6, Lidl 6, Waitrose 5 — the HHI is 1,440 on the percent scale regulators quote (0.1440 with shares as decimals, the form this course uses). Merge the two 15s into a 30 and it jumps to 1,890: up 2 × 15 × 15 = 450, because squaring rewards size (30² = 900, twice 15² + 15²). The four-firm ratio moves only from 67 to 75, and only because Aldi steps into the top four. The US agencies' 2023 merger guidelines give a sense of scale: above 1,800 a market counts as highly concentrated, and a merger that takes it there with a rise of more than 100 points is presumed to harm competition — exactly what this deal would have done (with Kantar's actual 15.4% and 15.3%, a rise of 471).

worked_example.problem: A firm in a perfectly competitive market sells at the market price of $18. At its profit-maximizing output — where marginal revenue (= price) equals marginal cost — it makes 2,000 units; at that output its average total cost is $20 and its average variable cost is $15. Should it keep producing in the short run? What happens in the long run?
steps: Total revenue = 18 × 2,000 = 36,000; total cost = 20 × 2,000 = 40,000; producing gives a profit of −4,000
Fixed cost = (ATC − AVC) × Q = (20 − 15) × 2,000 = 10,000, paid even at zero output, so shutting down loses 10,000
Producing covers all variable costs (15 × 2,000 = 30,000) and 6,000 of the fixed costs: the loss shrinks from 10,000 to 4,000
Rule: P = 18 ≥ AVC = 15, so operate in the short run; P = 18 < ATC = 20, so exit in the long run unless prices or costs change
It would break even only at P = ATC (zero economic profit)
worked_example.answer: Operate in the short run (loss 4,000 instead of 10,000); exit in the long run if P stays below ATC

days.title: Hedge-fund fees: from gross to net
days.concept: Hedge-fund investors earn the gross return minus a management fee and an incentive fee on profits above any hurdle and high-water mark, so a '2 and 20' fund must earn a large gross return just to match an index fund, and a fund of funds adds a second layer of fees.
los: Management fee on assets (beginning or ending NAV, or committed capital)
Incentive fee: on gross gains or net of the management fee; hard hurdle (fee on gains above the hurdle) vs soft hurdle (fee on all gains once the hurdle is cleared)
High-water mark: no incentive fee until previous peak NAV is regained
Fund-of-funds double fees
Gross vs net return; NAV per share = (assets − liabilities)/shares outstanding
Leveraged return R_L = R + (V_B/V_E)(R − r_D) (2027 coverage uncertain — insurance)

story_idea.candidate: In 2007 Warren Buffett bet Ted Seides of Protégé Partners $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a hand-picked group of five funds of hedge funds over the ten years 2008-2017. The index fund returned about 7.1% a year; the funds of funds averaged about 2.2%. Girls Inc. of Omaha received the winnings.
story_idea.why: Hedge-fund managers are often skilled. How can fees alone turn decent gross returns into poor net returns, and how big a gross return does '2 and 20' (plus another layer) require?

days.headline_hint: Buffett's $1 million bet: how "2 and 20" plus a second layer of fees eats a hedge fund's gains

story.title: The ten-year bet
story.hook: Warren Buffett had long argued that professional money managers, after their fees, would trail a plain index fund, and he offered to bet on it. Ted Seides of Protégé Partners took him on: over the ten years from 1 January 2008 to 31 December 2017, a low-cost S&P 500 index fund against five funds of hedge funds picked by Seides — funds that invest in other hedge funds and charge their own fees on top of theirs. The prize for the winner's charity, meant to be $1 million, ended up at about $2.2 million. Nine years in, Buffett reported the index fund compounding at about 7.1% a year against about 2.2% for the funds of funds; Seides conceded in 2017, and Girls Inc. of Omaha collected.
story.puzzle: Hedge-fund managers are often very skilled. How can fees alone turn decent gross returns into poor net ones — and what gross return does "2 and 20", with another layer on top, need just to keep up with an index fund?
story.payoff: Run the fees. Take illustrative terms: 2% of assets and 20% of profits at the hedge fund, then 1% and 10% at the fund of funds, each management fee on year-end assets and each incentive fee net of it. A 10% gross year becomes 6.24% after the first layer and 4.66% after the second, so 53% of the gain goes in fees. To hand the investor the index fund's 7.1%, the underlying hedge funds would have to earn about 13.49% gross, year after year. That is the arithmetic Buffett was betting on: two layers of fees set a bar that most skill cannot clear.

worked_example.problem: A fund starts the year with $200 million and ends with $230 million before fees. It charges a 1.5% management fee on beginning assets and a 15% incentive fee on gains before the management fee, with a 6% hurdle. Find the investor's net return if the hurdle is soft, and if it is hard.
steps: Gross gain = 230 − 200 = 30, a 15% return, which clears the 6% hurdle (12)
Soft hurdle: once cleared, the fee is on the whole gain: 15% × 30 = 4.50; net = 230 − 3.00 − 4.50 = 222.50, a net return of 11.25%
Hard hurdle: the fee is only on the gain above the hurdle: 15% × (30 − 12) = 2.70; net = 230 − 3.00 − 2.70 = 224.30, a net return of 12.15%
The hard hurdle saves the investor 1.80 million (0.90 percentage points)
worked_example.answer: Soft hurdle: 11.25% net; hard hurdle: 12.15% net

days.title: Private equity waterfalls, IRR and MOIC
days.concept: In private equity the distribution waterfall decides when the general partner earns carried interest — after investors have their capital and preferred return back, either across the whole fund (European) or deal by deal (American), with catch-up and clawback provisions — and performance is reported as IRR and the multiple of invested capital.

Preferred return (hurdle), full catch-up, carried interest
Clawback of excess carry paid early
MOIC = (realized value + unrealized value)/invested capital
IRR of the fund's cash flows (CF worksheet); IRR vs MOIC (time ignored)

LPs receive all contributed capital plus the preferred return before the GP earns carry

After the LPs' preferred return, the GP receives 100% of distributions until it holds its full carry share (e.g. 20%) of all profit; a partial catch-up gives it only part of each distribution

story_idea.candidate: When Blackstone filed to go public in 2007, an updated filing in June revealed that co-founder Stephen Schwarzman had received about $398 million for 2006, his share of the firm's profits and investment gains (the split between fees and carried interest was not checked).
story_idea.why: A private-equity manager's fee is supposedly '2 and 20'. How does a fund's profit actually flow between investors and managers, so that one manager can earn hundreds of millions in a year?

days.headline_hint: $398 million in one year: how private-equity profits flow down the waterfall

story.title: What the Blackstone prospectus revealed
story.hook: In March 2007 the private-equity firm Blackstone filed with the SEC to sell shares to the public. That first filing left out what its founders were paid; an updated filing on 11 June gave outsiders their first look. It showed that co-founder and chief executive Stephen Schwarzman had received about $398 million for 2006 — his share of the firm's profits and investment gains, which flow from the management fees its funds pay and the "carried interest", the managers' cut of the funds' gains. Ten days later Blackstone's units were priced at $31, raising about $4.1 billion.
story.puzzle: A buyout fund's headline terms are "2 and 20": a 2% fee and 20% of the profits. How do a fund's proceeds actually flow between the investors and the managers — and when does the 20% start?
story.payoff: Down a waterfall. In a whole-of-fund (European) waterfall the investors first get all their capital back plus a preferred return, often 8% a year; then the general partner "catches up" until it holds 20% of all the profit, and after that every dollar splits 80/20. In today's walkthrough fund, $150 contributed comes back as $250: the investors take the $40, the $90 and the first $55.18 of the final $120 (capital plus an 8% preferred return), the GP catches up with $8.79, the last $56.03 splits 80/20, and the GP ends with exactly $20.00 — 20% of the $100 profit. At 20%, every $1 billion of fund profit sends $200 million to the managers, which is how one partner's share can run into the hundreds of millions.

check_plan: c1 (num, calculator): a fund's cash flows are −80, −40, 0, +70, +110 (years 0-4): IRR = 13.1732%; percent to two decimals, tol 0.01; hint: only the cash flows change; the year-2 zero must be entered (C02 = 0), not skipped. MOIC = 180/120 = 1.50 noted. Solution with both keystroke lines (TI: irr(−80,{−40,0,70,110}))

c2 (mc, why): why is a deal-by-deal (American) waterfall better for the GP than a whole-of-fund (European) one? Right: carry is paid on each profitable deal as it exits, before the LPs have their whole fund's capital and preferred return back, so the GP is paid earlier — and may be paid on gains later wiped out by losing deals (hence clawbacks). Wrong: "because the carry percentage is higher" (it is the same 20%); "because the preferred return is lower" (the hurdle can be identical — timing is the difference)

c3 (num, twist — clawback): American waterfall, no hurdle, 20% carry. Deal 1: invested 50, exits at 80 (carry paid 6.00); deal 2: invested 50, exits at 30. Whole-fund profit = 10, so the GP is entitled to 2.00 and must give back 4.00; two decimals, tol 0.01

c4 (mc, exam): a fund invests 100 and returns 130 a year later; European waterfall with an 8% preferred return, 20% carry and full catch-up. The GP's carry is closest to: A 4.40 (ignored the catch-up: 20% of the 22 above the hurdle); B 5.68 (sized the catch-up as 20% of the preferred return, 1.60, instead of 8 × 20/80 = 2.00); C 6.00 (right: with a full catch-up the GP ends with 20% of the 30 profit)

c5 (explain, say it back): in two sentences, why can two funds with the same MOIC have very different IRRs? Points: (1) MOIC is total value over invested capital and ignores when the cash comes back; (2) the IRR discounts by time, so faster returns mean a higher IRR; (3) e.g. 1.6× in 3 years is 16.96% a year, 1.6× in 6 years only 8.15%
